faq.q: What does 福如东海 mean?

faq.a: 福如东海 is pronounced as "fú rú dōng hǎi" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 福如东海?

faq.q: When is 福如东海 used?

fu-ru-dong-hai.meaning: May your good fortune be boundless
fu-ru-dong-hai.meaning_metaphoric: May your good fortune be boundless
fu-ru-dong-hai.origin: 福 is 'blessing' or 'good fortune', 如 is 'like', and 东海 is the Eastern Sea, the ocean off China's east coast. The wish is for good fortune as boundless as the sea. It is an old formula of congratulation: the Hanyu dictionary cites a Dunhuang lecture text of 933 (《长兴四年中兴殿应圣节讲经文》), and later dramas such as 《荆钗记》 (Yuan–Ming era) show it already joined to its partner: 'may your fortune be like the Eastern Sea, your years like the Southern Mountains' (福如东海，寿比南山). The two halves are almost always said together, as a birthday wish for an elder, especially at a sixtieth, seventieth or eightieth. At Chinese New Year it is used the same way, for grandparents and older relatives. It sounds odd said to someone young.
fu-ru-dong-hai.title: 福如东海 (fú rú dōng hǎi) Meaning — Birthday Blessing for Elders, Explained

faq.q: When is 覆水难收 used?

fu-shui-nan-shou.origin: This descends from the story of Jiang Ziya, whose wife left him during his years of poverty and sought to return once he had risen. He poured a basin of water on the ground and invited her to gather it up. Water once overturned (覆水) cannot be recovered (难收). The story is unsentimental about the asymmetry: he is under no obligation, and the water is not coming back. An act whose consequences are not going to be taken back.
fu-shui-nan-shou.title: 覆水难收 (fu shui nan shou) — "Actions cannot be undone" | Meaning & Origin

fu-tang-dao-huo.example_en: He would go through fire and water for his family.
fu-tang-dao-huo.example_zh: 为了家人，他愿意赴汤蹈火。

fu-tang-dao-huo.literal: Go into boiling water step on fire
fu-tang-dao-huo.meaning: Go through fire and water; brave any danger
fu-tang-dao-huo.meaning_metaphoric: Go through fire and water; brave any danger
fu-tang-dao-huo.origin: To go into (赴) scalding water (汤) and tread (蹈) on fire (火). 汤 is boiling liquid rather than soup, as it is throughout classical Chinese, and the two elements are the standard pair of unsurvivable things. What is asserted is not bravery in the face of risk but willingness where the outcome is not in doubt. Declarations of loyalty and thanks carry it — 为你赴汤蹈火, I would go through fire for you — and it is hyperbole that both parties understand as hyperbole.
fu-tang-dao-huo.title: 赴汤蹈火 (fu tang dao huo) — "Go through fire and water; brave any danger" | Meaning & Origin

fu-wu-shuang-zhi.example_en: He realized that good luck is often fleeting and rare.
fu-wu-shuang-zhi.example_zh: 他意识到好运往往是短暂而稀有的。

faq.a: 福无双至 (fú wú shuāng zhì) literally means "Blessings do not come in pairs" and metaphorically means "Good luck does not repeat". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 福无双至 mean?

faq.q: How do you pronounce 福无双至?

faq.a: 福无双至 is used when He realized that good luck is often fleeting and rare..
faq.q: When is 福无双至 used?

fu-wu-shuang-zhi.literal: Blessings do not come in pairs
fu-wu-shuang-zhi.origin: Liu Xiang's Garden of Persuasions has the older form — 福不重至，祸必重来, blessings do not come twice, misfortunes certainly come again — which settled into the pairing used today: 福无双至，祸不单行. The Water Margin puts it in characters' mouths at exactly the moment their luck turns. The asymmetry is the whole point: good fortune (福) does not arrive doubled (无双至), while trouble comes in company. It is said with resignation rather than bitterness, most often by someone who has just had one good thing happen and is declining to expect a second.
fu-wu-shuang-zhi.title: 福无双至 (fu wu shuang zhi) — "Good luck does not repeat" | Meaning & Origin

faq.q: When is 福星高照 used?

fu-xing-gao-zhao.literal: The star of blessing shines high
fu-xing-gao-zhao.meaning: May good luck and blessings follow you
fu-xing-gao-zhao.meaning_metaphoric: May good luck and blessings follow you
fu-xing-gao-zhao.origin: A common New Year blessing wishing someone plenty of good luck. 福星 is the 'star of blessing': the Taiwan Ministry of Education dictionary identifies it with the planet Jupiter, whose position was held to bring good fortune, and in folk religion 福 is also the first of the three star gods 福禄寿 (blessing, rank and longevity) whose figures appear on New Year prints. 高照 means shining from on high. Zdic cites the phrase from the Qing novel 《儿女英雄传》 (chapter 39): 管保你这一瞧，就抵得个福星高照, 'one look from you is as good as having the star of blessing shine on us.' It is close to 吉星高照, but 吉星 is any lucky star, while 福星 is the specific star of blessing, and 福星 can also describe a person who brings others luck. Use it in cards and toasts to friends and family.
fu-xing-gao-zhao.title: 福星高照 (fu xing gao zhao) — "May good luck and blessings follow you" | Meaning & Origin

fu-yao-zhi-shang.example_en: Stock prices soared after the announcement.

faq.a: 扶摇直上 (fú yáo zhí shàng) literally means "Whirlwind spiraling straight up" and metaphorically means "Rise rapidly; soar straight up". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.

faq.q: When is 扶摇直上 used?

fu-yao-zhi-shang.origin: 扶摇 is a whirlwind that spirals upward, and in the Zhuangzi the vast Peng bird beats along it to ninety thousand li: 抟扶摇而上者九万里. To go straight (直) up (上) on it is therefore not to climb but to be carried, and the wind is doing the work. That is the picture Chinese keeps. Share prices, reputations and careers, with the implication of a rise too fast and too smooth to have been walked.
fu-yao-zhi-shang.title: 扶摇直上 (fu yao zhi shang) — "Rise rapidly; soar straight up" | Meaning & Origin

fu-zhong-qian-xing.example_en: Despite family obligations, she continued pursuing her education
fu-zhong-qian-xing.example_zh: 尽管有家庭责任，她仍然继续追求教育

faq.a: 负重前行 (fù zhòng qián xíng) literally means "Carry weight march forward" and metaphorically means "Progress despite difficulties". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 负重前行 mean?

faq.a: 负重前行 is pronounced as "fù zhòng qián xíng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 负重前行?

faq.q: When is 负重前行 used?

fu-zhong-qian-xing.origin: Carrying (负) a weight (重) and walking on (前行). This one is modern rather than classical, and it owes its currency to a line that circulates widely: if your days are quiet, it is because somebody else is carrying the load out of sight. Nothing in it marks the burden is deserved, or temporary, or noticed. That is what gives it its particular tone — said about people rather than by them, and aimed at parents, medical staff, soldiers, anybody whose effort would only become visible if it stopped.
fu-zhong-qian-xing.title: 负重前行 (fu zhong qian xing) — "Progress despite difficulties" | Meaning & Origin

faq.a: 负重致远 (fù zhòng zhì yuǎn) literally means "Bear weight reach far" and metaphorically means "Able to carry great responsibility". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 负重致远 mean?

faq.q: How do you pronounce 负重致远?

faq.a: 负重致远 is used when The CEO balanced daily operations while planning the company's future.
faq.q: When is 负重致远 used?

fu-zhong-zhi-yuan.origin: In the Records of the Three Kingdoms, Pang Tong assessed Gu Shao as an ox that could bear a heavy load (负重) over a long distance (致远) — steady rather than quick, and valuable for exactly that. In the same breath he called Lu Ji a nag with a turn of speed. Both are working animals, and the whole compliment lies in which kind of work each is fit for. The phrase names the capacity to carry serious responsibility over time, and it is said of the person an organisation hands its heaviest and slowest problems to.
fu-zhong-zhi-yuan.title: 负重致远 (fu zhong zhi yuan) — "Able to carry great responsibility" | Meaning & Origin

gai-guo-zi-xin.example_en: After realizing his errors, he decided to change his ways and improve.
gai-guo-zi-xin.example_zh: 意识到错误后，他决定改过自新。

faq.q: What does 改过自新 mean?

faq.a: 改过自新 is pronounced as "gǎi guò zì xīn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 改过自新?

gai-guo-zi-xin.meaning: Turn over a new leaf after wrongdoing
gai-guo-zi-xin.meaning_metaphoric: Turn over a new leaf after wrongdoing
gai-guo-zi-xin.origin: The Records of the Grand Historian tells of Chunyu Yi, sentenced to mutilation, whose youngest daughter Tiying travelled to the capital and petitioned the emperor: a punishment that removes a limb cannot be undone, so a man who later wishes to correct (改) his faults (过) and renew (新) himself (自) has no road back. Emperor Wen abolished the mutilating punishments. The phrase carries that argument inside it — the case for reform rests on the claim that the door must be left open.
gai-guo-zi-xin.title: 改过自新 (gai guo zi xin) — "Turn over a new leaf after wrongdoing" | Meaning & Origin

gai-tian-huan-di.example_en: Their innovative ideas have the potential to reshape the future.
gai-tian-huan-di.example_zh: 他们的创新理念有能力改天换地。

faq.q: What does 改天换地 mean?

gai-tian-huan-di.origin: To change (改) the heavens (天) and exchange (换) the earth (地). Unlike most of its neighbours this is a modern phrase, and it belongs to the vocabulary of twentieth-century Chinese politics, where it described the remaking of land and society by collective effort. That history gives it a heroic register that 翻天覆地 does not have: this one implies intention and agency, a transformation carried out rather than merely undergone, and it is still most at home in official language.
gai-tian-huan-di.title: 改天换地 (gai tian huan di) — "Profound transformation" | Meaning & Origin

gai-xie-gui-zheng.example_en: After the scandal, the company implemented strict ethical guidelines
gai-xie-gui-zheng.example_zh: 在丑闻之后，公司实施了严格的道德准则

faq.q: What does 改邪归正 mean?

faq.a: 改邪归正 is pronounced as "gǎi xié guī zhèng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 改邪归正?

faq.q: When is 改邪归正 used?

gai-xie-gui-zheng.literal: Turn from wrong return to right
gai-xie-gui-zheng.origin: Turning away (改) from what is wrong (邪) and returning (归) to what is right (正). The force sits in 归: rightness is treated as the place a person came from and can go back to, not somewhere new they have to be argued into. Vernacular fiction and drama supply the phrase, and there it marks a moment rather than a process — the bandit puts down the knife, the swindler shuts the shop. Chinese still uses it that way, with an expectation attached that the change is meant to be permanent, which is why it sounds far too heavy for ordinary self-improvement.
gai-xie-gui-zheng.title: 改邪归正 (gai xie gui zheng) — "Return to righteousness" | Meaning & Origin

gan-chang-cun-duan.example_en: The news of her departure left him heartbroken.
gan-chang-cun-duan.example_zh: 她的离去让他肝肠寸断。

faq.a: 肝肠寸断 (gān cháng cùn duàn) literally means "Liver and intestines cut inch by inch" and metaphorically means "Extreme sorrow". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 肝肠寸断 mean?

faq.a: 肝肠寸断 is pronounced as "gān cháng cùn duàn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 肝肠寸断?

faq.q: When is 肝肠寸断 used?

gan-chang-cun-duan.literal: Liver and intestines cut inch by inch
gan-chang-cun-duan.origin: A New Account of Tales of the World records an army passing through the gorges, where a soldier took a gibbon's infant aboard. The mother followed along the bank for a hundred li, crying, until she leapt onto the boat and died there. They cut her open and found 肠皆寸寸断 — the intestines (肠) severed (断) into inch (寸) lengths. The commander heard of it and dismissed the man. The four-character form adds the liver (肝), which the story does not mention, because 肝肠 is the ordinary Chinese pairing for the seat of feeling. The phrase describes grief as an internal injury, and it is kept for the real thing — bereavement, not disappointment.
gan-chang-cun-duan.title: 肝肠寸断 (gan chang cun duan) — "Extreme sorrow" | Meaning & Origin

gan-dan-xiang-zhao.example_en: The two friends shared everything with complete trust.
gan-dan-xiang-zhao.example_zh: 两位朋友肝胆相照，完全信任彼此。

faq.a: 肝胆相照 (gān dǎn xiāng zhào) literally means "Livers and galls illuminate each other" and metaphorically means "Share complete trust and loyalty". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 肝胆相照 mean?

faq.a: 肝胆相照 is pronounced as "gān dǎn xiāng zhào" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 肝胆相照?

faq.a: 肝胆相照 is used when The two friends shared everything with complete trust..
faq.q: When is 肝胆相照 used?

gan-dan-xiang-zhao.literal: Livers and galls illuminate each other
gan-dan-xiang-zhao.origin: Liver (肝) and gall (胆) lighting (照) one another (相). Chinese physiology seats courage in the gall and sincerity in the liver, so the phrase does not mean two friends know each other well — it means each is showing the other the organs that hold what they are made of. The image is deliberately visceral and slightly alarming, which is the point: what gets exposed is not information but nerve. Friendships formed under pressure, in the register of loyalty rather than of affection.
gan-dan-xiang-zhao.title: 肝胆相照 (gan dan xiang zhao) — "Share complete trust and loyalty" | Meaning & Origin

gan-nao-tu-di.example_en: He was willing to sacrifice everything for his friends, showing his true loyalty.
gan-nao-tu-di.example_zh: 为了朋友，他甘愿肝脑涂地，表现出真正的忠诚。

faq.a: 肝脑涂地 (gān nǎo tú dì) literally means "Livers and brains smeared" and metaphorically means "Ultimate sacrifice". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 肝脑涂地 mean?

faq.a: 肝脑涂地 is pronounced as "gān nǎo tú dì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 肝脑涂地?

faq.a: 肝脑涂地 is used when He was willing to sacrifice everything for his friends, showing his true loyalty..
faq.q: When is 肝脑涂地 used?

gan-nao-tu-di.origin: Lou Jing, arguing that Liu Bang should site his capital in the defensible Guanzhong rather than the exhausted central plain, described what the wars of the previous decade had actually left behind: fathers and sons with their livers (肝) and brains (脑) smeared (涂) on the ground (地). The phrase began as a description of massacre. It has since inverted into a pledge — I would give my liver and brains for this — and is now used to swear total commitment, usually to a ruler, a country or a cause. The original horror has drained out of it almost completely.
gan-nao-tu-di.title: 肝脑涂地 (gan nao tu di) — "Ultimate sacrifice" | Meaning & Origin

gao-feng-liang-jie.example_en: His actions reflected a high moral standard that inspired those around him.
gao-feng-liang-jie.example_zh: 他的行为展现了高风亮节，激励着周围的人。

faq.a: 高风亮节 (gāo fēng liàng jié) literally means "High character bright integrity" and metaphorically means "Noble and steadfast". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 高风亮节 mean?

faq.a: 高风亮节 is pronounced as "gāo fēng liàng jié" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 高风亮节?

faq.a: 高风亮节 is used when His actions reflected a high moral standard that inspired those around him..
faq.q: When is 高风亮节 used?

gao-feng-liang-jie.origin: High bearing (高风) and bright integrity (亮节). 节 is a bamboo joint before it is a moral term, and the metaphor is structural — the joints are what let the stem bend a long way and spring back without breaking. Chinese moral vocabulary leans on that image constantly. The phrase is reserved for character tested under pressure rather than merely admirable in comfort, which is why it attaches to figures like Su Wu, who kept his loyalty through nineteen years of detention among the Xiongnu.
gao-feng-liang-jie.title: 高风亮节 (gao feng liang jie) — "Noble and steadfast" | Meaning & Origin

gao-shan-liu-shui.example_en: The virtuoso's performance demonstrated perfect artistic harmony and expression
gao-shan-liu-shui.example_zh: 这位大师的表演展示了完美的艺术和谐与表现力

faq.a: 高山流水 (gāo shān liú shuǐ) literally means "High mountain flowing water" and metaphorically means "Perfect artistic understanding between friends". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 高山流水 mean?

faq.a: 高山流水 is pronounced as "gāo shān liú shuǐ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 高山流水?

faq.a: 高山流水 is used when The virtuoso's performance demonstrated perfect artistic harmony and expression.
faq.q: When is 高山流水 used?

gao-shan-liu-shui.origin: The Liezi records that Bo Ya played the qin and Zhong Ziqi listened. When Bo Ya's mind was on high (高) mountains (山), Zhong Ziqi said: how towering, like Mount Tai. When it turned to flowing (流) water (水), he said: how vast, like the Yangtze and the Yellow River. Whatever Bo Ya had in mind, Zhong Ziqi caught it. The Lüshi Chunqiu supplies the ending: when Zhong Ziqi died, Bo Ya broke his qin, cut the strings and never played again, holding that there was no longer anyone worth playing for. The phrase is used for understanding that needs no explaining, and 知音 — one who knows the tone — is still the Chinese word for that kind of friend.
gao-shan-liu-shui.title: 高山流水 (gao shan liu shui) — "Perfect artistic understanding between friends" | Meaning & Origin

gao-tan-kuo-lun.example_en: At the conference, he engaged in lofty discussions about philosophy and ethics.
gao-tan-kuo-lun.example_zh: 在会议上，他高谈阔论关于哲学和伦理的问题。

faq.a: 高谈阔论 (gāo tán kuò lùn) literally means "Lofty talk, expansive discussion" and metaphorically means "Empty grandiose talk". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 高谈阔论 mean?

faq.a: 高谈阔论 is pronounced as "gāo tán kuò lùn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 高谈阔论?

faq.a: 高谈阔论 is used when At the conference, he engaged in lofty discussions about philosophy and ethics..
faq.q: When is 高谈阔论 used?

gao-tan-kuo-lun.origin: Lofty (高) talk (谈) and expansive (阔) discussion (论). The two halves both describe scale — the altitude of the subject and the breadth of the sweep — and neither mentions substance, which is the joke. The phrase can occasionally be neutral, but in practice it is almost always dismissive: it describes the person who addresses the largest available questions at length, generally in a setting where a smaller and more answerable one was on the table.
gao-tan-kuo-lun.title: 高谈阔论 (gao tan kuo lun) — "Empty grandiose talk" | Meaning & Origin

gao-zhan-yuan-zhu.example_en: The leader's vision for the future was clear and inspiring, guiding the team toward long-term success.
gao-zhan-yuan-zhu.example_zh: 这位领导的远见卓识为团队指明了长期成功的方向。

faq.a: 高瞻远瞩 (gāo zhān yuǎn zhǔ) literally means "Look far from a high place" and metaphorically means "Foresight and vision". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 高瞻远瞩 mean?

faq.a: 高瞻远瞩 is pronounced as "gāo zhān yuǎn zhǔ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 高瞻远瞩?

faq.a: 高瞻远瞩 is used when The leader's vision for the future was clear and inspiring, guiding the team toward long-term success..
faq.q: When is 高瞻远瞩 used?

gao-zhan-yuan-zhu.literal: Look far from a high place
gao-zhan-yuan-zhu.origin: High (高) looking (瞻), far (远) gazing (瞩) — a person on high ground, seeing distance rather than detail. The compliment is specifically about scale of view, and Chinese distinguishes it from cleverness: someone can be 高瞻远瞩 and quite wrong about particulars, which is often exactly what is meant. It suits founders, planners and statesmen, and it appears constantly in official writing. In ordinary conversation it is grand enough that it can tip into irony if the plan in question has not worked.
gao-zhan-yuan-zhu.title: 高瞻远瞩 (gao zhan yuan zhu) — "Foresight and vision" | Meaning & Origin

gao-zhen-wu-you.example_en: After installing the security system, the homeowners slept without concern
gao-zhen-wu-you.example_zh: 安装了安全系统后，房主高枕无忧地睡觉

faq.a: 高枕无忧 (gāo zhěn wú yōu) literally means "High pillow no worry" and metaphorically means "Completely free from worry or concern". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 高枕无忧 mean?

faq.a: 高枕无忧 is pronounced as "gāo zhěn wú yōu" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 高枕无忧?

faq.a: 高枕无忧 is used when After installing the security system, the homeowners slept without concern.
faq.q: When is 高枕无忧 used?

gao-zhen-wu-you.meaning: Completely free from worry or concern
gao-zhen-wu-you.meaning_metaphoric: Completely free from worry or concern
gao-zhen-wu-you.origin: In the Strategies of the Warring States, Feng Xuan tells Lord Mengchang that a wily rabbit has three burrows and only just escapes with its life, and that with one refuge his lord 未得高枕而卧, cannot yet sleep on a high pillow (高枕). He builds the other two, and then tells him he may 高枕为乐, take his ease. 无忧 is the modern idiom's addition rather than the text's. The security is manufactured rather than given — this is the reward at the end of the work, not a description of a fortunate man. Resting easy because every contingency has already been covered.
gao-zhen-wu-you.title: 高枕无忧 (gao zhen wu you) — "Completely free from worry or concern" | Meaning & Origin

ge-an-guan-huo.example_en: The competing company observed their rival's crisis without offering assistance
ge-an-guan-huo.example_zh: 竞争公司隔岸观火，看着对手的危机而不提供帮助

faq.a: 隔岸观火 (gé àn guān huǒ) literally means "Watch fire from opposite shore" and metaphorically means "Observe troubles from safe distance". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 隔岸观火 mean?

faq.a: 隔岸观火 is pronounced as "gé àn guān huǒ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 隔岸观火?

faq.a: 隔岸观火 is used when The competing company observed their rival's crisis without offering assistance.
faq.q: When is 隔岸观火 used?

ge-an-guan-huo.origin: To watch (观) the fire (火) from across (隔) the bank (岸). It is the ninth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, where the advice is precise: when the enemy's internal disorder is growing, do not intervene, because pressure from outside will unite them and waiting will let the split do the work. So the detachment is tactical rather than callous in the original. Ordinary modern use has dropped the tactics and kept the coldness, and it now describes standing by while something burns.
ge-an-guan-huo.title: 隔岸观火 (ge an guan huo) — "Observe troubles from safe distance" | Meaning & Origin

ge-de-qi-suo.example_en: The reorganization helped each team member find their ideal role
ge-de-qi-suo.example_zh: 重组帮助每个团队成员找到了最适合的角色

faq.a: 各得其所 (gè dé qí suǒ) literally means "Each finds its place" and metaphorically means "Everything in right place". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 各得其所 mean?

faq.a: 各得其所 is pronounced as "gè dé qí suǒ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 各得其所?

faq.a: 各得其所 is used when The reorganization helped each team member find their ideal role.
faq.q: When is 各得其所 used?

ge-de-qi-suo.origin: Each (各) obtaining (得) its (其) proper place (所). The Book of Changes uses it of a market where everyone has exchanged what they came to exchange and gone home satisfied. That is the sense: not equality but fit, with the test being that nothing is left misplaced. Appointments, seating plans, settlements of a dispute: the standard way of saying an arrangement has worked out for everybody.
ge-de-qi-suo.title: 各得其所 (ge de qi suo) — "Everything in right place" | Meaning & Origin

ge-qiang-you-er.example_en: Be careful what you say; walls have ears in this office.
ge-qiang-you-er.example_zh: 在这个办公室里，你要小心说话，隔墙有耳。

faq.a: 隔墙有耳 (gé qiáng yǒu ěr) literally means "Walls have ears" and metaphorically means "Be discreet". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 隔墙有耳 mean?

faq.a: 隔墙有耳 is pronounced as "gé qiáng yǒu ěr" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 隔墙有耳?

faq.a: 隔墙有耳 is used when Be careful what you say; walls have ears in this office..
faq.q: When is 隔墙有耳 used?

ge-qiang-you-er.origin: Across (隔) the wall (墙) there are (有) ears (耳). Early statecraft texts carry the warning in the barer form 墙有耳, and Chinese and English arrived at almost the same image independently, which is unusual enough to be worth noticing. The phrase functions as an interruption rather than an observation: it is what one person says to another mid-conversation, and it means stop talking about this here, rather than commenting on anyone in particular.
ge-qiang-you-er.title: 隔墙有耳 (ge qiang you er) — "Be discreet" | Meaning & Origin

ge-shu-ji-jian.example_en: The committee chair encouraged all members to share their perspectives on the proposal
ge-shu-ji-jian.example_zh: 委员会主席鼓励所有成员分享他们对提案的看法

faq.a: 各抒己见 (gè shū jǐ jiàn) literally means "Each express own view" and metaphorically means "Everyone freely express their own opinions". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 各抒己见 mean?

faq.a: 各抒己见 is pronounced as "gè shū jǐ jiàn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 各抒己见?

faq.a: 各抒己见 is used when The committee chair encouraged all members to share their perspectives on the proposal.
faq.q: When is 各抒己见 used?

ge-shu-ji-jian.meaning: Everyone freely express their own opinions
ge-shu-ji-jian.meaning_metaphoric: Everyone freely express their own opinions
ge-shu-ji-jian.origin: Each (各) sets out (抒) their own (己) view (见). 抒 is to pour out or give voice to — the same character as in 抒情, to express feeling — so the phrase carries the sense of getting something said rather than merely registering a preference. What it names is a mode of discussion in which the whole range of opinion goes on the table before anyone converges, and Chinese uses it in exactly that setting: minutes of meetings, classroom instructions, and the sentence a chair says to open the floor. It is neutral about whether agreement follows, and often it does not.
ge-shu-ji-jian.title: 各抒己见 (ge shu ji jian) — "Everyone freely express their own opinions" | Meaning & Origin

ge-wu-zhi-zhi.example_en: He believes that thorough research leads to true knowledge.
ge-wu-zhi-zhi.example_zh: 他相信深入研究能获得真正的知识。

faq.a: 格物致知 (gé wù zhì zhī) literally means "Investigate things to gain knowledge" and metaphorically means "Pursue understanding". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 格物致知 mean?

faq.a: 格物致知 is pronounced as "gé wù zhì zhī" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 格物致知?

faq.a: 格物致知 is used when He believes that thorough research leads to true knowledge..
faq.q: When is 格物致知 used?

ge-wu-zhi-zhi.origin: Four characters from the Great Learning that Chinese philosophy then argued about for eight hundred years: investigate (格) things (物) and thereby extend (致) knowledge (知). The text gives no gloss, and the gap was filled in opposite directions — Zhu Xi read 格物 as the patient examination of things in the world, one at a time, while Wang Yangming, having sat staring at bamboo for a week and fallen ill without attaining anything, concluded that the investigation must be of the mind instead. Modern Chinese leans on Zhu Xi's reading, and the phrase is now used for empirical method and, sometimes, for science itself.
ge-wu-zhi-zhi.title: 格物致知 (ge wu zhi zhi) — "Pursue understanding" | Meaning & Origin

ge-xian-shen-tong.example_en: In the competition, each team showcased their unique strengths.

faq.a: 各显神通 (gè xiǎn shén tōng) literally means "Each displays divine powers" and metaphorically means "Each shows their special skills". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 各显神通 mean?

faq.a: 各显神通 is pronounced as "gè xiǎn shén tōng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 各显神通?

faq.a: 各显神通 is used when In the competition, each team showcased their unique strengths..
faq.q: When is 各显神通 used?

ge-xian-shen-tong.origin: Each one (各) displaying (显) their divine powers (神通). 神通 is a Buddhist technical term for the supernormal faculties attributed to the enlightened, and the phrase travels attached to the Eight Immortals crossing the sea, each getting across by their own method rather than sharing a boat. That story is the whole meaning: no common approach, no coordination, and everybody arrives. Situations where people have been left to solve something their own way — and the tone is cheerful about it.
ge-xian-shen-tong.title: 各显神通 (ge xian shen tong) — "Each shows their special skills" | Meaning & Origin

ge-xing-qi-shi.example_en: In a diverse team, everyone contributes their unique skills, leading to a well-rounded project.
ge-xing-qi-shi.example_zh: 在这个多元化的团队中，各行其是，大家各自发挥特长，最终完成了一个全面的项目。

faq.a: 各行其是 (gè xíng qí shì) literally means "Each does what he thinks is right" and metaphorically means "Disunity in action". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 各行其是 mean?

faq.a: 各行其是 is pronounced as "gè xíng qí shì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 各行其是?

faq.a: 各行其是 is used when In a diverse team, everyone contributes their unique skills, leading to a well-rounded project..
faq.q: When is 各行其是 used?

ge-xing-qi-shi.literal: Each does what he thinks is right
ge-xing-qi-shi.origin: Each (各) does (行) what they (其) think right (是). The final character is the trap for learners: 是 here means right or correct, not the copula, so the phrase describes people acting on their own judgement rather than merely acting separately. That is what makes it a criticism. The problem it names is not laziness or conflict but the absence of a settled common line, with everyone conscientiously pursuing their own version, and it is the standard Chinese diagnosis of a committee that has stopped functioning.
ge-xing-qi-shi.title: 各行其是 (ge xing qi shi) — "Disunity in action" | Meaning & Origin

ge-xue-sao-yang.example_en: The vague explanation failed to address the underlying problem
ge-xue-sao-yang.example_zh: 这个模糊的解释未能解决根本问题

faq.a: 隔靴搔痒 (gé xuē sāo yǎng) literally means "Scratch itch through boot" and metaphorically means "Ineffective indirect solution". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 隔靴搔痒 mean?

faq.a: 隔靴搔痒 is pronounced as "gé xuē sāo yǎng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 隔靴搔痒?

faq.a: 隔靴搔痒 is used when The vague explanation failed to address the underlying problem.
faq.q: When is 隔靴搔痒 used?

ge-xue-sao-yang.origin: To scratch (搔) an itch (痒) through (隔) the boot (靴). The image comes out of Chan writing, where it describes teaching that circles a matter without touching it. Everything about the action is correct except the one thing that matters, which is contact — and the phrase is precise that the effort is real and the frustration is caused by its being applied at one remove. Remedies, criticism and reforms that do not reach the thing they are aimed at.
ge-xue-sao-yang.title: 隔靴搔痒 (ge xue sao yang) — "Ineffective indirect solution" | Meaning & Origin

ge-you-suo-chang.example_en: Both candidates bring different but valuable skills to the position.
ge-you-suo-chang.example_zh: 两位候选人各有所长，都能为职位带来价值。

faq.a: 各有所长 (gè yǒu suǒ cháng) literally means "Each has their strengths" and metaphorically means "Different people, different strengths". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 各有所长 mean?

faq.a: 各有所长 is pronounced as "gè yǒu suǒ cháng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 各有所长?

faq.a: 各有所长 is used when Both candidates bring different but valuable skills to the position..
faq.q: When is 各有所长 used?

ge-you-suo-chang.origin: This idiom states that each person (各) has (有) their own (所) strengths (长). It acknowledges that different individuals excel in different areas, promoting appreciation for diversity of talents. The phrase appeared in Confucian texts discussing how wise rulers recognize and employ varied talents. It counters the tendency to rank people hierarchically. Modern usage encourages recognizing everyone's unique contributions and building teams that leverage complementary strengths.
ge-you-suo-chang.title: 各有所长 (ge you suo chang) — "Different people, different strengths" | Meaning & Origin

gen-shen-di-gu.example_en: The traditional beliefs remained entrenched in the community despite modernization
gen-shen-di-gu.example_zh: 尽管现代化，传统信仰在社区中仍根深蒂固

faq.a: 根深蒂固 (gēn shēn dì gù) literally means "Roots deep stem firm" and metaphorically means "Deeply entrenched and difficult to change". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 根深蒂固 mean?

faq.a: 根深蒂固 is pronounced as "gēn shēn dì gù" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 根深蒂固?

faq.a: 根深蒂固 is used when The traditional beliefs remained entrenched in the community despite modernization.
faq.q: When is 根深蒂固 used?

gen-shen-di-gu.meaning: Deeply entrenched and difficult to change
gen-shen-di-gu.meaning_metaphoric: Deeply entrenched and difficult to change
gen-shen-di-gu.origin: This comes from the Laozi, on deep roots and a firm base as the way of long life — 深根固柢. A plant whose roots run deep (根深) and whose stem is firmly set (蒂固) is not easily pulled up. Applied to habits and institutions the image is neutral in the original and unflattering now: what is hard to uproot is usually hard to reform. Something entrenched, and normally with the implication that it ought not to be.
gen-shen-di-gu.title: 根深蒂固 (gen shen di gu) — "Deeply entrenched and difficult to change" | Meaning & Origin

gong-bu-ying-qiu.example_en: The limited production capacity couldn't satisfy the overwhelming market interest
gong-bu-ying-qiu.example_zh: 有限的生产能力无法满足市场的巨大兴趣

faq.a: 供不应求 (gōng bù yìng qiú) literally means "Supply cannot meet demand" and metaphorically means "Demand exceeds available supply". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 供不应求 mean?

faq.a: 供不应求 is pronounced as "gōng bù yìng qiú" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 供不应求?

faq.a: 供不应求 is used when The limited production capacity couldn't satisfy the overwhelming market interest.
faq.q: When is 供不应求 used?

gong-bu-ying-qiu.origin: Supply (供) cannot (不) meet (应) demand (求). This is modern economic vocabulary rather than a classical idiom, and it is worth learning as such: it belongs to news reporting and business writing, and it has none of the literary texture of the phrases around it. The one thing worth noting is that it works as unambiguous praise when the subject is a product, where English 'we cannot meet demand' is at least half a complaint about logistics.
gong-bu-ying-qiu.title: 供不应求 (gong bu ying qiu) — "Demand exceeds available supply" | Meaning & Origin

gong-cheng-ming-jiu.example_en: After decades of work, he finally achieved recognition.
gong-cheng-ming-jiu.example_zh: 经过数十年的努力，他终于功成名就。

faq.a: 功成名就 (gōng chéng míng jiù) literally means "Merit achieved, name established" and metaphorically means "Achieve success and fame". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 功成名就 mean?

faq.a: 功成名就 is pronounced as "gōng chéng míng jiù" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 功成名就?

faq.a: 功成名就 is used when After decades of work, he finally achieved recognition..
faq.q: When is 功成名就 used?

gong-cheng-ming-jiu.origin: The work (功) completed (成) and the name (名) established (就). Both halves are achievements and the order is causal: the reputation follows the accomplishment rather than accompanying it. That is what makes the phrase retrospective. It describes a career that is finished rather than one going well, which is why it goes to people at the end of things — and why saying it of somebody still working can sound like a suggestion that they stop.
gong-cheng-ming-jiu.title: 功成名就 (gong cheng ming jiu) — "Achieve success and fame" | Meaning & Origin

gong-cheng-shen-tui.example_en: After completing his mission, he quietly stepped aside.
gong-cheng-shen-tui.example_zh: 完成使命后，他功成身退。

faq.a: 功成身退 (gōng chéng shēn tuì) literally means "Merit achieved, person withdraws" and metaphorically means "Retire after achieving success". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 功成身退 mean?

faq.a: 功成身退 is pronounced as "gōng chéng shēn tuì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 功成身退?

faq.a: 功成身退 is used when After completing his mission, he quietly stepped aside..
faq.q: When is 功成身退 used?

gong-cheng-shen-tui.origin: The Dao De Jing states it as a natural law rather than as advice: 功遂身退，天之道 — the work (功) done (成), the person (身) withdraws (退), and this is the way of heaven. The argument is that staying on after the thing is finished is what destroys the people who do it, and the classic case is the general who wins the war and is then killed by the king he won it for. Graceful exits claim it, and there is always a faint sense that the alternative was worse than obscurity.
gong-cheng-shen-tui.title: 功成身退 (gong cheng shen tui) — "Retire after achieving success" | Meaning & Origin

gong-de-yuan-man.example_en: After years of hard work, his project achieved a perfect conclusion

faq.a: 功德圆满 (gōng dé yuán mǎn) literally means "Merit and virtue complete" and metaphorically means "Successful completion". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 功德圆满 mean?

faq.a: 功德圆满 is pronounced as "gōng dé yuán mǎn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 功德圆满?

faq.a: 功德圆满 is used when After years of hard work, his project achieved a perfect conclusion.
faq.q: When is 功德圆满 used?

gong-de-yuan-man.origin: The expression came out of Buddhist practice, where the merit (功德) accumulated through a rite — sutras chanted, offerings made, a service carried to its proper end — is described as complete and round (圆满). 圆 is doing real work there: not merely finished but closed, with nothing left ragged. Secular Chinese borrowed the expression whole and now applies it to any undertaking brought to a clean end, a conference that ran its course, a project delivered. It keeps a faint ceremonial warmth, which is why it turns up in closing remarks far more often than in the middle of anything.
gong-de-yuan-man.title: 功德圆满 (gong de yuan man) — "Successful completion" | Meaning & Origin

gong-er-wang-si.example_en: She always puts the team's needs above her own, earning the respect of her colleagues.
gong-er-wang-si.example_zh: 她总是把团队的需求放在自己之上，赢得了同事们的尊重。

gong-er-wang-si.literal: For the public good, forget the private
gong-er-wang-si.meaning: Public duty crowds out private interest
gong-er-wang-si.meaning_metaphoric: Public duty crowds out private interest
gong-er-wang-si.origin: For the public good (公) and thereby forgetting (忘) the private (私). The Book of Han attaches the sentiment to Jia Yi, the young scholar-official whose memorials to Emperor Wen argued for reforms that cost him his position at court. The construction matters: not sacrificing self-interest, which implies a struggle, but forgetting it, which claims the interest never came up. That is a very high bar and the phrase knows it. It belongs to citations and memorials, and it is said about people more often than by them.
gong-er-wang-si.title: 公而忘私 (gong er wang si) — "Public duty crowds out private interest" | Meaning & Origin

faq.q: When is 功亏一篑 used?

gong-kui-yi-kui.meaning: Fail due to giving up near the end
gong-kui-yi-kui.meaning_metaphoric: Fail due to giving up near the end
gong-kui-yi-kui.origin: This one comes from the Book of Documents: 为山九仞，功亏一篑 — in raising a mound nine ren high, the work (功) fails (亏) for one basket (篑) of earth. Everything already carried counts for nothing if the last load is not. The image is deliberately cruel about proportion: the shortfall is trivial and the loss is total. Modern usage warns against abandoning something at the point where the remaining effort is smallest.
gong-kui-yi-kui.title: 功亏一篑 (gong kui yi kui) — "Fail due to giving up near the end" | Meaning & Origin

gong-qi-bu-bei.example_en: In the heat of competition, they decided to strike when their opponent was unprepared.
gong-qi-bu-bei.example_zh: 在竞争的激烈中，他们决定攻其不备。

faq.a: 攻其不备 (gōng qí bù bèi) literally means "Attack the unprepared" and metaphorically means "Surprise attack". It belongs to the Strategy & Action category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 攻其不备 mean?

faq.a: 攻其不备 is pronounced as "gōng qí bù bèi" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 攻其不备?

faq.a: 攻其不备 is used when In the heat of competition, they decided to strike when their opponent was unprepared..
faq.q: When is 攻其不备 used?

gong-qi-bu-bei.origin: Sun Tzu's first chapter ends with a pair: 攻其无备，出其不意 — attack (攻) where they (其) are unprepared (备), appear where you are not expected. The common modern form writes 不备 for his 无备; both negate preparation and the sense is unchanged. The two clauses are one instruction seen from either side. What the phrase adds to the ordinary idea of surprise is a target — it directs attention to the specific gap in the opponent's preparation, which has to be found before it can be struck. It is used freely in Chinese business and sport, and it survives translation better than most of Sun Tzu.
gong-qi-bu-bei.title: 攻其不备 (gong qi bu bei) — "Surprise attack" | Meaning & Origin

gong-wu-bu-ke.example_en: The army had never lost a battle.

gong-wu-bu-ke.literal: In attack, nothing is not taken
gong-wu-bu-ke.meaning: Win every battle; never fail in attacks
gong-wu-bu-ke.meaning_metaphoric: Win every battle; never fail in attacks
gong-wu-bu-ke.origin: In attacking (攻), there is nothing (无) not (不) taken (克). 克 is to overcome, and specifically to reduce a position, so the phrase concerns assaults rather than wars: every objective attempted was carried. It is normally the first half of a pair, 攻无不克，战无不胜, and using it alone is slightly unusual. Sales teams and litigators claim it as readily as armies, and the boast is about a record with no exceptions anywhere in it.
gong-wu-bu-ke.title: 攻无不克 (gong wu bu ke) — "Win every battle; never fail in attacks" | Meaning & Origin

gong-xi-fa-cai.example_en: Gung hei fat choi! Wishing you a prosperous New Year.
gong-xi-fa-cai.example_zh: 过年见到长辈，孩子们都笑着说：“恭喜发财，红包拿来！”

faq.a: 恭喜发财 (gōng xǐ fā cái) literally means "Congratulations, and may you make a fortune" and metaphorically means "Wishing you a prosperous New Year". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 恭喜发财 mean?

faq.a: 恭喜发财 is pronounced as "gōng xǐ fā cái" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 恭喜发财?

faq.a: 恭喜发财 is used when Gung hei fat choi! Wishing you a prosperous New Year..
faq.q: When is 恭喜发财 used?

gong-xi-fa-cai.literal: Congratulations, and may you make a fortune
gong-xi-fa-cai.meaning: Wishing you a prosperous New Year
gong-xi-fa-cai.meaning_metaphoric: Wishing you a prosperous New Year
gong-xi-fa-cai.origin: A folk New Year greeting with no classical source. 恭喜 means 'respectful congratulations' and 发财 'to make a fortune', so the phrase says, roughly, 'congratulations, and may you get rich'. It is young by idiom standards. One early literary appearance is in Wu Jianren's late-Qing novel 《二十年目睹之怪现状》 (chapter 8), serialised in the 1900s, where the narrator greets a friend with 'Congratulations, get rich!' (恭喜发财呢！). By the 1930s Lu Xun, in his essay 《过年》, could list it beside firecrackers, mahjong and New Year visits as a fixed part of the holiday. It is strongly associated with Cantonese-speaking communities, where it is said as 'gung hei fat choi', and Hong Kong films helped carry it overseas. Say it to anyone during the New Year period; children often add 红包拿来 ('now hand over the red envelope') as a joke.
gong-xi-fa-cai.title: 恭喜发财 (gōng xǐ fā cái) Meaning — "Gong Xi Fa Cai" Explained

faq.q: How do you pronounce 故步自封?

faq.a: 故步自封 is used when The firm kept its 1990s process and watched every rival overtake it.
faq.q: When is 故步自封 used?

gu-bu-zi-feng.meaning: Refuse to move beyond past methods
gu-bu-zi-feng.meaning_metaphoric: Refuse to move beyond past methods
gu-bu-zi-feng.origin: The standard form writes the first character 故, meaning old or former — the old (故) steps (步) one keeps taking, with oneself (自) sealed in (封). It is very often miswritten 固步自封, since 固 means fixed and seems to fit, and the error is common enough in China to be worth knowing about. The image is a person walking a route they have walked before and building a wall around it. It criticises not caution but the refusal to look at anything outside a method that once worked, and it is standard in Chinese writing about companies and institutions that stopped adapting.
gu-bu-zi-feng.title: 故步自封 (gu bu zi feng) — "Refuse to move beyond past methods" | Meaning & Origin

gu-ci-shi-bi.example_en: By focusing too much on minor details, he overlooked the bigger picture and missed the deadline.
gu-ci-shi-bi.example_zh: 他过于关注细节，顾此失彼，最终错过了截止日期。

faq.a: 顾此失彼 (gù cǐ shī bǐ) literally means "Attend to this, lose that" and metaphorically means "Unable to cover everything at once". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 顾此失彼 mean?

faq.a: 顾此失彼 is pronounced as "gù cǐ shī bǐ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 顾此失彼?

faq.a: 顾此失彼 is used when By focusing too much on minor details, he overlooked the bigger picture and missed the deadline..
faq.q: When is 顾此失彼 used?

gu-ci-shi-bi.meaning: Unable to cover everything at once
gu-ci-shi-bi.meaning_metaphoric: Unable to cover everything at once
gu-ci-shi-bi.origin: Attend to (顾) this one (此) and lose (失) that one (彼). The phrase names a specific failure mode rather than general carelessness: not neglect, but the impossibility of covering two things with resources sufficient for one, so that every correction opens a gap somewhere else. It is what you say about a defence stretched along too long a line, a team of three running four projects, or a budget being moved from one shortfall to another. The implication is always that the underlying allocation is wrong.
gu-ci-shi-bi.title: 顾此失彼 (gu ci shi bi) — "Unable to cover everything at once" | Meaning & Origin

gu-ming-diao-yu.example_en: His charity work seemed more about publicity than genuine help.

faq.q: What does 沽名钓誉 mean?

faq.a: 沽名钓誉 is pronounced as "gū míng diào yù" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 沽名钓誉?

faq.a: 沽名钓誉 is used when His charity work seemed more about publicity than genuine help..
faq.q: When is 沽名钓誉 used?

gu-ming-diao-yu.literal: Buy a name, angle for praise
gu-ming-diao-yu.origin: To buy (沽) a name (名) and angle (钓) for reputation (誉). Both verbs are transactional and one of them is patient — 钓 is fishing with a line, which implies bait, waiting, and a fish that does not know it is being caught. That is what the phrase alleges: not merely wanting to be well thought of, but building the conditions under which it will happen. Conspicuous charity and public resignations, and it is a serious accusation, because it claims to know the motive behind an act that was otherwise good.
gu-ming-diao-yu.title: 沽名钓誉 (gu ming diao yu) — "Seek fame through calculated actions" | Meaning & Origin

gu-rou-xiang-lian.example_en: Even after years apart, their bond remained strong, proving that flesh and blood are connected.
gu-rou-xiang-lian.example_zh: 即使多年未见，他们的纽带依然牢固，证明了骨肉相连。

faq.a: 骨肉相连 (gǔ ròu xiāng lián) literally means "Bones and flesh connected" and metaphorically means "Inseparable family bond". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 骨肉相连 mean?

faq.a: 骨肉相连 is pronounced as "gǔ ròu xiāng lián" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 骨肉相连?

faq.a: 骨肉相连 is used when Even after years apart, their bond remained strong, proving that flesh and blood are connected..
faq.q: When is 骨肉相连 used?

gu-rou-xiang-lian.origin: Bone (骨) and flesh (肉) joined (相连). 骨肉 is the ordinary Chinese word for close blood kin, so the phrase is not really a metaphor: it states that parents and children, brothers and sisters, are one body distributed across several people. Its force is that the connection is involuntary and cannot be dissolved by falling out. It appears constantly in writing about separated families, and in political language about territories claimed as inseparable.
gu-rou-xiang-lian.title: 骨肉相连 (gu rou xiang lian) — "Inseparable family bond" | Meaning & Origin

gu-ruo-jin-tang.example_en: The company's cybersecurity defenses were impenetrable to attackers
gu-ruo-jin-tang.example_zh: 公司的网络安全防御对攻击者来说固若金汤

faq.a: 固若金汤 (gù ruò jīn tāng) literally means "Metal walls, a moat of boiling water" and metaphorically means "Impenetrable defenses". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 固若金汤 mean?

faq.a: 固若金汤 is pronounced as "gù ruò jīn tāng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 固若金汤?

faq.a: 固若金汤 is used when The company's cybersecurity defenses were impenetrable to attackers.
faq.q: When is 固若金汤 used?

gu-ruo-jin-tang.literal: Metal walls, a moat of boiling water
gu-ruo-jin-tang.origin: In the Book of Han, Kuai Tong warns what will follow if the magistrate who surrendered first is put to death: the other border towns will hear of it, wall themselves up, and 皆为金城汤池，不可攻也 — all become walls of metal and moats of scalding water, and cannot be attacked. The warning is conditional and about what has not happened yet, not a report of cities already impregnable. 汤 is the trap for learners: here it is boiling liquid, not soup, and the moat is heated rather than merely wet. The four characters compress it — solid (固) as (若) metal (金) and scalding water (汤) — one defence passive and one active. Chinese uses the phrase for fortifications, for alibis with no hole in them, and for systems built with several independent layers.
gu-ruo-jin-tang.title: 固若金汤 (gu ruo jin tang) — "Impenetrable defenses" | Meaning & Origin

gu-shou-ru-chai.example_en: After months of illness, he looked so frail, with bones thin as firewood.
gu-shou-ru-chai.example_zh: 经过几个月的疾病，他看起来非常虚弱，骨瘦如柴。

faq.a: 骨瘦如柴 (gǔ shòu rú chái) literally means "Bones thin as sticks" and metaphorically means "Extremely thin". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 骨瘦如柴 mean?

faq.a: 骨瘦如柴 is pronounced as "gǔ shòu rú chái" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 骨瘦如柴?

faq.a: 骨瘦如柴 is used when After months of illness, he looked so frail, with bones thin as firewood..
faq.q: When is 骨瘦如柴 used?

gu-shou-ru-chai.origin: Bones (骨) thin (瘦) as (如) kindling (柴). 柴 is firewood, specifically the dry brushwood gathered for burning, so the comparison carries dryness and brittleness as well as thinness. The phrase is not a comment on physique but a description of a body that has been depleted, and Chinese uses it about illness, famine and grief. It is blunt and rather pitying, and it would not be used about someone who was merely slim.
gu-shou-ru-chai.title: 骨瘦如柴 (gu shou ru chai) — "Extremely thin" | Meaning & Origin

gu-tu-nan-li.example_en: Despite the opportunities elsewhere, he couldn't bring himself to leave.
gu-tu-nan-li.example_zh: 尽管别处有机会，他仍故土难离。

faq.a: 故土难离 (gù tǔ nán lí) literally means "Native soil hard to leave" and metaphorically means "Hard to leave one's homeland". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 故土难离 mean?

faq.a: 故土难离 is pronounced as "gù tǔ nán lí" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 故土难离?

faq.a: 故土难离 is used when Despite the opportunities elsewhere, he couldn't bring himself to leave..
faq.q: When is 故土难离 used?

gu-tu-nan-li.origin: Old (故) ground (土) is hard (难) to leave (离). 故土 is the earth one comes from, and 故 is the character in 故乡 and 故人 — what is old and one's own, rather than merely former. The phrase does not argue that leaving is wrong, only that it costs, which is why it turns up in accounts of migration and resettlement as an explanation of reluctance. The tone is sympathetic, and it is often said about people who left anyway.
gu-tu-nan-li.title: 故土难离 (gu tu nan li) — "Hard to leave one's homeland" | Meaning & Origin

gu-xi-yang-jian.example_en: The principal's leniency toward bullying only emboldened the perpetrators
gu-xi-yang-jian.example_zh: 校长对欺凌行为的宽容只会使行为人更加胆大妄为

faq.a: 姑息养奸 (gū xī yǎng jiān) literally means "Indulgence nurtures evildoers" and metaphorically means "Leniency encourages worse behavior". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 姑息养奸 mean?

faq.a: 姑息养奸 is pronounced as "gū xī yǎng jiān" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 姑息养奸?

faq.a: 姑息养奸 is used when The principal's leniency toward bullying only emboldened the perpetrators.
faq.q: When is 姑息养奸 used?

gu-xi-yang-jian.origin: 姑息 is indulgence of the temporary, accommodating kind — the Book of Rites contrasts loving someone with virtue against loving them with 姑息 — and the phrase adds what it produces: nurturing (养) what is corrupt (奸). The verb is the sharp part, since 养 is what you do deliberately to something you want to grow. Discipline, policy and parenting, and the claim is always that the leniency was not neutral but causal.
gu-xi-yang-jian.title: 姑息养奸 (gu xi yang jian) — "Leniency encourages worse behavior" | Meaning & Origin

gu-zhu-yi-zhi.example_en: He decided to invest all his savings in the startup, believing it was his best chance for success.
gu-zhu-yi-zhi.example_zh: 他决定孤注一掷，把所有的积蓄都投资在这个初创公司上，认为这是他成功的最佳机会。

faq.a: 孤注一掷 (gū zhù yī zhì) literally means "Stake everything on one throw" and metaphorically means "All-in risk". It belongs to the Strategy & Action category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 孤注一掷 mean?

faq.a: 孤注一掷 is pronounced as "gū zhù yī zhì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 孤注一掷?

faq.a: 孤注一掷 is used when He decided to invest all his savings in the startup, believing it was his best chance for success..
faq.q: When is 孤注一掷 used?

gu-zhu-yi-zhi.origin: The History of Song records the slander that Wang Qinruo laid before Emperor Zhenzong about Kou Zhun, who had pushed the emperor to the front at the Chanyuan campaign: a gambler down to his last stake (孤注) throws (掷) everything on one cast, and Your Majesty was that stake. The accusation worked and Kou Zhun fell. The phrase keeps the gambling table exactly. It describes the move made because no further moves remain, and it is neutral about courage — the same act reads as decisive or desperate depending only on the result.
gu-zhu-yi-zhi.title: 孤注一掷 (gu zhu yi zhi) — "All-in risk" | Meaning & Origin

gua-gu-liao-du.example_en: He had to scrape bones to cure the poison of his past mistakes.
gua-gu-liao-du.example_zh: 他不得不刮骨疗毒，以治愈过去错误的毒害。

faq.a: 刮骨疗毒 (guā gǔ liáo dú) literally means "Scrape bone to cure poison" and metaphorically means "Radical problem-solving". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 刮骨疗毒 mean?

faq.a: 刮骨疗毒 is pronounced as "guā gǔ liáo dú" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 刮骨疗毒?

faq.a: 刮骨疗毒 is used when He had to scrape bones to cure the poison of his past mistakes..
faq.q: When is 刮骨疗毒 used?

gua-gu-liao-du.origin: The Records of the Three Kingdoms says that Guan Yu, hit by a poisoned arrow, was told the poison had reached the bone and that the arm must be opened and the bone scraped (刮骨) to cure (疗) the poison (毒). He held out his arm and went on eating and drinking with his officers while the surgeon worked, with the blood filling the dish beneath. The history does not name the doctor — Hua Tuo is the novel's addition. The phrase means treating a problem at its source, accepting that the cure will be worse than living with it.
gua-gu-liao-du.title: 刮骨疗毒 (gua gu liao du) — "Radical problem-solving" | Meaning & Origin

gua-mu-xiang-kan.example_en: After her breakthrough performance, critics had to reassess her artistic abilities
gua-mu-xiang-kan.example_zh: 在她的突破性表演之后，评论家们不得不重新评估她的艺术才能

faq.a: 刮目相看 (guā mù xiāng kàn) literally means "Scrape eyes look anew" and metaphorically means "Reassess someone who has improved". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 刮目相看 mean?

gua-mu-xiang-kan.origin: Lü Meng was a Wu general dismissed as unlettered muscle until his sovereign told him to read. When Lu Su next passed through and talked strategy with him, he was astonished, and Lü Meng answered with the line that became the idiom: 士别三日，即更刮目相待 — when a man has been apart three days, you must scrape (刮) your eyes (目) and look (看) at him afresh. Pei Songzhi's commentary to the Records of the Three Kingdoms preserves it, quoting the Jiangbiao Zhuan. What it asks for is the effort of dropping an assessment that has gone stale, and it is used of people who have been underestimated.
gua-mu-xiang-kan.title: 刮目相看 (gua mu xiang kan) — "Reassess someone who has improved" | Meaning & Origin

gua-shu-di-luo.origin: When the melon (瓜) is ripe (熟), the stem (蒂) drops (落) of itself. The observation is agricultural and precise: a melon taken early has to be pulled, and one left to its time separates without force. The phrase is used of anything that cannot usefully be hurried — a negotiation, a diagnosis, a decision someone else has to reach — and its implicit advice is about the person waiting rather than the melon. It pairs naturally with 水到渠成.
gua-shu-di-luo.title: 瓜熟蒂落 (gua shu di luo) — "Things happen when ready" | Meaning & Origin

The counsel is not about honesty but about appearances: the man is innocent, and that is precisely why he must not be seen doing it. Modern usage warns against putting yourself in a position that invites suspicion, however clean your hands are.

gua-yang-tou-mai-gou-rou.origin: The oldest version is in the 《晏子春秋》, where the minister Yanzi rebukes a ruler with the image of an ox head hung at the gate while horse meat is sold inside. The sheep-and-dog form settled later and stuck, because it is funnier and because the two were priced so differently that the swindle is instantly legible. It remains the standard Chinese phrase for the gap between the sign and the goods — advertising, political promises, a job description that turns out to describe a different job — and its force comes from the fact that nobody is lying outright. The head really is hanging there.

guai-wan-mo-jiao.origin: Turning corners (拐弯) and skirting angles (抹角) — the phrase describes a route through a crowded old quarter, where nothing runs straight and progress is made by a series of small deflections. Applied to speech it means arriving at the point eventually and never directly. The tone is mildly impatient, and the commonest form is the imperative: 别拐弯抹角, stop going round the houses, which is close to the English idiom in both sense and tone.

guan-kui-li-ce.origin: Dongfang Shuo, deflecting a challenge, wrote of looking at the sky through a tube (管窥) and measuring the sea with a gourd dipper (蠡测). Both instruments work: the tube does show sky and the ladle does hold water, which is exactly why the error is worth naming — the method returns a real answer to a question far larger than it can address. The phrase is used self-deprecatingly to preface an opinion, and it is a standard modesty formula in Chinese academic writing.

guan-men-zhuo-zei.origin: The twenty-second of the Thirty-Six Stratagems: against a small and mobile enemy, close the escape first and fight second, because a force you cannot catch will simply return. Shut (关) the door (门) and take (捉) the thief (贼). The stratagem is careful to limit itself to a weak opponent — cornering a strong one produces the desperate resistance the tactic is meant to avoid — and that qualification is generally lost when the phrase is used outside its source.

faq.q: When is 光明磊落 used?

guang-ming-lei-luo.origin: Bright (光) and clear (明), open and unhidden (磊落). 磊 is three stones stacked out in the open, and the word keeps that sense of everything being where it can be counted. What the phrase claims is not that somebody has done no wrong but that nothing in their conduct is arranged to be hidden, which is a different and more testable virtue. References and obituaries are full of it, and it is the standard defence of somebody under suspicion — the argument being that a life run this way could not have concealed the thing alleged.
guang-ming-lei-luo.title: 光明磊落 (guang ming lei luo) — "Upright and open; above board" | Meaning & Origin

guang-zong-yao-zu.origin: To bring light (光) to the clan (宗) and make the ancestors (祖) shine (耀). The direction is what matters: achievement is not the individual's to keep but flows backwards up the line, and in a system of ancestral rites the dead have a real stake in it. That is why examination success was a family event. The phrase is still used in earnest and also, increasingly, ironically by younger Chinese speakers describing the weight of expectation that comes attached to it.
guang-zong-yao-zu.title: 光宗耀祖 (guang zong yao zu) — "Bring family pride" | Meaning & Origin

faq.a: 鬼斧神工 (guǐ fǔ shén gōng) literally means "Ghostly axe, divine work" and metaphorically means "Supernatural craftsmanship". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 鬼斧神工 mean?

faq.a: 鬼斧神工 is pronounced as "guǐ fǔ shén gōng" in Mandarin Chinese.

gui-fu-shen-gong.origin: The Zhuangzi tells of the woodworker Qing, whose bell-stand was so fine that people said no human hand had made it. Asked his secret, he described fasting: after three days he no longer thought about reward or rank, after five about praise or blame, after seven he had forgotten he had a body and a court to serve. Only then did he go into the forest, look at the trees as they were, and see the finished stand standing in one of them; then he set his hand to it. Ghost (鬼) axe (斧) and spirit (神) work (工) is what the onlookers concluded. Craftsmanship, and natural formations that look designed.
gui-fu-shen-gong.title: 鬼斧神工 (gui fu shen gong) — "Supernatural craftsmanship" | Meaning & Origin

gui-gen-dao-di.origin: Returning (归) to the root (根) and getting to (到) the bottom (底). Both halves point downward, one botanical and one spatial, and the phrase is used to introduce a conclusion rather than to describe an investigation — it signals that everything said so far is about to be reduced to one thing. Chinese speakers use it as a discourse marker, roughly where English says 'at the end of the day', and what follows it is the speaker's actual position.
gui-gen-dao-di.title: 归根到底 (gui gen dao di) — "Fundamentally or in the final analysis" | Meaning & Origin

faq.a: 过河拆桥 (guò hé chāi qiáo) literally means "Cross river, dismantle bridge" and metaphorically means "Abandoning those who helped you". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 过河拆桥 mean?

faq.a: 过河拆桥 is pronounced as "guò hé chāi qiáo" in Mandarin Chinese.

faq.q: When is 过河拆桥 used?

guo-he-chai-qiao.origin: The History of Yuan records the abolition of the examinations. Xu Youren had argued against it and lost, and was then placed at the head of the officials made to kneel and hear the edict read — he had himself entered office through those examinations. As they rose, a censor said to him: the vice-councillor may be called a man who crosses (过) the river (河) and pulls down (拆) the bridge (桥). What the image supplies beyond ordinary ingratitude is the destruction. The bridge is not left behind but dismantled, so nobody follows and the crosser cannot go back — which is why it is most often said of institutions that shut the route they came in by.

guo-tai-min-an.origin: The state (国) in right order (泰) and the people (民) secure (安). 泰 is the Yijing hexagram of things standing in proper relation, heaven and earth in communication, so the first half claims order rather than mere quiet. The two halves are offered as a single outcome and not as a trade, which is the argument inside the phrase. It is the standard formula in blessings, on temple plaques and at new year, and it is what governments have always claimed to be delivering.
guo-tai-min-an.title: 国泰民安 (guo tai min an) — "National peace and public security" | Meaning & Origin

guo-you-bu-ji.origin: Zigong asked Confucius which of two disciples was the better; one went too far and one fell short. Asked whether going too far was therefore better, Confucius answered 过犹不及 — overshooting (过) is just like (犹) falling short (不及). The point is that they are the same kind of error, not that one is preferable. That is what the phrase claims, and it is aimed at overcorrection above all, where the reply to one excess is another.
guo-you-bu-ji.title: 过犹不及 (guo you bu ji) — "Moderation in all things" | Meaning & Origin

Investigations, lost files, and looking for one person in a large city.

hai-ku-shi-lan.meaning_metaphoric: Until the end of time; eternal love
hai-ku-shi-lan.origin: Seas (海) drying (枯) and stones (石) crumbling (烂). Both are chosen for being the slowest imaginable changes rather than impossible ones, which is where the scale comes from — this is deep time, not never. It lives inside oaths, in the form 海枯石烂不变心, unchanged until the seas dry and the stones crumble. Promises between lovers claim it almost exclusively, and it is old-fashioned enough now that saying it is usually a little self-aware.
hai-ku-shi-lan.title: 海枯石烂 (hai ku shi lan) — "Until the end of time; eternal love" | Meaning & Origin

Of conversation it means something closer to rambling — 聊得海阔天空 is talk that has gone everywhere and settled nowhere — and that second sense is at least as common in speech.

hai-na-bai-chuan.origin: The sea (海) takes in (纳) a hundred (百) rivers (川) and is still the sea — that is the whole argument, and it is why the image is the sea and not a lake. The line is Lin Zexu's, the first half of a couplet normally quoted whole: 海纳百川，有容乃大；壁立千仞，无欲则刚 — the sea admits a hundred rivers, and capacity is what makes it great; the cliff stands a thousand fathoms, and wanting nothing is what makes it unyielding. He wrote it in 1839, in the weeks before the opium seizures at Humen. The people it describes can absorb difference without losing their own shape.
hai-na-bai-chuan.title: 海纳百川 (hai na bai chuan) — "Accept all with open mind" | Meaning & Origin

hai-qun-zhi-ma.origin: In the Zhuangzi the Yellow Emperor, lost and asking a boy herding horses how to govern the empire, is told it is no different from tending horses: 去其害马者而已矣, remove whatever is harming (害) the horses (马), and nothing more. The 群 of the modern idiom is a later addition that reads the herd into it. The answer's force is in its brevity — the boy declines the grandeur of the question. The individual whose conduct is damaging a whole group.

han-dan-xue-bu.origin: The Zhuangzi asks whether you have not heard about the young man of Shouling who went to Handan (邯郸) to learn how they walked there (学步). He never acquired their gait, and lost his own along the way, and had to crawl home. That is the whole story and it is two lines long. The phrase describes imitation that costs the imitator what they already had, and it is sharper than simply copying badly — the loss is the point.
han-dan-xue-bu.title: 邯郸学步 (han dan xue bu) — "Lose abilities through misguided imitation" | Meaning & Origin

han-niu-chong-dong.meaning: So many books they cannot be housed
han-niu-chong-dong.meaning_metaphoric: So many books they cannot be housed
han-niu-chong-dong.origin: Books enough that the ox hauling them sweats (汗牛) and the house is filled to the rafters (充栋). Liu Zongyuan coined it in a memorial inscription, complaining about the sheer volume of commentary that had accumulated on a single classic — so the phrase began as a complaint, not a compliment. That edge is largely gone. Any enormous body of writing will do now, though a careful writer can still let the original exasperation show through.
han-niu-chong-dong.title: 汗牛充栋 (han niu chong dong) — "So many books they cannot be housed" | Meaning & Origin

han-xin-ru-ku.literal: Hold the acrid, swallow the bitter
han-xin-ru-ku.origin: 茹 is to swallow, and 辛 is pungent rather than bitter — the sharpness of ginger and pepper. So the phrase is about holding (含) something acrid in the mouth and swallowing (茹) something bitter (苦), which is a more physical image than English 'endure hardship'. Its usage is strongly gendered by custom: it attaches above all to mothers, and specifically to years of unremarked domestic effort on someone else's behalf. It is a phrase of gratitude, most often said too late.
han-xin-ru-ku.title: 含辛茹苦 (han xin ru ku) — "Persevere through adversity" | Meaning & Origin

hao-gao-wu-yuan.example_zh: 他的雄心壮志常常在现实面前让他失望。

faq.a: 好高骛远 (hào gāo wù yuǎn) literally means "Fond of high and distant goals" and metaphorically means "Unrealistic aspirations". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 好高骛远 mean?

hao-gao-wu-yuan.literal: Fond of high and distant goals
hao-gao-wu-yuan.origin: To be fond of (好) the high (高) and chase (骛) the distant (远). Song neo-Confucian writing uses it as a complaint about students who find the near and low beneath them and reach straight for the profound. 骛 is a horse galloping, and it carries the flavour of the whole phrase — not ambition but ambition that will not stay still long enough to do the groundwork. It is one of the most common criticisms in Chinese education, aimed at the person who wants the result without the sequence that produces it.
hao-gao-wu-yuan.title: 好高骛远 (hao gao wu yuan) — "Unrealistic aspirations" | Meaning & Origin

hao-hao-dang-dang.example_en: The reform movement swept through the industry like a mighty wave

faq.a: 浩浩荡荡 (hào hào dàng dàng) literally means "Vast mighty flow" and metaphorically means "Moving in overwhelming numbers". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 浩浩荡荡 mean?

faq.q: How do you pronounce 浩浩荡荡?

faq.q: When is 浩浩荡荡 used?

hao-hao-dang-dang.origin: Vast (浩浩) and sweeping (荡荡) — a doubling that Chinese uses for water in volume, and the Yueyang Tower essay applies a close variant to the lake stretching past any shore. The sound is doing much of the work, four syllables of open vowels that take a long time to say. It describes mass in motion: a river in flood, a procession, an army, a crowd. Applied to human affairs it carries a suggestion of inevitability, which is why official language is fond of it.
hao-hao-dang-dang.title: 浩浩荡荡 (hao hao dang dang) — "Moving in overwhelming numbers" | Meaning & Origin

hao-hao-xian-sheng.meaning: Person who agrees with everyone to avoid conflict
hao-hao-xian-sheng.meaning_metaphoric: Person who agrees with everyone to avoid conflict
hao-hao-xian-sheng.origin: Sima Hui of the late Han would not speak ill of anybody, and answered whatever he was told, good or terrible, with the word 'good' (好). A visitor came to tell him his own son had died; Sima Hui said 'very good.' His wife rounded on him — people confide in you because they think you have virtue, and you say 'good' when you hear a man's son is dead? To which he answered that her words too were very good. A 'Mr Good-Good' (好好先生) offends nobody and is of use to nobody. Somebody who agrees with everybody and will not take a position.
hao-hao-xian-sheng.title: 好好先生 (hao hao xian sheng) — "Person who agrees with everyone to avoid conflict" | Meaning & Origin

hao-shi-duo-mo.example_en: She faced numerous challenges before finally achieving her dream job.
hao-shi-duo-mo.example_zh: 她在实现梦想的过程中，好事多磨，经历了无数挑战。

faq.a: 好事多磨 (hǎo shì duō mó) literally means "Good things meet much grinding" and metaphorically means "Good things come with setbacks". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 好事多磨 mean?

faq.a: 好事多磨 is pronounced as "hǎo shì duō mó" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 好事多磨?

faq.a: 好事多磨 is used when She faced numerous challenges before finally achieving her dream job..
faq.q: When is 好事多磨 used?

hao-shi-duo-mo.origin: Good things (好事) meet much (多) grinding (磨). 磨 is the millstone, and the abrasion is the point: the phrase does not say good things are delayed but that they are worn against something on the way. Its natural home is romance and marriage, where Chinese uses it almost as a superstition — the courtship that keeps hitting obstacles is being tested rather than warned off. It is offered as consolation, and it implies the good thing is still coming.
hao-shi-duo-mo.title: 好事多磨 (hao shi duo mo) — "Good things come with setbacks" | Meaning & Origin

hao-wu-yi-wen.example_en: The evidence clearly established the defendant's innocence beyond any doubt
hao-wu-yi-wen.example_zh: 证据清楚地证明被告无罪，毫无疑问

faq.a: 毫无疑问 (háo wú yí wèn) literally means "Not slightest doubt" and metaphorically means "Absolutely certain without any doubt". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 毫无疑问 mean?

faq.a: 毫无疑问 is pronounced as "háo wú yí wèn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 毫无疑问?

faq.a: 毫无疑问 is used when The evidence clearly established the defendant's innocence beyond any doubt.
faq.q: When is 毫无疑问 used?

hao-wu-yi-wen.origin: Without (无) so much as a fine hair (毫) of doubt (疑问). 毫 is a real unit — the finest hair of an animal's winter coat, used in classical Chinese as the smallest measurable quantity, and it survives in 一丝一毫 and in 差之毫厘，谬以千里. Here it sets the threshold as low as the language can put it: not the smallest measurable doubt remains. The four-character phrase itself is modern rather than classical, with no source text behind it, and in use it functions less as a description than as a discourse marker — the Chinese equivalent of opening a sentence with the English phrase there is no question that.
hao-wu-yi-wen.title: 毫无疑问 (hao wu yi wen) — "Absolutely certain without any doubt" | Meaning & Origin

faq.q: What does 好逸恶劳 mean?

faq.a: 好逸恶劳 is used when The team's productivity suffered from members who avoided challenging tasks.
faq.q: When is 好逸恶劳 used?

hao-yi-wu-lao.origin: To love (好) ease (逸) and hate (恶) toil (劳). The two verbs are the point: this is not laziness as a failing of will but as a preference, something the phrase presents as the ordinary human default rather than a vice peculiar to the person being described. That makes it a diagnosis more than an insult. Arguments about incentives and education turn on it, the assumption being that effort has to be built against the grain rather than simply expected.
hao-yi-wu-lao.title: 好逸恶劳 (hao yi wu lao) — "Shirk effort by preference" | Meaning & Origin

he-fa-tong-yan.example_en: The 90-year-old professor maintained youthful energy despite his white hair

faq.a: 鹤发童颜 (hè fà tóng yán) literally means "Crane hair, child face" and metaphorically means "Youthful despite old age". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.

faq.q: When is 鹤发童颜 used?

he-fa-tong-yan.origin: Hair (发) white as a crane's (鹤) with the face (颜) of a child (童). Both halves are drawn from Daoist longevity literature, where the crane is a standard emblem of long life and the retained childlike complexion is what successful cultivation was supposed to produce. The phrase does not simply mean old and healthy. It describes a specific and slightly uncanny combination, and it is a warm compliment paid to the vigorous old — most often to a teacher or a doctor.
he-fa-tong-yan.title: 鹤发童颜 (he fa tong yan) — "Youthful despite old age" | Meaning & Origin

he-jia-huan-le.example_en: We ended our video call to Grandma with the usual wish: may the whole family be happy and together this year.
he-jia-huan-le.example_zh: 祝您新春快乐，阖家欢乐，身体健康！

faq.a: 阖家欢乐 (hé jiā huān lè) literally means "The whole family happy together" and metaphorically means "May your whole family be happy". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 阖家欢乐 mean?

faq.a: 阖家欢乐 is pronounced as "hé jiā huān lè" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 阖家欢乐?

faq.a: 阖家欢乐 is used when We ended our video call to Grandma with the usual wish: may the whole family be happy and together this year..

he-jia-huan-le.meaning: May your whole family be happy
he-jia-huan-le.meaning_metaphoric: May your whole family be happy
he-jia-huan-le.origin: A New Year wish for the whole household rather than one person. 阖 originally meant a door leaf and came to mean 'whole' or 'entire', so 阖家 is the entire family; 欢乐 means joy and happiness. There is no single classical source, but the phrase is old. It closes the Yuan-dynasty zaju play 《相国寺公孙合汗衫》, whose verdict verse announces 张员外阖家欢乐, 'the Zhang household is joyful once more,' and it recurs as a happy-ending formula in Ming and Qing novels. Because it addresses the family, it suits greetings to colleagues, clients or friends whose relatives you do not know well. It is often paired with 身体健康 or 万事如意, and in writing people sometimes use the homophone 合家欢乐.
he-jia-huan-le.title: 阖家欢乐 (he jia huan le) — "May your whole family be happy" | Meaning & Origin

he-li-ji-qun.origin: This one comes from the Shishuo Xinyu, on Ji Shao, of whom an onlooker said that seeing him in a crowd was like seeing a crane (鹤) standing (立) among chickens (鸡群). The remark was reported to his father's friend, who replied that the onlooker had never seen the father. The distinction it names is bearing rather than rank. Somebody conspicuously above the company they are standing in — and the compliment is to bearing rather than to rank.
he-li-ji-qun.title: 鹤立鸡群 (he li ji qun) — "Stand out from crowd" | Meaning & Origin

heng-xing-ba-dao.example_en: His arrogant attitude made him many enemies in the workplace.
heng-xing-ba-dao.example_zh: 他的横行霸道让他在职场上结下了许多敌人。
