faq.a: 天伦之乐 (tiān lún zhī lè) literally means "Heavenly family joy" and metaphorically means "Family happiness". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 天伦之乐 mean?

faq.a: 天伦之乐 is pronounced as "tiān lún zhī lè" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 天伦之乐?

faq.a: 天伦之乐 is used when The holiday season is a time for the joy of family reunion, where laughter and love fill the air..
faq.q: When is 天伦之乐 used?

tian-lun-zhi-le.origin: Li Bai wrote it in the preface to a spring night's drinking with his cousins in a garden of peach and plum blossom: the joys (乐) of natural relation (天伦), set out among the flowers, with the wine going round and the poems being made. 天伦 is the bond you did not choose — parents, siblings, children — as against relations built by agreement. That is what gives the phrase its warmth and also its limit. It describes the pleasure of family gathered and doing nothing in particular, and it is what Chinese reaches for at New Year.
tian-lun-zhi-le.title: 天伦之乐 (tian lun zhi le) — "Family happiness" | Meaning & Origin

tian-luo-di-wang.example_en: The police set up a dragnet to catch the fugitives.
tian-luo-di-wang.example_zh: 警方布下天罗地网抓捕逃犯。

faq.a: 天罗地网 (tiān luó dì wǎng) literally means "Nets of heaven and earth" and metaphorically means "Inescapable net; dragnet". It belongs to the Strategy & Action category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 天罗地网 mean?

faq.a: 天罗地网 is pronounced as "tiān luó dì wǎng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 天罗地网?

faq.a: 天罗地网 is used when The police set up a dragnet to catch the fugitives..
faq.q: When is 天罗地网 used?

tian-luo-di-wang.origin: A net (罗) over heaven (天) and a net (网) across earth (地). Two different words for a net are used, one for catching birds and one for fish, so the pair covers the air and the ground and the phrase leaves no medium unaccounted for. That completeness is the claim. Manhunts and surveillance, from the perspective of whoever set the nets — a fugitive is caught in one, never described as having laid it.
tian-luo-di-wang.title: 天罗地网 (tian luo di wang) — "Inescapable net; dragnet" | Meaning & Origin

tian-ma-xing-kong.example_en: His imagination knows no bounds, creating worlds that captivate everyone.
tian-ma-xing-kong.example_zh: 他的想象力无穷无尽，创造出迷住每一个人的世界。

faq.a: 天马行空 (tiān mǎ xíng kōng) literally means "Heavenly horse crossing the sky" and metaphorically means "Unrestrained creativity". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 天马行空 mean?

faq.a: 天马行空 is pronounced as "tiān mǎ xíng kōng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 天马行空?

faq.a: 天马行空 is used when His imagination knows no bounds, creating worlds that captivate everyone..
faq.q: When is 天马行空 used?

tian-ma-xing-kong.origin: Han China imported horses from the far west and wrote about them extravagantly, as celestial creatures that sweated blood and could cover impossible distances; a heavenly horse (天马) moving through empty sky (行空) is that reputation taken to its limit. Later critics borrowed the image for writing that goes where it likes without harness. The phrase carries both readings still. Applied to imagination it is admiring, and applied to an argument or a plan it usually means that nothing in it is attached to the ground.
tian-ma-xing-kong.title: 天马行空 (tian ma xing kong) — "Unrestrained creativity" | Meaning & Origin

tian-wai-you-tian.example_en: The champion was talented, but he knew there were even better players out there
tian-wai-you-tian.example_zh: 这位冠军很有天赋，但他知道还有更厉害的选手

faq.a: 天外有天 (tiān wài yǒu tiān) literally means "Skies beyond skies" and metaphorically means "Always someone better". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 天外有天 mean?

faq.a: 天外有天 is pronounced as "tiān wài yǒu tiān" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 天外有天?

faq.a: 天外有天 is used when The champion was talented, but he knew there were even better players out there.
faq.q: When is 天外有天 used?

tian-wai-you-tian.origin: Beyond (外) the sky (天) there is another sky (天). It travels as half of a pair — 天外有天，人外有人, and beyond any person there is another person — and the second clause is what the first is for. The construction is deliberately recursive: no matter which sky you have reached, the sentence can be applied again. Its job is to puncture complacency, and it is most often said to somebody who has just won something.
tian-wai-you-tian.title: 天外有天 (tian wai you tian) — "Always someone better" | Meaning & Origin

tian-xia-wu-nan-shi.example_en: With determination and hard work, he believes that nothing is impossible.
tian-xia-wu-nan-shi.example_zh: 他相信，只要努力，就天下无难事。

faq.a: 天下无难事 (tiān xià wú nán shì) literally means "Nothing in the world is difficult" and metaphorically means "Perseverance conquers all". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 天下无难事 mean?

faq.a: 天下无难事 is pronounced as "tiān xià wú nán shì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 天下无难事?

faq.a: 天下无难事 is used when With determination and hard work, he believes that nothing is impossible..
faq.q: When is 天下无难事 used?

tian-xia-wu-nan-shi.literal: Nothing in the world is difficult
tian-xia-wu-nan-shi.origin: The idiom 天下无难事 (tiān xià wú nán shì) is commonly used in classical Chinese literature to express the idea that nothing in the world is inherently difficult if one is determined to overcome it. The full expression is 天下无难事，只怕有心人, which translates to 'Nothing in the world is difficult, only afraid of those with determination.' This idiom emphasizes the power of human will and perseverance in overcoming obstacles. It first appeared in the Ming dynasty work 《韩夫人题红记·花阴私祝》 by Wang Jide and gained popularity through its inclusion in the Qing dynasty novel 《红楼梦》 (Dream of the Red Chamber) by Cao Xueqin. The idiom is often used in motivational contexts to encourage persistence and resolve in the face of challenges.
tian-xia-wu-nan-shi.title: 天下无难事 (tian xia wu nan shi) — "Perseverance conquers all" | Meaning & Origin

tian-ya-hai-jiao.example_en: They traveled to the farthest reaches of the world in search of adventure.
tian-ya-hai-jiao.example_zh: 他们走遍天涯海角，寻找冒险。

faq.a: 天涯海角 (tiān yá hǎi jiǎo) literally means "Sky's edge, sea's corner" and metaphorically means "Distant separation". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 天涯海角 mean?

faq.a: 天涯海角 is pronounced as "tiān yá hǎi jiǎo" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 天涯海角?

faq.a: 天涯海角 is used when They traveled to the farthest reaches of the world in search of adventure..
faq.q: When is 天涯海角 used?

tian-ya-hai-jiao.origin: The edge (涯) of the sky and the corner (角) of the sea. Han Yu's lament for his dead nephew has the source of the sentiment — one of us at heaven's edge, one at earth's corner — and the phrase names the farthest place there is. Two uses dominate: separation, where it measures how far apart people are, and commitment, in promises to follow someone anywhere. There is also a real cape on Hainan called 天涯海角, which is where Chinese tourists go to stand at the end of the world.
tian-ya-hai-jiao.title: 天涯海角 (tian ya hai jiao) — "Distant separation" | Meaning & Origin

tian-yi-wu-feng.example_en: The integration of the two companies was so perfect no operational disruptions occurred
tian-yi-wu-feng.example_zh: 两家公司的整合如此完美，没有发生任何运营中断

faq.a: 天衣无缝 (tiān yī wú fèng) literally means "Heavenly garment without seams" and metaphorically means "Flawless and perfectly seamless". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 天衣无缝 mean?

faq.a: 天衣无缝 is pronounced as "tiān yī wú fèng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 天衣无缝?

faq.a: 天衣无缝 is used when The integration of the two companies was so perfect no operational disruptions occurred.
faq.q: When is 天衣无缝 used?

tian-yi-wu-feng.origin: This is from a Tang tale in which a man meets a weaver girl from heaven and notices that her robe (天衣) has no (无) seam (缝) anywhere; asked about it, she explains that heavenly clothes are not made with needle and thread. The perfection is not fine workmanship but the absence of joins altogether. A plan or an argument with no visible join anywhere for an opponent to get at.
tian-yi-wu-feng.title: 天衣无缝 (tian yi wu feng) — "Flawless and perfectly seamless" | Meaning & Origin

tie-chu-cheng-zhen.example_en: Through years of practice, the amateur artist became a master
tie-chu-cheng-zhen.example_zh: 通过多年练习，这位业余艺术家成为了大师

faq.a: 铁杵成针 (tiě chǔ chéng zhēn) literally means "Iron rod becomes needle" and metaphorically means "Success through persistence". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 铁杵成针 mean?

faq.a: 铁杵成针 is pronounced as "tiě chǔ chéng zhēn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 铁杵成针?

faq.a: 铁杵成针 is used when Through years of practice, the amateur artist became a master.
faq.q: When is 铁杵成针 used?

tie-chu-cheng-zhen.origin: Li Bai, the story goes, had given up on his studies and was walking away when he met an old woman grinding down an iron pestle (铁杵). Asked what she was doing, she said she was making a needle (针). He went back to his books. The tale is attached to a stream near Meizhou and is told mainly to children, which suits it. It is normally quoted with the conditional that carries the whole argument: 只要功夫深，铁杵磨成针 — given deep enough effort, an iron pestle is ground into a needle.
tie-chu-cheng-zhen.title: 铁杵成针 (tie chu cheng zhen) — "Success through persistence" | Meaning & Origin

tie-zheng-ru-shan.example_en: The prosecution presented overwhelming evidence against the defendant.
tie-zheng-ru-shan.example_zh: 控方提出了铁证如山的证据。

faq.a: 铁证如山 (tiě zhèng rú shān) literally means "Iron evidence like a mountain" and metaphorically means "Irrefutable evidence; conclusive proof". It belongs to the Strategy & Action category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 铁证如山 mean?

faq.a: 铁证如山 is pronounced as "tiě zhèng rú shān" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 铁证如山?

faq.a: 铁证如山 is used when The prosecution presented overwhelming evidence against the defendant..
faq.q: When is 铁证如山 used?

tie-zheng-ru-shan.origin: Proof (证) as iron (铁), immovable as a mountain (如山). The two comparisons are doing different work: iron for what cannot be bent, the mountain for what cannot be shifted or overlooked. Together they claim that the evidence is both sound and unavoidable. The phrase belongs to legal and journalistic language and is stronger than anything English uses casually — it is asserted about a case already made, not about evidence still being weighed.
tie-zheng-ru-shan.title: 铁证如山 (tie zheng ru shan) — "Irrefutable evidence; conclusive proof" | Meaning & Origin

tong-bing-xiang-lian.example_en: Having experienced similar losses, they truly understood each other.
tong-bing-xiang-lian.example_zh: 经历过类似的失去，他们同病相怜。

faq.a: 同病相怜 (tóng bìng xiāng lián) literally means "Same illness mutually sympathize" and metaphorically means "Sympathize with those sharing similar troubles". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 同病相怜 mean?

faq.a: 同病相怜 is pronounced as "tóng bìng xiāng lián" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 同病相怜?

faq.a: 同病相怜 is used when Having experienced similar losses, they truly understood each other..
faq.q: When is 同病相怜 used?

tong-bing-xiang-lian.meaning: Sympathize with those sharing similar troubles
tong-bing-xiang-lian.meaning_metaphoric: Sympathize with those sharing similar troubles
tong-bing-xiang-lian.origin: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue gives it to Wu Zixu, explaining why he had taken in another exile from Chu whose family had also been destroyed: those with the same affliction (同病) pity one another (相怜), those with the same anxiety help one another. The sequel is worth knowing — the man he sheltered later helped bring about his death. Chinese still uses the phrase warmly, for the solidarity that comes from shared trouble, though the source is unusually clear-eyed about its limits.
tong-bing-xiang-lian.title: 同病相怜 (tong bing xiang lian) — "Sympathize with those sharing similar troubles" | Meaning & Origin

tong-gai-qian-fei.example_en: After the incident, he resolved to completely change his ways.
tong-gai-qian-fei.example_zh: 事件之后，他决心痛改前非。

faq.a: 痛改前非 (tòng gǎi qián fēi) literally means "Thoroughly change past wrongs" and metaphorically means "Sincerely repent and reform". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 痛改前非 mean?

faq.a: 痛改前非 is pronounced as "tòng gǎi qián fēi" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 痛改前非?

faq.a: 痛改前非 is used when After the incident, he resolved to completely change his ways..
faq.q: When is 痛改前非 used?

tong-gai-qian-fei.origin: To change (改) former (前) wrongs (非) thoroughly (痛). 痛 is the trap for learners: it is not 'painfully' here but 'completely, right through' — the same sense as in 痛击 and 痛快 — and dictionaries warn specifically against reading pain into it. What the phrase demands is therefore the extent of the reform rather than its emotional cost: not some of the conduct amended, but all of it, and not provisionally. It belongs to formal contexts, to apologies and to accounts of somebody's return from a bad period, and it cannot be used lightly about a small correction.
tong-gai-qian-fei.title: 痛改前非 (tong gai qian fei) — "Sincerely repent and reform" | Meaning & Origin

tong-qiang-tie-bi.example_en: Their defenses were so strong that no enemy could breach them.
tong-qiang-tie-bi.example_zh: 他们的防御如铜墙铁壁，敌人无法攻破。

faq.a: 铜墙铁壁 (tóng qiáng tiě bì) literally means "Copper wall iron wall" and metaphorically means "Impenetrable defense". It belongs to the Strategy & Action category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 铜墙铁壁 mean?

faq.a: 铜墙铁壁 is pronounced as "tóng qiáng tiě bì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 铜墙铁壁?

faq.a: 铜墙铁壁 is used when Their defenses were so strong that no enemy could breach them..
faq.q: When is 铜墙铁壁 used?

tong-qiang-tie-bi.origin: Walls (墙) of bronze (铜) and ramparts (壁) of iron (铁). The phrase belongs to vernacular fiction and describes fortification that cannot be breached. What is worth noticing is how readily Chinese moves it off physical defences: it is used of an alibi with no hole in it, of a bureaucracy that cannot be got past, and — most commonly in modern political language — of a population described as an unbreachable wall, where the metal is people rather than masonry.
tong-qiang-tie-bi.title: 铜墙铁壁 (tong qiang tie bi) — "Impenetrable defense" | Meaning & Origin

tong-sou-wu-qi.example_en: The shop is known for its honesty, treating everyone fairly.
tong-sou-wu-qi.example_zh: 这家店童叟无欺，所有顾客都能得到公正的对待。

faq.a: 童叟无欺 (tóng sǒu wú qī) literally means "No deception of young or old" and metaphorically means "Honest business practices". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 童叟无欺 mean?

faq.a: 童叟无欺 is pronounced as "tóng sǒu wú qī" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 童叟无欺?

faq.a: 童叟无欺 is used when The shop is known for its honesty, treating everyone fairly..
faq.q: When is 童叟无欺 used?

tong-sou-wu-qi.literal: No deception of young or old
tong-sou-wu-qi.origin: A shop sign before it was an idiom, and still most at home painted on one: neither children (童) nor the old (叟) are cheated (无欺). The pairing names the two customers easiest to short-change, one too inexperienced to check and one assumed unable to, so honesty toward them is offered as proof of honesty toward everyone. It is a merchant's claim about himself, which gives it a faint period flavour in modern use, and Chinese speakers deploy it half-ironically about anyone insisting a little too firmly on their own fairness.
tong-sou-wu-qi.title: 童叟无欺 (tong sou wu qi) — "Honest business practices" | Meaning & Origin

tong-xiao-da-dan.example_en: The medical team worked continuously until they stabilized all emergency patients
tong-xiao-da-dan.example_zh: 医疗团队连续工作，直到所有急诊患者病情稳定

faq.a: 通宵达旦 (tōng xiāo dá dàn) literally means "Through night reach dawn" and metaphorically means "Work through the entire night". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 通宵达旦 mean?

faq.a: 通宵达旦 is pronounced as "tōng xiāo dá dàn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 通宵达旦?

faq.a: 通宵达旦 is used when The medical team worked continuously until they stabilized all emergency patients.
faq.q: When is 通宵达旦 used?

tong-xiao-da-dan.origin: Through (通) the night (宵) and reaching (达) daybreak (旦). 旦 is a picture of the sun above the horizon line, so the phrase names its own endpoint: the work stops when the light comes, not when it is finished. That is the difference between this and simply working late. Examination cramming, emergency response, deadlines — and it carries neither approval nor criticism, only the fact that the night was not slept.
tong-xiao-da-dan.title: 通宵达旦 (tong xiao da dan) — "Work through the entire night" | Meaning & Origin

tong-zhou-gong-ji.example_en: The community united to help those affected by the disaster
tong-zhou-gong-ji.example_zh: 社区团结起来帮助受灾群众

faq.a: 同舟共济 (tóng zhōu gòng jì) literally means "Cross river in same boat" and metaphorically means "Face challenges together". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 同舟共济 mean?

faq.a: 同舟共济 is pronounced as "tóng zhōu gòng jì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 同舟共济?

faq.a: 同舟共济 is used when The community united to help those affected by the disaster.
faq.q: When is 同舟共济 used?

tong-zhou-gong-ji.origin: This idiom shares deep connections with China's river-centric civilization, where crossing (济) together (共) in the same boat (同舟) was often a matter of life and death. Ancient texts tell of strangers becoming allies when facing treacherous waters, especially along the mighty Yangtze. During the Three Kingdoms period, multiple accounts describe opposing armies cooperating to navigate dangerous rapids. The imagery powerfully conveys mutual dependence and collective survival. Modern applications extend to corporate partnerships, international cooperation on global challenges, and community resilience during crises. The idiom emphasizes that differences become secondary when facing shared challenges – whether environmental disasters, economic hardships, or social upheavals.
tong-zhou-gong-ji.title: 同舟共济 (tong zhou gong ji) — "Face challenges together" | Meaning & Origin

tou-liang-huan-zhu.example_en: The investigation revealed that key data had been subtly altered
tou-liang-huan-zhu.example_zh: 调查显示关键数据被巧妙地篡改了

faq.a: 偷梁换柱 (tōu liáng huàn zhù) literally means "Steal beam swap pillar" and metaphorically means "Deceive by substitution". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 偷梁换柱 mean?

faq.a: 偷梁换柱 is pronounced as "tōu liáng huàn zhù" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 偷梁换柱?

faq.a: 偷梁换柱 is used when The investigation revealed that key data had been subtly altered.
faq.q: When is 偷梁换柱 used?

tou-liang-huan-zhu.origin: This is the twenty-fifth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems: stealing (偷) the beams (梁) and swapping (换) the pillars (柱) while the building still stands. The substitution is made inside a structure that keeps its outward form, so that nothing appears to have changed until weight is put on it. A quiet swap of something load-bearing behind a surface that still looks right — and the discovery always comes late.
tou-liang-huan-zhu.title: 偷梁换柱 (tou liang huan zhu) — "Deceive by substitution" | Meaning & Origin

tou-shu-ji-qi.example_en: In negotiations, he was cautious, knowing that aggressive tactics could backfire.

tou-shu-ji-qi.origin: Jia Yi, arguing that senior officials should not be punished like common criminals, quoted a village proverb: you want to throw something at the rat (投鼠) but you think of the vessel (忌器) it is sitting beside. The Book of Han preserves the argument. The phrase names the specific paralysis of having a clear target that cannot be struck without breaking something valuable next to it, and it is used of hostage situations, of dismissing an executive with client relationships, and of any strike whose collateral is the real constraint.
tou-shu-ji-qi.title: 投鼠忌器 (tou shu ji qi) — "Held back from striking by fear of collateral damage" | Meaning & Origin

tou-tou-shi-dao.origin: A Chan expression before it was anything else, meaning that the Way (道) is present at every point (头头) — wherever you put your hand down, that is it. Secularised, it describes speech in which every part connects to every other and the whole thing hangs together. The compliment is about structure rather than truth, and that is the catch: Chinese quite often uses 说得头头是道 of someone whose reasoning is beautifully organised and whose conclusion is wrong.
tou-tou-shi-dao.title: 头头是道 (tou tou shi dao) — "Logical and organized" | Meaning & Origin

tu-si-gou-peng.meaning: Discard allies once they are useless
tu-si-gou-peng.meaning_metaphoric: Discard allies once they are useless
tu-si-gou-peng.origin: Fan Li, having helped Goujian of Yue destroy Wu, left at once and wrote to his colleague Wen Zhong telling him to do the same: 飞鸟尽，良弓藏；狡兔死，走狗烹 — when the birds are gone the good bow is put away, when the cunning hares are dead the running hounds are cooked. Goujian, he warned, was a man to share hardship with but not ease. Wen Zhong stayed and was ordered to kill himself. Han Xin quoted the same lines at his own arrest centuries later. The other half, 鸟尽弓藏, is used interchangeably.
tu-si-gou-peng.title: 兔死狗烹 (tu si gou peng) — "Discard allies once they are useless" | Meaning & Origin

faq.q: When is 退避三舍 used?

tui-bi-san-she.origin: Chong'er of Jin, sheltering in Chu as an exile, was asked what he would give in return and answered that if the two states ever met in battle he would withdraw three stages (退避三舍). A 舍 was a day's march, thirty li. Years later, as Duke Wen, he was facing Chu at Chengpu and did exactly that — and the withdrawal drew the Chu army out of position and into the defeat that followed. The Zuo Zhuan tells it. The phrase means yielding ground on purpose, and the story is careful that the yielding was also the tactic.
tui-bi-san-she.title: 退避三舍 (tui bi san she) — "Make concessions to avoid conflict" | Meaning & Origin

tui-bo-zhu-lan.literal: Push the waves, raise the billows
tui-bo-zhu-lan.origin: To push (推) the waves (波) and help (助) the swell (澜). Wang Tong uses it alongside a second image, letting the wind loose to stop a fire, and both describe intervening in a way that adds to what is already moving. The phrase says nothing about who started it: the force being amplified was there first, and the person named merely fed it. Media coverage, speculation, and anyone whose contribution made a developing situation worse.
tui-bo-zhu-lan.title: 推波助澜 (tui bo zhu lan) — "Amplifying existing trends or momentum" | Meaning & Origin

faq.a: 推陈出新 (tuī chén chū xīn) literally means "Push old produce new" and metaphorically means "Create new from old". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 推陈出新 mean?

faq.a: 推陈出新 is pronounced as "tuī chén chū xīn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 推陈出新?

faq.a: 推陈出新 is used when The designer combined traditional elements with modern technology.
faq.q: When is 推陈出新 used?

tui-chen-chu-xin.origin: Pushing out (推) the stale (陈) so that the new (新) can come forth (出). The early sense is physical, used of the body and of stored grain long before it meant anything about art or policy: clearing what has gone old to make room. That history settles what the phrase does not mean. The old is displaced by the new arriving, not cleared away in advance to make space for it, and Chinese therefore uses it of reform that grows out of existing practice — approving in a way that its words for wholesale replacement are not.
tui-chen-chu-xin.title: 推陈出新 (tui chen chu xin) — "Create new from old" | Meaning & Origin

tui-xin-zhi-fu.example_en: They had a heart-to-heart talk about their concerns.
tui-xin-zhi-fu.example_zh: 他们推心置腹地谈论了彼此的担忧。

faq.a: 推心置腹 (tuī xīn zhì fù) literally means "Push heart, place in belly" and metaphorically means "Speak from the heart; confide completely". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 推心置腹 mean?

faq.a: 推心置腹 is used when They had a heart-to-heart talk about their concerns..
faq.q: When is 推心置腹 used?

tui-xin-zhi-fu.meaning: Speak from the heart; confide completely
tui-xin-zhi-fu.meaning_metaphoric: Speak from the heart; confide completely
tui-xin-zhi-fu.origin: Liu Xiu, then still King of Xiao and not yet Emperor Guangwu, had taken the surrender of a large force that remained uneasy about its position. He rode out through the ranks on light horse to inspect them, and the surrendered men said to one another that he 推赤心置人腹中, pushed his own red heart into other men's bellies — so how could they not throw their lives away for him? The idiom keeps the gesture: pushing out (推) the heart (心) and setting it (置) inside somebody else (腹). What it describes is trust extended first and without security, which is why it is a leader's phrase. The conversation in which one side deliberately goes first.
tui-xin-zhi-fu.title: 推心置腹 (tui xin zhi fu) — "Speak from the heart; confide completely" | Meaning & Origin

tuo-shou-ke-de.example_en: The promotion seemed like a prize just waiting to be claimed.
tuo-shou-ke-de.example_zh: 这个晋升机会唾手可得。

faq.a: 唾手可得 (tuò shǒu kě dé) literally means "Spit on the palms and it can be had" and metaphorically means "Easily attainable". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 唾手可得 mean?

faq.a: 唾手可得 is pronounced as "tuò shǒu kě dé" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 唾手可得?

faq.a: 唾手可得 is used when The promotion seemed like a prize just waiting to be claimed..
faq.q: When is 唾手可得 used?

tuo-shou-ke-de.literal: Spit on the palms and it can be had
tuo-shou-ke-de.origin: 唾手 is spitting on the palms, the gesture a labourer makes before taking hold of a handle — so the phrase is not about spit but about the moment just before gripping. What can be had (可得) at that point takes no more effort than closing the hand. The Later Han histories put it in the mouth of an over-confident commander. It carries that flavour still: Chinese often uses it of something described as easy by the person who has not yet had to do it.
tuo-shou-ke-de.title: 唾手可得 (tuo shou ke de) — "Easily attainable" | Meaning & Origin

tuo-ying-er-chu.example_en: Among hundreds of applicants, she stood out from the crowd.

faq.a: 脱颖而出 (tuō yǐng ér chū) literally means "Tip of awl emerges from bag" and metaphorically means "Stand out; distinguish oneself". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 脱颖而出 mean?

faq.a: 脱颖而出 is pronounced as "tuō yǐng ér chū" in Mandarin Chinese.

faq.a: 脱颖而出 is used when Among hundreds of applicants, she stood out from the crowd..
faq.q: When is 脱颖而出 used?

tuo-ying-er-chu.literal: Tip of awl emerges from bag
tuo-ying-er-chu.origin: The Lord of Pingyuan used the awl to dismiss Mao Sui: a man of ability in the world is like an awl in a bag, and its point shows at once — three years, and nothing has been heard of you. Mao Sui turned it round. Had he been put in the bag earlier, he said, the whole blade would have come through (颖脱而出), not merely the tip. The Records of the Grand Historian keeps both halves, and the idiom is built from Mao Sui's reply rather than from the original jibe.
tuo-ying-er-chu.title: 脱颖而出 (tuo ying er chu) — "Stand out; distinguish oneself" | Meaning & Origin

faq.q: What does 完璧归赵 mean?

faq.q: How do you pronounce 完璧归赵?

faq.q: When is 完璧归赵 used?

wan-bi-gui-zhao.origin: Qin offered fifteen cities for Zhao's famous jade disc, and everyone understood the cities would never be handed over. Lin Xiangru carried the jade (璧) to Qin, watched the king pass it round his court without a word about payment, and said there was a flaw he would point out — got it back into his own hands, stood against a pillar and promised to shatter it and his own skull together. While Qin stalled, he had the jade smuggled back to Zhao (赵) whole (完), and offered his own life instead. The Records of the Grand Historian tells it. He was not killed, and he had returned (归) it intact.
wan-bi-gui-zhao.title: 完璧归赵 (wan bi gui zhao) — "Return something perfect" | Meaning & Origin

wan-ma-ben-teng.example_en: After the announcement, the stock market surged with unprecedented trading volume

faq.a: 万马奔腾 (wàn mǎ bēn téng) literally means "Ten thousand horses galloping" and metaphorically means "Powerful unstoppable momentum". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 万马奔腾 mean?

faq.a: 万马奔腾 is pronounced as "wàn mǎ bēn téng" in Mandarin Chinese.

faq.q: When is 万马奔腾 used?

wan-ma-ben-teng.origin: Ten thousand (万) horses (马) at full gallop (奔腾). Chinese uses 万 as an intensifier rather than a count, and what the image supplies beyond mere numbers is the ground noise — a mass of animals moving as one thing, felt before it is seen. Poets applied it to rivers in flood and to surf. Modern usage is mostly figurative and often official, describing an economy or a national effort, and it always implies collective momentum rather than individual speed.
wan-ma-ben-teng.title: 万马奔腾 (wan ma ben teng) — "Powerful unstoppable momentum" | Meaning & Origin

wan-shi-ru-yi.example_en: Happy New Year — may everything go just the way you wish.

faq.q: What does 万事如意 mean?

faq.a: 万事如意 is pronounced as "wàn shì rú yì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 万事如意?

faq.a: 万事如意 is used when Happy New Year — may everything go just the way you wish..
faq.q: When is 万事如意 used?

wan-shi-ru-yi.literal: Ten thousand things as you wish
wan-shi-ru-yi.meaning: May everything go the way you want
wan-shi-ru-yi.meaning_metaphoric: May everything go the way you want
wan-shi-ru-yi.origin: Probably the most-used Chinese New Year wish of all. 万事 is 'ten thousand matters', meaning everything, and 如意 means 'as one wishes' — the same 如意 as the ruyi sceptre, a curved ornamental object given as a token of good fortune. A well-known early appearance is in Dream of the Red Chamber (《红楼梦》, chapter 53), inside a New Year letter of greetings from an estate steward to the Jia family: 'a great and happy spring, honour and peace, promotion and prosperity, and all things as you wish' (新春大喜大福，荣贵平安，加官进禄，万事如意). The line is already a New Year greeting, three centuries ago. Use it at the end of almost any greeting, to anyone.
wan-shi-ru-yi.title: 万事如意 (wàn shì rú yì) — "May Everything Go Your Way" | Chinese New Year Greeting

wan-wu-yi-shi.example_en: The plan was designed to be absolutely foolproof.

faq.a: 万无一失 (wàn wú yī shī) literally means "Ten thousand without one failure" and metaphorically means "Absolutely sure; foolproof". It belongs to the Strategy & Action category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 万无一失 mean?

faq.a: 万无一失 is pronounced as "wàn wú yī shī" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 万无一失?

faq.a: 万无一失 is used when The plan was designed to be absolutely foolproof..
faq.q: When is 万无一失 used?

wan-wu-yi-shi.origin: Ten thousand (万) and not (无) one (一) miss (失). 万 is the standard Chinese figure for an uncountable number rather than a literal count, so what the phrase claims is a rate rather than a record. That makes it a statement about design: the thing has been arranged so that failure has no route in. Preparations and plans, very often in the negative or under pressure: 万无一失 is what a superior demands rather than what an engineer volunteers.
wan-wu-yi-shi.title: 万无一失 (wan wu yi shi) — "Absolutely sure; foolproof" | Meaning & Origin

wan-xiang-geng-xin.example_en: The first morning of the new year felt like a fresh start, as if everything around us had been renewed.
wan-xiang-geng-xin.example_zh: 一元复始，万象更新，愿新的一年一切顺利。

faq.a: 万象更新 (wàn xiàng gēng xīn) literally means "Ten thousand scenes all renewed" and metaphorically means "Everything starts fresh with the new year". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 万象更新 mean?

faq.a: 万象更新 is pronounced as "wàn xiàng gēng xīn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 万象更新?

faq.a: 万象更新 is used when The first morning of the new year felt like a fresh start, as if everything around us had been renewed..
faq.q: When is 万象更新 used?

wan-xiang-geng-xin.meaning: Everything starts fresh with the new year
wan-xiang-geng-xin.meaning_metaphoric: Everything starts fresh with the new year
wan-xiang-geng-xin.origin: A phrase for the fresh start of a new year or a new spring. 万象 is 'ten thousand phenomena', everything in view, and 更新 means to renew. It is best known in the New Year couplet 一元复始，万象更新, 'the first day returns, and everything is renewed.' Some online sources credit the phrase to 《红楼梦》, but it could not be found in the novel's text, so treat that claim with caution. One verified older use is in the Ming physician Zhang Jiebin's (张介宾) 《类经》, a commentary on the Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic, where he glosses the lines on the three months of spring with the note 万象更新也, 'all things are renewed.' That link to spring suits the Spring Festival well. Use it in speeches, cards and New Year messages that look forward to a new start.
wan-xiang-geng-xin.title: 万象更新 (wan xiang geng xin) — "Everything starts fresh with the new year" | Meaning & Origin

wan-zi-qian-hong.example_en: The garden in spring is a riot of colors, showcasing nature's beauty.
wan-zi-qian-hong.example_zh: 春天的花园里万紫千红，展示了大自然的美丽。

faq.a: 万紫千红 (wàn zǐ qiān hóng) literally means "Ten thousand purples, thousand reds" and metaphorically means "Diverse and flourishing". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 万紫千红 mean?

faq.a: 万紫千红 is pronounced as "wàn zǐ qiān hóng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 万紫千红?

faq.a: 万紫千红 is used when The garden in spring is a riot of colors, showcasing nature's beauty..
faq.q: When is 万紫千红 used?

wan-zi-qian-hong.origin: Zhu Xi's poem on a spring day ends with the line: once you know the face of the east wind, the ten thousand purples (万紫) and thousand reds (千红) are all of them spring. The image is a hillside in flower, and the argument is that the variety is one thing underneath. That double sense survives in use. The phrase describes profusion and diversity together, and it goes to gardens, to festivals and, in official language, to a cultural scene doing well.
wan-zi-qian-hong.title: 万紫千红 (wan zi qian hong) — "Diverse and flourishing" | Meaning & Origin

wang-chuan-qiu-shui.example_en: She waited at the station, gazing through autumn waters for his return.
wang-chuan-qiu-shui.example_zh: 她在车站望穿秋水，等待他的归来。

faq.a: 望穿秋水 (wàng chuān qiū shuǐ) literally means "Gazing through autumn waters" and metaphorically means "To eagerly await someone or something". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 望穿秋水 mean?

faq.a: 望穿秋水 is pronounced as "wàng chuān qiū shuǐ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 望穿秋水?

faq.a: 望穿秋水 is used when She waited at the station, gazing through autumn waters for his return..
faq.q: When is 望穿秋水 used?

wang-chuan-qiu-shui.meaning: To eagerly await someone or something
wang-chuan-qiu-shui.meaning_metaphoric: To eagerly await someone or something
wang-chuan-qiu-shui.origin: This descends from drama and verse of the Yuan and after, where autumn water (秋水) is a standing figure for clear bright eyes. To look until the autumn waters are worn through (望穿) is to watch for someone so long and so hard that the eyes themselves give out. The hyperbole is about duration, and the one waiting is always the one who cannot act. Longing for somebody's arrival with exhausting intensity.
wang-chuan-qiu-shui.title: 望穿秋水 (wang chuan qiu shui) — "To eagerly await someone or something" | Meaning & Origin

wang-en-fu-yi.example_en: He forgot all the help he received and acted selfishly, showing his true colors.
wang-en-fu-yi.example_zh: 他忘恩负义，完全不记得曾经的帮助。

faq.a: 忘恩负义 (wàng ēn fù yì) literally means "Forget kindness betray loyalty" and metaphorically means "Ungrateful betrayal". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 忘恩负义 mean?

faq.a: 忘恩负义 is pronounced as "wàng ēn fù yì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 忘恩负义?

faq.a: 忘恩负义 is used when He forgot all the help he received and acted selfishly, showing his true colors..
faq.q: When is 忘恩负义 used?

wang-en-fu-yi.origin: Forget (忘) the kindness (恩) and turn your back on (负) what is owed (义). 义 is the load-bearing character: not loyalty as sentiment but obligation as a moral fact, the thing a person owes whether or not they feel like it. That is why the phrase bites. It charges someone not with coldness but with breaking a real debt, and Chinese treats it as among the more serious things you can say about a person's character, well beyond ordinary rudeness or neglect.
wang-en-fu-yi.title: 忘恩负义 (wang en fu yi) — "Ungrateful betrayal" | Meaning & Origin

wang-hu-suo-yi.example_en: He was so engrossed in the concert that he lost track of time.
wang-hu-suo-yi.example_zh: 他陶醉于音乐会中，忘乎所以，完全忘记了时间。

faq.a: 忘乎所以 (wàng hū suǒ yǐ) literally means "Forget one's place" and metaphorically means "Carried away by success". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.

It belongs to vernacular fiction and describes a specific failure: not arrogance in general but the temporary kind produced by a success, elation or flattery, in which someone's sense of proportion goes missing for an evening. People who have just been promoted, praised in public, or allowed to talk for too long.

Every mouth in the ranks began to water, and on that they reached the next source. The New Account of Tales of the World files the story under Deceptions, which is the right heading: the plums were not there, and the saliva was. What it names is relief supplied by anticipation alone, and the tone is dry.

The physical imagery of looking up at someone so far ahead that you can only see their back emerged from scholarly traditions where disciples would literally follow behind their teachers. Today, it's used to describe the experience of admiring someone's achievements while acknowledging the significant gap in skills or accomplishments, particularly relevant in professional mentorship and personal development contexts.

wang-yang-bu-lao.origin: The Strategies of the Warring States gives it to the minister Zhuang Xin, speaking to the King of Chu after part of the kingdom has already been lost: seeing the hare and turning to call the hound is not too late, and mending (补) the pen (牢) after losing (亡) the sheep (羊) is not too late either — 亡羊补牢，未为迟也. Modern speech usually completes it as 亡羊补牢，为时未晚. The proverb concedes the loss and refuses to treat it as final, and it urges fixing the fault that caused it rather than dwelling on what is gone.

wang-yang-de-niu.literal: Lose a sheep, gain an ox
wang-yang-de-niu.meaning: A small loss that yields a greater gain
wang-yang-de-niu.meaning_metaphoric: A small loss that yields a greater gain
wang-yang-de-niu.origin: From 《淮南子·说山训》: to lose (亡) a sheep (羊) and gain (得) an ox (牛) is a loss no one would refuse. The phrase is the optimistic twin of the far better-known 亡羊补牢, and it makes a different argument — not that damage can be repaired, but that a loss can be the price of something larger, and that the accounting only makes sense once you can see both sides of it. It is a useful thing to say to someone still grieving the sheep, and a dangerous thing to say too early, before the ox has actually arrived.
wang-yang-de-niu.title: 亡羊得牛 (wang yang de niu) — "A small loss that yields a greater gain" | Meaning & Origin

faq.q: When is 望洋兴叹 used?

wang-yang-xing-tan.literal: Look up in awe and sigh
wang-yang-xing-tan.origin: In the Zhuangzi, the Lord of the Yellow River, proud of his swollen autumn flood, travels east until he reaches the North Sea and can find no end to it. He turns his face about and 望洋向若而叹 — looks up in awe (望洋) toward Ruo, the sea god, and sighs (叹). The idiom adds 兴, to raise or set going, so the modern form is raising (兴) that sigh. 望洋 is a binome for gazing upward, not the two characters read separately, which is the trap: there is no ocean in it. The sigh is not defeat but the moment his sense of his own scale collapses. Recognising that something is past your reach is the whole of it, and there is more humility in that than despair.
wang-yang-xing-tan.title: 望洋兴叹 (wang yang xing tan) — "Feel overwhelmed by greatness" | Meaning & Origin

wang-zi-fei-bo.origin: Zhuge Liang, in the memorial written before his first northern campaign, tells the young Liu Shan not to 妄自菲薄 — not to belittle (菲薄) himself (自) without cause (妄) — and not to reach for improper analogies, since either would close off the path of honest advice. The context is worth keeping: it is addressed to somebody who had real authority and was not using it. 妄 is the load-bearing character, marking the self-deprecation as unwarranted rather than modest, and Chinese still uses the phrase to tell somebody their humility has turned into a way of not trying.
wang-zi-fei-bo.title: 妄自菲薄 (wang zi fei bo) — "Underestimate oneself; excessive self-deprecation" | Meaning & Origin

wang-zi-zun-da.meaning: Be conceited; have an inflated ego
wang-zi-zun-da.meaning_metaphoric: Be conceited; have an inflated ego
wang-zi-zun-da.origin: Ma Yuan, sent to take the measure of the warlord Gongsun Shu, came back and reported that the man was a frog at the bottom of a well who nonetheless made himself out to be honoured and great (尊大) without cause (妄). The judgement became the phrase, and it sits exactly opposite 妄自菲薄 — the same 妄自 construction marking a self-assessment as unwarranted, with the error running the other way. A person or an institution whose sense of its own standing is not shared by anybody outside it.
wang-zi-zun-da.title: 妄自尊大 (wang zi zun da) — "Be conceited; have an inflated ego" | Meaning & Origin

wei-bian-san-jue.origin: Books in Confucius's day were bamboo slips strung together with leather (韦) thongs. The Records of the Grand Historian says that in his later years he so loved the Book of Changes that the thongs binding (编) his copy wore through and snapped (绝) three (三) separate times, and that he remarked he would master the book if granted a few more years. The image is precise about what devotion looked like before paper: not a note in a margin but a volume physically destroyed by rereading. It is reserved for study pursued to that depth, and stays closer to high praise than to an everyday compliment.
wei-bian-san-jue.title: 韦编三绝 (wei bian san jue) — "Diligent, repeated study" | Meaning & Origin

wei-bu-xian-zhi.origin: 卜 is divination by heat-cracked bone and shell, the oldest recorded Chinese writing system's original purpose. To know (知) first (先) without having divined (未卜) is therefore to reach the answer without the apparatus. The phrase comes from Yuan drama and is usually light in tone — it is what you say to someone who guessed correctly, or, in the negative, to disclaim any special insight: 我又不是未卜先知, I'm not a fortune-teller.
wei-bu-xian-zhi.title: 未卜先知 (wei bu xian zhi) — "Foresight or intuition" | Meaning & Origin

The construction sets a threshold — there is an amount below which a thing does not merit mention — and puts the subject under it. That gives the phrase two quite separate lives. Said of one's own contribution it is the standard modest deflection of thanks; said of somebody else's it is dismissive to the point of rudeness. Chinese speakers use the first constantly and the second with care.
wei-bu-zu-dao.title: 微不足道 (wei bu zu dao) — "Too slight to weigh at all" | Meaning & Origin

faq.a: 围而不攻 is pronounced as "wéi ér bù gōng" in Mandarin Chinese.

wei-er-bu-gong.origin: To surround (围) and yet (而) not (不) attack (攻). The tactic is old and the logic is set out in Sun Zi, which rates taking a state whole above breaking it and warns the commander to leave a besieged army an apparent way out rather than corner it into fighting to the death — encirclement works by pressure, supply and time, and an assault throws that advantage away. The four-character phrase itself is a plain military description rather than a classical set idiom, and modern Chinese uses it mostly by analogy: keeping a rival boxed in, or holding a position of strength without forcing a confrontation you would win more cheaply by waiting.
wei-er-bu-gong.title: 围而不攻 (wei er bu gong) — "Strategic patience" | Meaning & Origin

faq.q: What does 唯利是图 mean?

faq.q: How do you pronounce 唯利是图?

faq.a: 唯利是图 is used when In business, he is known for his ruthless pursuit of profit above all else..

wei-li-shi-tu.origin: The Zuo Zhuan gives the phrase as 唯利是视, only profit is looked to, and it is Qin's own oath quoted back at it: Chu reported to Jin that Qin had sworn that whatever it did with Jin it would look only to advantage, and Jin's envoy Lü Xiang read the oath out in the formal denunciation that broke the alliance. The grammar repays attention: 唯…是… is a classical construction that pulls the object in front of the verb for emphasis, so the literal shape is only (唯) profit (利) is what is sought (图), with 是 a grammatical marker rather than the verb to be. It is a hard-edged accusation in modern Chinese, standard in criticism of companies and of people who have priced a friendship.
wei-li-shi-tu.title: 唯利是图 (wei li shi tu) — "Selfish pursuit of gain" | Meaning & Origin

wei-wei-jiu-zhao.meaning: Relieve pressure by attacking the source
wei-wei-jiu-zhao.meaning_metaphoric: Relieve pressure by attacking the source
wei-wei-jiu-zhao.origin: When Wei besieged the Zhao capital in 354 BCE, Qi sent an army under Tian Ji, and Sun Bin argued against marching to Zhao's relief at all: strike at Wei's own capital, and the Wei army will have to come home. It did — 魏果去邯郸 — and Qi met it in the field at Guiling and broke it. Besieging (围) Wei (魏) to rescue (救) Zhao (赵) became the second of the Thirty-Six Stratagems and the standard name for relieving pressure by threatening what an opponent cannot afford to leave undefended. The insight is that a besieger is weak precisely because they are committed somewhere else.
wei-wei-jiu-zhao.title: 围魏救赵 (wei wei jiu zhao) — "Relieve pressure by attacking the source" | Meaning & Origin

wei-yu-chou-mou.literal: Mend the windows before it rains
wei-yu-chou-mou.origin: This one comes from the Book of Songs, where a bird strips mulberry roots to bind (绸缪) its window and door before (未) the rain (雨) comes. The bird is speaking after already losing its young, which gives the image its urgency: preparation is described by something that has learned the hard way. Note it is the Book of Songs, not the Book of Changes. Precautions taken while there is still time to take them, with the note of hard experience still attached.
wei-yu-chou-mou.title: 未雨绸缪 (wei yu chou mou) — "Prepare before problems arise" | Meaning & Origin

The 点 is the dot a writer made to strike out an error, so the claim is that there were none to make. It praises writing that came out finished, which is a claim about the draft rather than about the result, and it is the compliment paid to somebody who does not appear to revise.
wen-bu-jia-dian.title: 文不加点 (wen bu jia dian) — "Perfect execution without revision" | Meaning & Origin

wen-cao-sheng-quan.meaning: Have victory in the bag; be certain to win
wen-cao-sheng-quan.meaning_metaphoric: Have victory in the bag; be certain to win
wen-cao-sheng-quan.origin: A 券 was a tally — a contract split in two so that each party held half, and holding your half was the proof of your claim. To grip (操) the winning (胜) half securely (稳) is therefore not confidence but documentation: what the phrase asserts is that the outcome has already been established and the remaining play is a formality. Elections, negotiations and matches, and it is a strong claim, which is why it turns up so often in accounts of somebody who turned out to be wrong.
wen-cao-sheng-quan.title: 稳操胜券 (wen cao sheng quan) — "Have victory in the bag; be certain to win" | Meaning & Origin

wen-gu-zhi-xin.origin: Confucius, in the Analects: 温故而知新，可以为师矣 — one who warms (温) the old (故) and thereby knows (知) the new (新) is fit to be a teacher. 温 is the word for reheating food, so the image is of returning to what you already have rather than acquiring more. The claim is specific and quite demanding: review alone is not enough, and the test is whether something new comes out of it. The final clause is why the phrase belongs to teaching, and it is usually left off in modern use.
wen-gu-zhi-xin.title: 温故知新 (wen gu zhi xin) — "Learn new through studying old" | Meaning & Origin

wen-guo-ze-xi.example_en: A good leader welcomes constructive criticism.
wen-guo-ze-xi.example_zh: 好的领导者闻过则喜，欢迎建设性批评。

faq.a: 闻过则喜 (wén guò zé xǐ) literally means "Hear faults, then rejoice" and metaphorically means "Welcome criticism; embrace feedback". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 闻过则喜 mean?

faq.a: 闻过则喜 is pronounced as "wén guò zé xǐ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 闻过则喜?

faq.a: 闻过则喜 is used when A good leader welcomes constructive criticism..
faq.q: When is 闻过则喜 used?

wen-guo-ze-xi.origin: The Mencius says of Zilu that when people told him he had a fault (过), he was glad (喜) — 人告之以有过则喜. The 闻 of the four-character form is the hearing of it, and the fault being heard about is one's own, which is the whole difficulty. Mencius sets him at the bottom of a short ascending series: Zilu welcomed correction, Yu the Great bowed when he heard a good word, and Shun went further than either. Being pleased to be corrected is treated as an achievement rather than a temperament. Somebody who takes criticism as information rather than as an attack, which is rare enough to be worth remarking on.
wen-guo-ze-xi.title: 闻过则喜 (wen guo ze xi) — "Welcome criticism; embrace feedback" | Meaning & Origin

wen-ji-qi-wu.example_en: She practiced piano every morning before dawn to master her craft
wen-ji-qi-wu.example_zh: 她每天黎明前练习钢琴以精进技艺

faq.a: 闻鸡起舞 (wén jī qǐ wǔ) literally means "Hear the rooster, rise and drill the sword" and metaphorically means "Practice with determination". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 闻鸡起舞 mean?

faq.a: 闻鸡起舞 is pronounced as "wén jī qǐ wǔ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 闻鸡起舞?

faq.a: 闻鸡起舞 is used when She practiced piano every morning before dawn to master her craft.
faq.q: When is 闻鸡起舞 used?

wen-ji-qi-wu.literal: Hear the rooster, rise and drill the sword
wen-ji-qi-wu.origin: Zu Ti and Liu Kun shared a bed as junior officials and shared an ambition to see the north recovered. The History of the Jin records that in the middle of the night Zu Ti heard (闻) a cock (鸡) crowing out of hours — an omen ordinarily counted unlucky — kicked Liu Kun awake and said this is not an evil sound. They got up (起) and drilled with their swords (舞) in the dark. The phrase is used of self-imposed discipline begun before anyone is watching, and both men went on to command armies.
wen-ji-qi-wu.title: 闻鸡起舞 (wen ji qi wu) — "Practice with determination" | Meaning & Origin

wen-jing-zhi-jiao.example_en: They pledged loyalty to each other through thick and thin.
wen-jing-zhi-jiao.example_zh: 他们是刎颈之交，发誓同甘共苦。

faq.a: 刎颈之交 (wěn jǐng zhī jiāo) literally means "Friendship of severed necks" and metaphorically means "Be sworn friends; absolute loyalty". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 刎颈之交 mean?

faq.a: 刎颈之交 is pronounced as "wěn jǐng zhī jiāo" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 刎颈之交?

faq.a: 刎颈之交 is used when They pledged loyalty to each other through thick and thin..
faq.q: When is 刎颈之交 used?

wen-jing-zhi-jiao.origin: Lian Po, a general, had been publicly slighting Lin Xiangru, a courtier promoted over him; Lin kept out of his way, explaining that Zhao survived because the two of them both existed and that a quarrel would finish it. Lian Po came to his gate carrying a rod and asked to be beaten with it. They became 刎颈之交 — friends (交) who would give the throat (刎颈) for one another. What the phrase claims is not affection but a bond in which the other's life outweighs one's own, and it is reserved accordingly.
wen-jing-zhi-jiao.title: 刎颈之交 (wen jing zhi jiao) — "Be sworn friends; absolute loyalty" | Meaning & Origin

wen-xin-wu-kui.example_en: She felt a sense of peace knowing she had acted with integrity in the situation.
wen-xin-wu-kui.example_zh: 她心里问心无愧，知道自己在这个问题上做得很对。

faq.a: 问心无愧 (wèn xīn wú kuì) literally means "Ask heart without guilt" and metaphorically means "Clear conscience". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 问心无愧 mean?

faq.a: 问心无愧 is pronounced as "wèn xīn wú kuì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 问心无愧?

faq.a: 问心无愧 is used when She felt a sense of peace knowing she had acted with integrity in the situation..
faq.q: When is 问心无愧 used?

wen-xin-wu-kui.origin: To ask (问) the heart (心) and find nothing to be ashamed of (无愧). The construction places the tribunal inside the person, which is the whole point: the phrase is used precisely when external judgement has gone against you, and it asserts a standard that the verdict did not reach. After a loss, an accusation or a decision that cost something — closer to a defence than a boast.
wen-xin-wu-kui.title: 问心无愧 (wen xin wu kui) — "Clear conscience" | Meaning & Origin

wen-zha-wen-da.example_en: The company grew through careful, steady expansion.
wen-zha-wen-da.example_zh: 公司稳扎稳打，稳步扩张。

faq.a: 稳扎稳打 (wěn zhā wěn dǎ) literally means "Stable camp, stable attack" and metaphorically means "Proceed steadily; consolidate before advancing". It belongs to the Strategy & Action category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 稳扎稳打 mean?

faq.a: 稳扎稳打 is pronounced as "wěn zhā wěn dǎ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 稳扎稳打?

faq.a: 稳扎稳打 is used when The company grew through careful, steady expansion..
faq.q: When is 稳扎稳打 used?

wen-zha-wen-da.origin: Pitching camp (扎) firmly (稳) and striking (打) firmly (稳). The doubled 稳 is the whole instruction: both the halting and the advancing are to be done from a secure position, so no ground is taken that could not be held if the next move failed. It is the same thinking as 步步为营 with the emphasis on soundness rather than on pace. Business expansion, study plans, and anybody being told — usually kindly — to stop trying to skip ahead.
wen-zha-wen-da.title: 稳扎稳打 (wen zha wen da) — "Proceed steadily; consolidate before advancing" | Meaning & Origin

wen-zhi-bin-bin.example_en: His eloquent speech and polished demeanor impressed everyone at the gala.
wen-zhi-bin-bin.example_zh: 他在晚会上文质彬彬的演讲给大家留下了深刻的印象。

faq.a: 文质彬彬 (wén zhì bīn bīn) literally means "Polish and substance evenly matched" and metaphorically means "Balanced character". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 文质彬彬 mean?

faq.a: 文质彬彬 is pronounced as "wén zhì bīn bīn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 文质彬彬?

faq.a: 文质彬彬 is used when His eloquent speech and polished demeanor impressed everyone at the gala..
faq.q: When is 文质彬彬 used?

wen-zhi-bin-bin.origin: Confucius set two things against each other in the Analects: 质, raw substance, and 文, cultivation and polish. Substance overrunning polish gives you a boor; polish overrunning substance gives you a clerk. Only when the two are 彬彬 — evenly matched, neither showing through the other — is there a gentleman. The phrase has drifted somewhat in modern use, where it tends to describe a scholarly, mild-mannered appearance, and the balance Confucius insisted on is often reduced to just the polished half.
wen-zhi-bin-bin.title: 文质彬彬 (wen zhi bin bin) — "Balanced character" | Meaning & Origin

wo-hu-cang-long.example_en: This quiet neighborhood is full of hidden talent — a true case of crouching tiger, hidden dragon.
wo-hu-cang-long.example_zh: 江湖里卧虎藏龙，人心里何尝不是？

faq.a: 卧虎藏龙 (wò hǔ cáng lóng) literally means "Crouching tiger, hidden dragon" and metaphorically means "Hidden talents or extraordinary people in an unassuming place". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 卧虎藏龙 mean?

faq.a: 卧虎藏龙 is pronounced as "wò hǔ cáng lóng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 卧虎藏龙?

faq.a: 卧虎藏龙 is used when This quiet neighborhood is full of hidden talent — a true case of crouching tiger, hidden dragon..
faq.q: When is 卧虎藏龙 used?

wo-hu-cang-long.meaning: Hidden talents or extraordinary people in an unassuming place
wo-hu-cang-long.meaning_metaphoric: Hidden talents or extraordinary people in an unassuming place
wo-hu-cang-long.origin: Yu Xin of the Northern Zhou wrote 暗石疑藏虎，盘根似卧龙 — dark stones seem to hide tigers, gnarled roots resemble a reclining dragon — and the halves were later compressed into one phrase: a crouching (卧) tiger (虎), a hidden (藏) dragon (龙). It names a place where formidable people are present and unrecognised, which is how Zhuge Liang is remembered before Liu Bei found him living on Wolong Hill. Ang Lee's 2000 film took the title, and the pun is in the names: Yu Jiaolong (玉娇龙) carries the dragon and Lo Xiaohu (罗小虎) the tiger. An organisation or a small town whose people turn out to be far more capable than the surface suggests.
wo-hu-cang-long.title: 卧虎藏龙 (wo hu cang long) — "Hidden talents or extraordinary people in an unassuming place" | Meaning & Origin

wo-xin-chang-dan.example_en: After losing the championship, the athlete trained with extraordinary dedication for years to finally win
wo-xin-chang-dan.example_zh: 失去冠军后，这位运动员多年来以非凡的奉献精神训练，最终获胜

faq.a: 卧薪尝胆 (wò xīn cháng dǎn) literally means "Sleep on firewood, taste gall" and metaphorically means "Endure hardship for future success". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 卧薪尝胆 mean?

faq.a: 卧薪尝胆 is pronounced as "wò xīn cháng dǎn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 卧薪尝胆?

faq.a: 卧薪尝胆 is used when After losing the championship, the athlete trained with extraordinary dedication for years to finally win.
faq.q: When is 卧薪尝胆 used?

wo-xin-chang-dan.origin: Goujian of Yue, beaten and made to serve Fuchai of Wu, was let home and set about not forgetting it. The Records of the Grand Historian describes what he did: he hung a gall bladder (胆) where he sat, and looked up at it whenever he sat or lay down, and tasted (尝) it before every meal. The brushwood is not in that account — 卧薪, sleeping (卧) on firewood (薪), attached itself to the story later, and the four characters together first turn up in a Song essay of Su Shi's, written in the voice of Sun Quan. Goujian did destroy Wu, twenty years on.
wo-xin-chang-dan.title: 卧薪尝胆 (wo xin chang dan) — "Endure hardship for future success" | Meaning & Origin

wu-bian-wu-ji.example_en: The ocean stretched out before us, vast and limitless, inviting exploration.
wu-bian-wu-ji.example_zh: 大海无边无际，令人感到渺小而敬畏。

faq.a: 无边无际 (wú biān wú jì) literally means "Boundless and limitless" and metaphorically means "Vast beyond any limit". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 无边无际 mean?

faq.a: 无边无际 is pronounced as "wú biān wú jì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 无边无际?

faq.a: 无边无际 is used when The ocean stretched out before us, vast and limitless, inviting exploration..
faq.q: When is 无边无际 used?

wu-bian-wu-ji.origin: Without (无) edge (边), without (无) boundary (际). Chinese doubles the negation for scale, and the two nouns are not synonyms — 边 is the rim of a thing and 际 is where two things meet — so between them they deny both the object's own limit and any point at which something else begins. Oceans, deserts and night skies, and figuratively anything unmeasurable, from grief to possibility.
wu-bian-wu-ji.title: 无边无际 (wu bian wu ji) — "Vast beyond any limit" | Meaning & Origin

wu-di-zi-rong.example_en: The public exposure left him feeling deeply ashamed.
wu-di-zi-rong.example_zh: 公开曝光让他无地自容。

faq.a: 无地自容 (wú dì zì róng) literally means "No ground to contain oneself" and metaphorically means "Extremely ashamed; wish to disappear". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 无地自容 mean?

faq.a: 无地自容 is pronounced as "wú dì zì róng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 无地自容?

faq.a: 无地自容 is used when The public exposure left him feeling deeply ashamed..
faq.q: When is 无地自容 used?

wu-di-zi-rong.origin: No (无) ground (地) in which to put (容) oneself (自). 容 is to hold or contain, so the image is of the earth declining to make room: there is nowhere to stand that is out of view. That is more specific than embarrassment — what the phrase describes is shame with an audience, the exposure being the intolerable part. Public humiliation, and somebody caught in a thing they had denied; it is strong enough to be rarely used lightly.
wu-di-zi-rong.title: 无地自容 (wu di zi rong) — "Extremely ashamed; wish to disappear" | Meaning & Origin

wu-dong-yu-zhong.example_en: He remained unmoved by all the emotional appeals.
wu-dong-yu-zhong.example_zh: 面对所有情感诉求，他无动于衷。

faq.a: 无动于衷 (wú dòng yú zhōng) literally means "No movement in the heart" and metaphorically means "Unmoved; indifferent". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 无动于衷 mean?

faq.a: 无动于衷 is pronounced as "wú dòng yú zhōng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 无动于衷?

faq.a: 无动于衷 is used when He remained unmoved by all the emotional appeals..
faq.q: When is 无动于衷 used?

wu-dong-yu-zhong.origin: No (无) movement (动) in (于) what is innermost (衷). 衷 is specifically the inside of a person, the part not on display, so the phrase reports an absence at a depth the observer cannot actually see — which is why it is always an inference and sometimes an unjust one. Chinese uses it far more often as a criticism than as praise: the situation called for a reaction and none came. Composure is available as a reading, but it is not the one anybody reaches for first.
wu-dong-yu-zhong.title: 无动于衷 (wu dong yu zhong) — "Unmoved; indifferent" | Meaning & Origin

wu-du-you-ou.example_en: Many people share similar experiences, proving that we are not alone in our struggles.
wu-du-you-ou.example_zh: 在这个问题上，无独有偶，很多人都有相似的经历。

faq.a: 无独有偶 (wú dú yǒu ǒu) literally means "Not alone but in pairs" and metaphorically means "Unexpected similarity". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 无独有偶 mean?

faq.a: 无独有偶 is pronounced as "wú dú yǒu ǒu" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 无独有偶?

faq.a: 无独有偶 is used when Many people share similar experiences, proving that we are not alone in our struggles..
faq.q: When is 无独有偶 used?

wu-du-you-ou.origin: Not (无) single (独) but having (有) a counterpart (偶). What makes it worth learning is the tone, which learners consistently get wrong. It is not a neutral word for coincidence: Chinese uses it when the second instance makes the first one worse, revealing that what looked like a one-off is a pattern. A second embezzlement, a second identical complaint, a second company doing the same thing. It introduces the second item and implies there may be more.
wu-du-you-ou.title: 无独有偶 (wu du you ou) — "Unexpected similarity" | Meaning & Origin

wu-fu-lin-men.example_en: May all five blessings arrive at your door this New Year.
wu-fu-lin-men.example_zh: 大年初一，家家户户门上都贴着“五福临门”的春联。

faq.a: 五福临门 (wǔ fú lín mén) literally means "Five blessings arrive at the door" and metaphorically means "May every kind of good fortune come to your home". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 五福临门 mean?

faq.a: 五福临门 is pronounced as "wǔ fú lín mén" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 五福临门?

faq.a: 五福临门 is used when May all five blessings arrive at your door this New Year..
faq.q: When is 五福临门 used?

wu-fu-lin-men.literal: Five blessings arrive at the door
wu-fu-lin-men.meaning: May every kind of good fortune come to your home
wu-fu-lin-men.meaning_metaphoric: May every kind of good fortune come to your home
wu-fu-lin-men.origin: The five blessings come from the Book of Documents. The 'Great Plan' chapter (《尚书·洪范》) lists them: 'The five blessings: first, long life; second, wealth; third, health and peace; fourth, love of virtue; fifth, a natural death at the end of a full life' (五福：一曰寿，二曰富，三曰康宁，四曰攸好德，五曰考终命). The four-character phrase itself is a later folk formula with no single classical source; 临门 means 'arriving at the gate'. A late-Qing story collection, 《俗话倾谈》, observes that people commonly write 五福临门 over their doorways and explains the five from the classic. In everyday use the list is often replaced by a looser five, such as good fortune, official salary, longevity, joy and wealth (福禄寿喜财). It is above all a phrase for doors and couplets, and a generous wish for a whole household.
wu-fu-lin-men.title: 五福临门 (wu fu lin men) — "May every kind of good fortune come to your home" | Meaning & Origin

wu-gu-feng-deng.example_en: The village New Year banner wished everyone a bumper harvest in the coming year.
wu-gu-feng-deng.example_zh: 祝大家新的一年风调雨顺，五谷丰登！

faq.a: 五谷丰登 (wǔ gǔ fēng dēng) literally means "The five grains ripen in abundance" and metaphorically means "May the year bring abundance". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 五谷丰登 mean?

faq.a: 五谷丰登 is pronounced as "wǔ gǔ fēng dēng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 五谷丰登?

faq.a: 五谷丰登 is used when The village New Year banner wished everyone a bumper harvest in the coming year..
faq.q: When is 五谷丰登 used?

wu-gu-feng-deng.literal: The five grains ripen in abundance
wu-gu-feng-deng.origin: 五谷 is 'the five grains', a traditional term for all staple crops (lists vary, but usually include millet, rice, wheat and beans), 丰 is 'abundant' and 登 here means 'to ripen' or 'be harvested'. The phrase means a good harvest of every crop. The idea is old: the strategy text 《六韬》 speaks of seasonable wind and rain bringing 五谷丰熟, 'the five grains ripen in abundance'. The exact wording 五谷丰登 appears in later fiction, including Journey to the West (《西游记》, chapter 44). In a farming society a good harvest meant a good year, so it became a standard New Year wish, often paired with 风调雨顺 (favourable wind and rain) on couplets and village gates. Today it is used as a general wish for abundance, and fits greetings to families, communities and anyone with rural roots.
wu-gu-feng-deng.title: 五谷丰登 (wu gu feng deng) — "May the year bring abundance" | Meaning & Origin

wu-hua-ba-men.example_en: The market offers a bewildering variety of products.
wu-hua-ba-men.example_zh: 市场上的产品五花八门，令人眼花缭乱。

faq.a: 五花八门 (wǔ huā bā mén) literally means "Five flowers and eight gates" and metaphorically means "A bewildering variety; all kinds of". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 五花八门 mean?

faq.a: 五花八门 is pronounced as "wǔ huā bā mén" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 五花八门?

faq.a: 五花八门 is used when The market offers a bewildering variety of products..
faq.q: When is 五花八门 used?

wu-hua-ba-men.meaning: A bewildering variety; all kinds of
wu-hua-ba-men.meaning_metaphoric: A bewildering variety; all kinds of
wu-hua-ba-men.origin: This idiom has roots in ancient Chinese military strategy, where 'five flowers' (五花) referred to five tactical formations and 'eight gates' (八门) to eight strategic positions. The phrase originally described the complexity of battlefield tactics. Over time, it evolved to describe any diverse or varied collection. Some scholars also trace it to the five-element theory and eight trigrams of Chinese philosophy. In modern usage, it describes a wide variety of things, often with a connotation of being overwhelming or confusingly diverse.
wu-hua-ba-men.title: 五花八门 (wu hua ba men) — "A bewildering variety; all kinds of" | Meaning & Origin

wu-ji-bi-fan.example_en: After the market peaked, a correction was inevitable
wu-ji-bi-fan.example_zh: 市场达到顶峰后，调整是不可避免的
