yin-guo-bao-ying.meaning: Good and evil deeds repaid in kind
yin-guo-bao-ying.meaning_metaphoric: Good and evil deeds repaid in kind
yin-guo-bao-ying.origin: Cause (因), effect (果), and the returning repayment (报应). The vocabulary is Buddhist and entered Chinese with the translated sutras, bringing with it a moral mechanics quite different from the older Chinese idea of heaven's mandate: consequence here is impersonal, exact, and not necessarily settled within one lifetime. That last part is what the ordinary Chinese use has dropped. Today it usually means simply that what someone did has caught up with them, and it is said with satisfaction more often than with piety.
yin-guo-bao-ying.title: 因果报应 (yin guo bao ying) — "Good and evil deeds repaid in kind" | Meaning & Origin

yin-huo-de-fu.example_en: Sometimes, setbacks can lead to unexpected opportunities.
yin-huo-de-fu.example_zh: 有时候，挫折能带来意想不到的机会。

faq.a: 因祸得福 (yīn huò dé fú) literally means "Gain fortune from misfortune" and metaphorically means "Benefit from adversity". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 因祸得福 mean?

faq.a: 因祸得福 is pronounced as "yīn huò dé fú" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 因祸得福?

faq.a: 因祸得福 is used when Sometimes, setbacks can lead to unexpected opportunities..
faq.q: When is 因祸得福 used?

yin-huo-de-fu.origin: The thought is a commonplace of Warring States argument — that the same event is a disaster or a windfall depending on where you are standing in time, and that a skilled person converts one into the other. Chinese has a fuller story for it in 塞翁失马, the old man whose lost horse, returned horse, and injured son each reverse the previous judgement. This phrase is the compressed version: by way of (因) misfortune (祸) one obtains (得) blessing (福). It is normally said in retrospect, about a setback that turned out to have opened something, and it is the standard consolation offered to someone who has just lost a job.
yin-huo-de-fu.title: 因祸得福 (yin huo de fu) — "Benefit from adversity" | Meaning & Origin

yin-huo-shao-shen.example_en: His questionable business practices eventually led to his downfall
yin-huo-shao-shen.example_zh: 他不当的商业行为最终导致了自己的垮台

faq.a: 引火烧身 (yǐn huǒ shāo shēn) literally means "Draw fire burn self" and metaphorically means "Bring trouble upon oneself". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 引火烧身 mean?

faq.a: 引火烧身 is pronounced as "yǐn huǒ shāo shēn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 引火烧身?

faq.a: 引火烧身 is used when His questionable business practices eventually led to his downfall.
faq.q: When is 引火烧身 used?

yin-huo-shao-shen.origin: To draw (引) the fire (火) and have it burn (烧) yourself (身). The phrase describes an action aimed outward that returns on the person who took it, and Chinese distinguishes it carefully from simple bad luck: the fire was fetched deliberately. It has a second and quite different use in political language, where 引火烧身 means volunteering yourself for criticism — inviting the fire onto your own head in order to start a discussion that otherwise would not happen.
yin-huo-shao-shen.title: 引火烧身 (yin huo shao shen) — "Bring trouble upon oneself" | Meaning & Origin

yin-shui-si-yuan.example_en: After achieving success, she created a scholarship at her old school
yin-shui-si-yuan.example_zh: 在成功之后，她在母校设立了奖学金

faq.a: 饮水思源 (yǐn shuǐ sī yuán) literally means "Drink water think source" and metaphorically means "Remember your roots". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 饮水思源 mean?

faq.a: 饮水思源 is pronounced as "yǐn shuǐ sī yuán" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 饮水思源?

faq.a: 饮水思源 is used when After achieving success, she created a scholarship at her old school.
faq.q: When is 饮水思源 used?

yin-shui-si-yuan.origin: Yu Xin, writing in the sixth century, put it as 落其实者思其树，饮其流者怀其源 — who eats the fruit thinks of the tree, who drinks from the stream remembers its source. The four-character form keeps the second half: drink (饮) the water (水), think (思) of the source (源). It concerns debts owed rather than gratitude in the abstract, and in practice it is aimed at people who have arrived somewhere and stopped mentioning how. Teachers, parents, the place somebody came from — usually invoked at the exact moment when forgetting would be most convenient.
yin-shui-si-yuan.title: 饮水思源 (yin shui si yuan) — "Remember your roots" | Meaning & Origin

yin-zhen-zhi-ke.example_en: Choosing to ignore the problem may provide temporary relief, but it ultimately leads to greater consequences.
yin-zhen-zhi-ke.example_zh: 选择忽视问题可能会带来暂时的缓解，但最终会导致更大的后果。

faq.a: 饮鸩止渴 (yǐn zhèn zhǐ kě) literally means "Drink poison to quench thirst" and metaphorically means "Short-sighted solution". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 饮鸩止渴 mean?

faq.a: 饮鸩止渴 is pronounced as "yǐn zhèn zhǐ kě" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 饮鸩止渴?

faq.a: 饮鸩止渴 is used when Choosing to ignore the problem may provide temporary relief, but it ultimately leads to greater consequences..
faq.q: When is 饮鸩止渴 used?

yin-zhen-zhi-ke.origin: The 鸩 is a poisonous bird of legend whose feathers, steeped in wine, made a reliable and untraceable method of murder. Huo Xu, defending his uncle against a capital charge, argued to the authorities that no man would do what was alleged, since it would be like drinking (饮) that wine to stop (止) thirst (渴) — relief for a moment, death immediately after. The History of the Later Han preserves the plea. The phrase describes a remedy whose cost is larger than the problem, and it is standard in Chinese discussion of debt.
yin-zhen-zhi-ke.title: 饮鸩止渴 (yin zhen zhi ke) — "Short-sighted solution" | Meaning & Origin

ying-jie-bu-xia.example_en: The sudden influx of customers left the staff overwhelmed.
ying-jie-bu-xia.example_zh: 突然涌入的顾客让员工应接不暇。

faq.a: 应接不暇 (yìng jiē bù xiá) literally means "Responding and receiving without leisure" and metaphorically means "More to take in than one can keep up with". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 应接不暇 mean?

faq.a: 应接不暇 is pronounced as "yìng jiē bù xiá" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 应接不暇?

faq.a: 应接不暇 is used when The sudden influx of customers left the staff overwhelmed..
faq.q: When is 应接不暇 used?

ying-jie-bu-xia.meaning: More to take in than one can keep up with
ying-jie-bu-xia.meaning_metaphoric: More to take in than one can keep up with
ying-jie-bu-xia.origin: Wang Xianzhi said that travelling the road through Shanyin, with the hills and rivers throwing the light back at one another, left a person 应接不暇 — no leisure (不暇) left over from meeting (应) and taking in (接) it all. The original is about abundance rather than pressure: the eye cannot keep up because there is too much worth looking at. Chinese has since carried it over to work and to visitors, where the abundance is less welcome, but the flattering sense survives — a shop can be 应接不暇 and its owner delighted.
ying-jie-bu-xia.title: 应接不暇 (ying jie bu xia) — "More to take in than one can keep up with" | Meaning & Origin

ying-nan-er-shang.example_en: In the face of adversity, she chose to confront the challenges head-on
ying-nan-er-shang.example_zh: 面对困难，她选择迎难而上

faq.a: 迎难而上 (yíng nán ér shàng) literally means "Face difficulties head-on" and metaphorically means "Persevere through challenges". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 迎难而上 mean?

faq.a: 迎难而上 is pronounced as "yíng nán ér shàng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 迎难而上?

faq.a: 迎难而上 is used when In the face of adversity, she chose to confront the challenges head-on.
faq.q: When is 迎难而上 used?

ying-nan-er-shang.origin: To meet (迎) the difficulty (难) and go up (上) into it. It belongs to the vocabulary of official encouragement — work reports, campaign slogans, school assemblies. What distinguishes it from ordinary perseverance is direction: 迎 is movement toward the thing, so the phrase describes choosing the harder route while an easier one is available. Its natural opposite is 知难而退, and Chinese sets the two against each other constantly.
ying-nan-er-shang.title: 迎难而上 (ying nan er shang) — "Persevere through challenges" | Meaning & Origin

ying-ren-er-jie.example_en: Once we identified the root cause, the problem was easily solved.
ying-ren-er-jie.example_zh: 一旦找到根本原因，问题就迎刃而解了。

faq.a: 迎刃而解 (yíng rèn ér jiě) literally means "Split apart upon meeting the blade" and metaphorically means "Easily solved once properly approached". It belongs to the Strategy & Action category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 迎刃而解 mean?

faq.a: 迎刃而解 is pronounced as "yíng rèn ér jiě" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 迎刃而解?

faq.a: 迎刃而解 is used when Once we identified the root cause, the problem was easily solved..
faq.q: When is 迎刃而解 used?

ying-ren-er-jie.literal: Split apart upon meeting the blade
ying-ren-er-jie.origin: With Wu's capital nearly taken, Du Yu's officers proposed halting until the following winter. He answered them in council that the army's might was already roused, and that the thing was now like splitting bamboo: after the first few joints the rest comes apart on meeting (迎) the blade (刃) and falls open (解), with nowhere left to lay a hand. The physical claim is accurate — bamboo resists the first cut and then splits its whole length along the grain. What the phrase adds to the ordinary idea of an easy solution is the condition attached: the ease is available only after the hard part, and only along the right line. Problems that dissolve once the correct approach is found — never problems that were easy to begin with.
ying-ren-er-jie.title: 迎刃而解 (ying ren er jie) — "Easily solved once properly approached" | Meaning & Origin

yong-guan-san-jun.example_en: His courage in the face of adversity made him a leader among his peers.
yong-guan-san-jun.example_zh: 他在逆境中的勇气使他成为同龄人中的领袖。

faq.a: 勇冠三军 (yǒng guàn sān jūn) literally means "Bravery crowns the army" and metaphorically means "Unmatched bravery". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 勇冠三军 mean?

faq.a: 勇冠三军 is pronounced as "yǒng guàn sān jūn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 勇冠三军?

faq.a: 勇冠三军 is used when His courage in the face of adversity made him a leader among his peers..
faq.q: When is 勇冠三军 used?

yong-guan-san-jun.origin: 三军 is the full establishment of an ancient army, its three divisions, so to crown (冠) all three with one's courage (勇) is to be the bravest man in the entire force. The phrase comes from the letter attributed to Li Ling writing to Su Wu, praising the general Li Guang. It has stayed close to its origins and remains distinctly martial. Genuine physical courage is the sense, and applying it to a boardroom would sound like deliberate hyperbole.
yong-guan-san-jun.title: 勇冠三军 (yong guan san jun) — "Unmatched bravery" | Meaning & Origin

yong-ren-zi-rao.example_en: She created imaginary problems and spent days worrying about scenarios that never materialized
yong-ren-zi-rao.example_zh: 她创造了想象中的问题，花了好几天担心那些从未发生的情况

faq.a: 庸人自扰 (yōng rén zì rǎo) literally means "Mediocre person self-disturbs" and metaphorically means "Creating unnecessary troubles for oneself". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 庸人自扰 mean?

faq.a: 庸人自扰 is pronounced as "yōng rén zì rǎo" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 庸人自扰?

faq.a: 庸人自扰 is used when She created imaginary problems and spent days worrying about scenarios that never materialized.
faq.q: When is 庸人自扰 used?

yong-ren-zi-rao.origin: This is from the New Book of Tang, on the official Lu Xiangxian, who held that the world is fundamentally without trouble and that mediocre people (庸人) stir it up (自扰) into vexation. The diagnosis is unkind and specific: the difficulty is manufactured, and manufactured by the person now complaining of it. Somebody working themselves up over a difficulty that is not there.
yong-ren-zi-rao.title: 庸人自扰 (yong ren zi rao) — "Creating unnecessary troubles for oneself" | Meaning & Origin

yong-wang-zhi-qian.example_en: Despite the obstacles, she bravely forged ahead with her plans for the new business.
yong-wang-zhi-qian.example_zh: 尽管有障碍，她勇往直前地推进新业务的计划。

faq.a: 勇往直前 (yǒng wǎng zhí qián) literally means "Courageously advance forward" and metaphorically means "Persevere with courage". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 勇往直前 mean?

faq.a: 勇往直前 is pronounced as "yǒng wǎng zhí qián" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 勇往直前?

faq.a: 勇往直前 is used when Despite the obstacles, she bravely forged ahead with her plans for the new business..
faq.q: When is 勇往直前 used?

yong-wang-zhi-qian.origin: Four characters doing exactly what they say: brave (勇), going (往), straight (直), forward (前). The phrase is built from the plainest available parts, and its force comes from the complete absence of sideways motion in it. What it rules out is not fear but hesitation and detour. It belongs to exhortation: coaches, commanders, graduation speeches, and the sort of encouragement offered to someone who has already decided and is casting about for a reason not to.
yong-wang-zhi-qian.title: 勇往直前 (yong wang zhi qian) — "Persevere with courage" | Meaning & Origin

you-bei-wu-huan.example_en: By planning ahead, she ensured that potential problems would not derail her project.
you-bei-wu-huan.example_zh: 有备无患的原则让她的计划顺利进行。

faq.a: 有备无患 (yǒu bèi wú huàn) literally means "Preparedness averts disaster" and metaphorically means "Trouble skips the prepared". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 有备无患 mean?

faq.a: 有备无患 is pronounced as "yǒu bèi wú huàn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 有备无患?

faq.a: 有备无患 is used when By planning ahead, she ensured that potential problems would not derail her project..
faq.q: When is 有备无患 used?

you-bei-wu-huan.origin: The Book of Documents states it flatly: attend to your affairs, and in preparation there is no calamity — have the preparation (有备) and you are without trouble (无患). It is the last clause of the chain quoted in the Zuo Zhuan as 居安思危，思则有备，有备无患, where Wei Jiang tells the ruler of Jin that peace is exactly when danger should be considered, since prosperity rather than crisis is what stops people looking. The phrase is not about anxiety. It is about doing the work while it is still cheap, and it is what Chinese says over insurance and fire drills.
you-bei-wu-huan.title: 有备无患 (you bei wu huan) — "Trouble skips the prepared" | Meaning & Origin

you-jiao-wu-lei.example_en: The scholarship program aims to make education accessible to all.
you-jiao-wu-lei.example_zh: 奖学金项目旨在有教无类，让所有人都能接受教育。

faq.a: 有教无类 (yǒu jiào wú lèi) literally means "Provide education without discrimination" and metaphorically means "Teach anyone, whatever their station". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 有教无类 mean?

faq.a: 有教无类 is pronounced as "yǒu jiào wú lèi" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 有教无类?

faq.a: 有教无类 is used when The scholarship program aims to make education accessible to all..
faq.q: When is 有教无类 used?

you-jiao-wu-lei.origin: In teaching (教) there are (有) no (无) categories (类). Confucius said it in a society where 类 meant birth and rank, so the claim was substantive rather than pious: he declined to sort applicants by where they came from, and his students included the poor and the disreputable. It remains the standard Chinese banner for educational access, and it is worth reading as the negative it is — not that everybody must be taught alike, but that nobody is to be sorted out beforehand.
you-jiao-wu-lei.title: 有教无类 (you jiao wu lei) — "Teach anyone, whatever their station" | Meaning & Origin

you-kou-jie-bei.example_en: His contributions to the community were recognized by all, earning him widespread acclaim.
you-kou-jie-bei.example_zh: 他对社区的贡献得到了大家的认可，有口皆碑。

faq.a: 有口皆碑 (yǒu kǒu jiē bēi) literally means "Every mouth is a monument" and metaphorically means "Universally praised". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 有口皆碑 mean?

faq.a: 有口皆碑 is pronounced as "yǒu kǒu jiē bēi" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 有口皆碑?

faq.a: 有口皆碑 is used when His contributions to the community were recognized by all, earning him widespread acclaim..
faq.q: When is 有口皆碑 used?

you-kou-jie-bei.origin: The Song Buddhist compilation Wudeng Huiyuan has the line: do not trouble to carve the stubborn stone, for the mouths of travellers on the road are the tablet. Chinese practice was to record a good official's deeds on an inscribed stele; the argument here is that what people say about you unprompted does the same work and cannot be commissioned. Hence every mouth (有口皆) a monument (碑). Reputation that has clearly not been bought, which is precisely the kind worth having.
you-kou-jie-bei.title: 有口皆碑 (you kou jie bei) — "Universally praised" | Meaning & Origin

you-mu-gong-du.example_en: The evidence of his hard work is clear for everyone to see.
you-mu-gong-du.example_zh: 他努力工作的证据有目共睹。

faq.a: 有目共睹 (yǒu mù gòng dǔ) literally means "With eyes, seen by all" and metaphorically means "Undeniably obvious". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 有目共睹 mean?

faq.a: 有目共睹 is pronounced as "yǒu mù gòng dǔ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 有目共睹?

faq.a: 有目共睹 is used when The evidence of his hard work is clear for everyone to see..
faq.q: When is 有目共睹 used?

you-mu-gong-du.origin: Having (有) eyes (目), all together (共) see it (睹). The construction is worth noticing: the claim is not that everyone agrees, but that possessing eyes is the only qualification required, which forecloses the argument rather than winning it. That is exactly how it is used. It appears in Chinese official and commercial language about achievements, and its rhetorical function is to treat a contested claim as though it were a matter of plain observation. A learner who meets it in a sales pitch should read it as a signal that no evidence is going to follow.
you-mu-gong-du.title: 有目共睹 (you mu gong du) — "Undeniably obvious" | Meaning & Origin

you-ren-you-yu.example_en: The experienced chef handled the busy kitchen effortlessly.
you-ren-you-yu.example_zh: 经验丰富的厨师在繁忙的厨房游刃有余。

faq.a: 游刃有余 (yóu rèn yǒu yú) literally means "Moving blade with room to spare" and metaphorically means "Handle with ease; have skill to spare". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 游刃有余 mean?

you-sheng-lie-tai.origin: The superior (优) prevail (胜), the inferior (劣) are washed out (汰). This is not a classical idiom: it entered Chinese in the late Qing through Yan Fu's translation of Huxley, in the wave of thinking about survival and struggle that reached China at the moment it was losing wars to industrial powers. That history is why the phrase carries such force in Chinese and why it is applied so readily to nations and firms. 汰 is the word for panning or rinsing away, so the elimination is a sorting rather than a defeat.

you-sheng-you-se.origin: Having (有) sound (声) and having (有) colour (色). The phrase began in literary criticism, praising writing that engaged more than one sense at once, and it has widened to any performance or undertaking carried off with energy and visible effect. What it praises is presentation rather than substance, which leaves a small opening for irony — a project described as running 有声有色 is definitely making an impression, and the phrase does not by itself say whether it is working.

you-shi-you-zhong.literal: Have a beginning and an end
you-shi-you-zhong.origin: A plain statement of a virtue: there is (有) a beginning (始) and there is an end (终). Its weight comes instead from its opposites, which Chinese has in abundance: 有头无尾, a head with no tail; 虎头蛇尾, a tiger's head on a snake's tail; 半途而废, abandoned at the halfway point. Against that company, finishing is treated as the harder and rarer half of any undertaking. It is applied to people rather than to projects, as a judgement on character, and it is among the plainest compliments in the language.
you-shi-you-zhong.title: 有始有终 (you shi you zhong) — "Persevere to completion" | Meaning & Origin

The image is structural — the threads are orderly because something holds them in relation to each other, not because each was tidied separately. Work or an argument that is orderly because something holds it together, not because it was tidied afterwards.
you-tiao-bu-wen.title: 有条不紊 (you tiao bu wen) — "Methodical and well-organized action" | Meaning & Origin

you-tou-wu-wei.origin: Four characters that describe exactly what they name: 有 (have) 头 (head) 无 (lack) 尾 (tail). The picture is of a thing that begins and then simply stops — no ending arrives, not even a poor one. That is what separates it from its close cousin 虎头蛇尾, 'tiger head, snake tail', where a finish does arrive but arrives feeble; here there is no finish at all. It is the flat opposite of 有始有终, and the two are used as a matched pair of judgements about a person's character rather than about any one abandoned task. The phrase travelled well beyond Mandarin: Hokkien speakers say it as ū thâu bô bué, and a learner is as likely to meet it in Taiwan, Fujian or Singapore as in Beijing.
you-tou-wu-wei.title: 有头无尾 (you tou wu wei) — "Started but never finished" | Meaning & Origin

you-zhi-zhe-shi-jing-cheng.example_en: With determination and hard work, she finally reached her goals.

you-zhi-zhe-shi-jing-cheng.origin: The idiom 有志者事竟成 (yǒu zhì zhě shì jìng chéng) originates from the historical account of Geng Yan, a general under the Eastern Han dynasty's Emperor Guangwu. Geng Yan was tasked with defeating the formidable warlord Zhang Bu. Despite being outnumbered and wounded in battle, Geng Yan's unwavering determination led to a decisive victory. Emperor Guangwu praised him, acknowledging that 'those with determination (有志者) will see their tasks (事) through to completion (竟成).' This idiom emphasizes the power of perseverance and resolve. In modern usage, it encourages individuals to pursue their goals with tenacity, suggesting that success is attainable through steadfast effort.

yu-bang-xiang-zheng.origin: A snipe stabbed at the flesh of an open clam and the shell closed on its beak. Neither would let go: no rain today or tomorrow, said the bird, and you are a dead clam; no release today or tomorrow, said the clam, and you are a dead bird. A fisherman walking the bank took both. Su Dai told the story to the King of Zhao to argue him out of attacking Yan, with Qin as the fisherman, and the Strategies of the Warring States records it. The saying is nearly always given whole: 鹬蚌相争，渔翁得利 — while snipe and clam fight, the fisherman profits.

yu-gong-yi-shan.origin: The Liezi tells of an old man of ninety whose way out was blocked by two mountains, and who began shifting (移) them (山) away a basket at a time. A widowed neighbour's small son ran over to help. The Wise Old Man of Hequ laughed at him and told him to stop, and he answered that when he died his sons would remain, and their sons after them, while the mountains would not grow any higher — 子子孙孙无穷匮也，而山不加增. A spirit heard him and had the mountains carried away. The names are the joke: 愚公 is the Foolish (愚) Old Man (公) and 智叟 the Wise Old Man, and the story hands the argument to the fool, whose foolishness turns out to be arithmetic the wise man had not done.
yu-gong-yi-shan.title: 愚公移山 (yu gong yi shan) — "Persistence overcomes huge obstacles" | Meaning & Origin

So the phrase claims speed and number together, and specifically the kind that appears without anyone planting anything. Start-ups, coffee shops and copycat products.

What the phrase names is not a hard negotiation but an impossible one: the thing being asked for is the counterparty's existence, so no terms exist at which they could agree.

The phrase describes a group whose members are of very unequal quality, and it is mildly disapproving. It suits open markets, unvetted crowds and any profession with no barrier to entry.

What the phrase adds beyond simple counterfeiting is the mixing: the fakes are distributed among genuine articles so that the batch as a whole passes. Goods, credentials and people all qualify.

Jade is not found finished; it is cut and ground, and the phrase treats hardship as that grinding rather than as misfortune. It is a consolation, but an unsentimental one. The claim is causal rather than merely cautionary: the haste is the thing that prevents the arrival. Projects, learning, and anybody visibly cutting the stages short.

faq.q: When is 与众不同 used?

yu-zhong-bu-tong.origin: Not (不) the same as (同) the crowd (众), with 与 marking the comparison. Chinese has long been ambivalent about the condition this names, and the ambivalence survives inside the phrase: it is a compliment when the speaker approves of the difference and a diagnosis when they do not, and nothing in the four characters settles which. That makes it more useful than English 'unique', which has worn down to mean merely good. Design, a person's manner, and children whose difference has not yet been decided about.
yu-zhong-bu-tong.title: 与众不同 (yu zhong bu tong) — "Unique; distinctive" | Meaning & Origin

faq.q: When is 语重心长 used?

yu-zhong-xin-chang.origin: Words (语) that are weighty (重) and a heart (心) that reaches far (长). The two halves describe different things: the speech is serious, and the concern behind it extends beyond the present moment. That combination is what makes the phrase specific. Advice from somebody older who has thought about your life for longer than you have — and it is nearly always said in retrospect, about a conversation whose point arrived years later.
yu-zhong-xin-chang.title: 语重心长 (yu zhong xin chang) — "Heartfelt advice" | Meaning & Origin

yuan-jiao-jin-gong.example_en: In the game of politics, forming alliances with distant nations while undermining local rivals can be a winning strategy.
yuan-jiao-jin-gong.example_zh: 在政治博弈中，远交近攻的策略常常能取得胜利。

faq.a: 远交近攻 (yuǎn jiāo jìn gōng) literally means "Befriend distant, attack nearby" and metaphorically means "Strategic prioritization". It belongs to the Strategy & Action category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 远交近攻 mean?

faq.a: 远交近攻 is pronounced as "yuǎn jiāo jìn gōng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 远交近攻?

faq.a: 远交近攻 is used when In the game of politics, forming alliances with distant nations while undermining local rivals can be a winning strategy..
faq.q: When is 远交近攻 used?

yuan-jiao-jin-gong.origin: Fan Ju arrived in Qin and told King Zhaoxiang that his campaigns made no sense: Qin was attacking distant states and leaving neighbours intact, so every victory produced land it could not hold. Ally with the far (远交) and attack the near (近攻), he argued, and each conquest is contiguous and keepable. The Strategies of the Warring States records it, and Qin's unification of China followed the policy for decades. It remains a genuinely useful principle about the order of operations, in business as much as in war.
yuan-jiao-jin-gong.title: 远交近攻 (yuan jiao jin gong) — "Strategic prioritization" | Meaning & Origin

yuan-mu-qiu-yu.example_en: The company sought manufacturing efficiency by hiring more managers instead of upgrading equipment

faq.q: How do you pronounce 缘木求鱼?

faq.a: 缘木求鱼 is used when The company sought manufacturing efficiency by hiring more managers instead of upgrading equipment.
faq.q: When is 缘木求鱼 used?

yuan-mu-qiu-yu.meaning: Using completely wrong method for a task
yuan-mu-qiu-yu.meaning_metaphoric: Using completely wrong method for a task
yuan-mu-qiu-yu.origin: Mencius said it to King Xuan of Qi, who wanted to extend his territory by force and expected contentment to follow. To pursue what you want by those means, Mencius told him, is to climb a tree (缘木) to look for fish (求鱼) — and worse, because climbing a tree and finding no fish does you no harm, whereas the king's method would end in ruin. The complaint is not that the effort is insufficient. It is that the effort is being made in the wrong medium altogether. The phrase stays useful wherever energy is being spent generously on a method that could not work however hard it were pushed.
yuan-mu-qiu-yu.title: 缘木求鱼 (yuan mu qiu yu) — "Using completely wrong method for a task" | Meaning & Origin

yuan-yuan-liu-chang.example_en: Chinese civilization has ancient roots and continues to thrive today.

faq.a: 源远流长 is used when Chinese civilization has ancient roots and continues to thrive today..
faq.q: When is 源远流长 used?

yuan-yuan-liu-chang.meaning: Having deep roots and long history
yuan-yuan-liu-chang.meaning_metaphoric: Having deep roots and long history
yuan-yuan-liu-chang.origin: A source (源) far off (远) and a current (流) that runs long (长). Both halves describe the same river from opposite ends, and what they claim together is continuity rather than mere age: the water arriving now is connected to the spring, and nothing in between has been cut. That is why it is applied to traditions, disciplines and family lines rather than to old objects. The register is official and ceremonial, and it is very often the opening sentence of a piece about a craft.
yuan-yuan-liu-chang.title: 源远流长 (yuan yuan liu chang) — "Having deep roots and long history" | Meaning & Origin

yun-chou-wei-wo.example_en: The CEO quietly developed the company's expansion strategy

faq.a: 运筹帷幄 is used when The CEO quietly developed the company's expansion strategy.
faq.q: When is 运筹帷幄 used?

yun-chou-wei-wo.literal: Work the counting rods in the command tent
yun-chou-wei-wo.origin: Liu Bang, asked why he had won the empire when Xiang Yu was the better soldier, named three men he could not equal. Of Zhang Liang he said: 运筹帷幄之中，决胜千里之外 — turning the counting rods inside the tent curtains (帷幄), he decides victory a thousand li away. The Records of the Grand Historian keeps the speech, and the two clauses are normally quoted together, since the second is what the first is for. 运筹 is literally working the counting rods, so the image is calculation rather than inspiration.
yun-chou-wei-wo.title: 运筹帷幄 (yun chou wei wo) — "Plan strategy carefully" | Meaning & Origin

faq.a: 再接再厉 is used when After narrowly missing the championship, the team redoubled their training efforts for next season.
faq.q: When is 再接再厉 used?

zai-jie-zai-li.literal: Engage again, whet the beak again
zai-jie-zai-li.origin: This is from a linked poem by Han Yu and Meng Jiao on cockfighting: between rounds the bird engages again (再接) and again whets (再厉) its beak on the ground. 厉 is sharpening, not encouragement, and the bird is resharpening between bouts rather than being urged on. Modern usage tells someone to keep going and do better still, usually after a success rather than a defeat.
zai-jie-zai-li.title: 再接再厉 (zai jie zai li) — "Continue efforts with undiminished enthusiasm" | Meaning & Origin

zao-bi-tou-guang.example_en: The student studied by streetlight when electricity was unavailable

faq.q: When is 凿壁偷光 used?

zao-bi-tou-guang.origin: Kuang Heng's family could not afford lamp oil, so he bored (凿) a hole in the party wall (壁) and stole (偷) the light (光) that came through from the neighbour's side. The account is in the Miscellany of the Western Capital, which adds that he hired himself out to a rich household and asked to be paid in access to their books rather than in money. He rose to be chancellor. The phrase is used of study pursued without the means for it, and Chinese schoolchildren still learn it.
zao-bi-tou-guang.title: 凿壁偷光 (zao bi tou guang) — "Study despite poverty" | Meaning & Origin

zhan-ding-jie-tie.example_en: The judge made a decisive ruling that left no room for appeal or interpretation
zhan-ding-jie-tie.example_zh: 法官做出了一个斩钉截铁的裁决，不留上诉或解释的余地

faq.a: 斩钉截铁 (zhǎn dīng jié tiě) literally means "Chop nail cut iron" and metaphorically means "Decisively and firmly without hesitation". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 斩钉截铁 mean?

faq.a: 斩钉截铁 is pronounced as "zhǎn dīng jié tiě" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 斩钉截铁?

faq.a: 斩钉截铁 is used when The judge made a decisive ruling that left no room for appeal or interpretation.
faq.q: When is 斩钉截铁 used?

zhan-ding-jie-tie.origin: Yunju Daoying, in the Jingde Records, tells his assembly that a person who studies the Buddha-dharma must be like one cutting through a nail (斩钉) and severing iron (截铁) — nothing tentative, nothing left half-done. Both objects resist cutting, so the force is in the decisiveness rather than in any ease. It transferred from that demand on a student to speech and manner generally: speaking or deciding with no hedge left anywhere in the sentence.
zhan-ding-jie-tie.title: 斩钉截铁 (zhan ding jie tie) — "Decisively and firmly without hesitation" | Meaning & Origin

zhan-wu-bu-sheng.example_en: Their legal team has never lost a case.
zhan-wu-bu-sheng.example_zh: 他们的法律团队战无不胜。

faq.a: 战无不胜 (zhàn wú bù shèng) literally means "In battle, nothing is not won" and metaphorically means "Win every battle; be undefeated". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 战无不胜 mean?

faq.a: 战无不胜 is pronounced as "zhàn wú bù shèng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 战无不胜?

faq.a: 战无不胜 is used when Their legal team has never lost a case..
faq.q: When is 战无不胜 used?

zhan-wu-bu-sheng.literal: In battle, nothing is not won
zhan-wu-bu-sheng.origin: In battle (战), there is nothing (无) not (不) won (胜). The partner phrase to 攻无不克, and the division of labour between them is real: that one covers the taking of objectives and this one the engagements, so together they claim a record with no failure at either scale. The Strategies of the Warring States attaches a warning to the idea — 战无不胜而不知止者身且死, the man who wins every battle and does not know when to stop will die of it — which the modern phrase has dropped.
zhan-wu-bu-sheng.title: 战无不胜 (zhan wu bu sheng) — "Win every battle; be undefeated" | Meaning & Origin

zhao-cai-jin-bao.example_en: Wishing your business a year that keeps the money coming in.
zhao-cai-jin-bao.example_zh: 老板在店门口贴上“招财进宝”，盼着新的一年生意红火。

faq.a: 招财进宝 (zhāo cái jìn bǎo) literally means "Beckon wealth, bring in treasure" and metaphorically means "May money and valuables flow in". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 招财进宝 mean?

faq.a: 招财进宝 is pronounced as "zhāo cái jìn bǎo" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 招财进宝?

faq.q: When is 招财进宝 used?

zhao-cai-jin-bao.meaning: May money and valuables flow in
zhao-cai-jin-bao.meaning_metaphoric: May money and valuables flow in
zhao-cai-jin-bao.origin: 招 means 'to beckon' and 进 'to bring in', so the phrase invites wealth and treasure into the house. An early recorded use is in the Yuan-dynasty zaju play 《降桑椹蔡顺奉母》 by Liu Tangqing, where the earth god introduces himself with the line 'beckoning wealth and bringing in treasure, I bring fine omens; the whole household is free of worry and kept safe' (招财进宝臻佳瑞，阖家无虑保安存). The phrase is best known in written form. The four characters are often merged into one composite character, with shared components and the 辶 stroke of 进 sweeping under the rest, and this is written on square red paper and pasted on doors, counters or cabinets at New Year. It is a greeting for businesses and shopkeepers above all, and a natural partner to 恭喜发财.
zhao-cai-jin-bao.title: 招财进宝 (zhao cai jin bao) — "May money and valuables flow in" | Meaning & Origin

zhao-qi-peng-bo.example_en: The startup team tackled challenges with youthful enthusiasm and boundless energy
zhao-qi-peng-bo.example_zh: 创业团队以年轻的热情和无限的精力应对挑战

faq.a: 朝气蓬勃 (zhāo qì péng bó) literally means "Morning vigor flourishing" and metaphorically means "Vibrant youthful energy and enthusiasm". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 朝气蓬勃 mean?

faq.a: 朝气蓬勃 is pronounced as "zhāo qì péng bó" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 朝气蓬勃?

faq.a: 朝气蓬勃 is used when The startup team tackled challenges with youthful enthusiasm and boundless energy.
faq.q: When is 朝气蓬勃 used?

zhao-qi-peng-bo.origin: 朝气 is the vigour of the early morning, set in Chinese against 暮气, the flatness of evening, and the pair is used of people rather than of times of day. 蓬勃 is the vocabulary of plants growing thickly. So the phrase claims the energy of a morning and the growth of a spring together, and it is applied to the young, to new organisations and to periods rather than to individuals in isolation. Its opposite, 暮气沉沉, is what Chinese says about an institution that has stopped.
zhao-qi-peng-bo.title: 朝气蓬勃 (zhao qi peng bo) — "Vibrant youthful energy and enthusiasm" | Meaning & Origin

zhao-qin-mu-chu.meaning: Constantly shifting loyalty for personal gain
zhao-qin-mu-chu.meaning_metaphoric: Constantly shifting loyalty for personal gain
zhao-qin-mu-chu.origin: Qin in the morning (朝秦), Chu by evening (暮楚). The states named are the two great powers between which the small central states, and the travelling persuaders who served them, spent the Warring States period choosing sides. The phrase is not about mere inconsistency: it names loyalty treated as a position to be taken up and put down according to advantage. Politicians, contractors, and anyone whose allegiance has been observed to track the odds.
zhao-qin-mu-chu.title: 朝秦暮楚 (zhao qin mu chu) — "Constantly shifting loyalty for personal gain" | Meaning & Origin

zhao-san-mu-si.example_en: His indecisiveness led to constant changes in plans, leaving everyone confused.
zhao-san-mu-si.example_zh: 他的优柔寡断导致计划不断变化，让大家感到困惑。

faq.a: 朝三暮四 (zhāo sān mù sì) literally means "Three in the morning, four at night" and metaphorically means "Fickle and inconsistent". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 朝三暮四 mean?

faq.a: 朝三暮四 is pronounced as "zhāo sān mù sì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 朝三暮四?

faq.a: 朝三暮四 is used when His indecisiveness led to constant changes in plans, leaving everyone confused..
faq.q: When is 朝三暮四 used?

zhao-san-mu-si.literal: Three in the morning, four at night
zhao-san-mu-si.origin: The Zhuangzi tells of a monkey keeper who, running short, told his monkeys they would have three acorns in the morning (朝三) and four at night (暮四). The monkeys were furious. He offered four in the morning and three at night, and they were delighted. Zhuangzi's point is about the sage, who wearies neither himself nor others by disputing over what is in substance identical. The modern meaning has drifted well away from that: today 朝三暮四 nearly always means fickle and changeable, and the arithmetic in the story has been forgotten.
zhao-san-mu-si.title: 朝三暮四 (zhao san mu si) — "Fickle and inconsistent" | Meaning & Origin

zhao-si-mu-xiang.example_en: He constantly thinks about his family back home.
zhao-si-mu-xiang.example_zh: 他朝思暮想着远方的家人。

faq.a: 朝思暮想 (zhāo sī mù xiǎng) literally means "Think in morning, yearn at night" and metaphorically means "Think about constantly; yearn for". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 朝思暮想 mean?

faq.a: 朝思暮想 is pronounced as "zhāo sī mù xiǎng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 朝思暮想?

faq.a: 朝思暮想 is used when He constantly thinks about his family back home..
faq.q: When is 朝思暮想 used?

zhao-si-mu-xiang.literal: Think in morning, yearn at night
zhao-si-mu-xiang.origin: Thinking (思) at dawn (朝) and thinking again (想) at dusk (暮). The two verbs are near-synonyms and the two times are the ends of the waking span, so the phrase covers a day by naming its edges. It is plainer than 魂牵梦萦 and correspondingly commoner in speech. Absent people, a place somebody wants to get back to, and — quite ordinarily — something they have been wanting to buy for months.
zhao-si-mu-xiang.title: 朝思暮想 (zhao si mu xiang) — "Think about constantly; yearn for" | Meaning & Origin

zhen-feng-xiang-dui.example_en: During the debate, each candidate responded with immediate sharp counterarguments
zhen-feng-xiang-dui.example_zh: 辩论中，每位候选人都以即时尖锐的反驳作为回应

faq.a: 针锋相对 (zhēn fēng xiāng duì) literally means "Needle points facing each other" and metaphorically means "Sharp, direct confrontation in argument". It belongs to the Strategy & Action category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 针锋相对 mean?

faq.a: 针锋相对 is pronounced as "zhēn fēng xiāng duì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 针锋相对?

faq.a: 针锋相对 is used when During the debate, each candidate responded with immediate sharp counterarguments.
faq.q: When is 针锋相对 used?

zhen-feng-xiang-dui.origin: Needle point (针锋) meeting needle point (相对). The expression comes out of Chan Buddhist dialogue, where the exchange of question and answer was described in exactly these terms — two points meeting precisely, with nothing wasted on either side. That origin explains its flavour. It describes opposition that is exactly matched and exactly aimed, rather than merely hostile, and it gets used of debates and negotiations where each move answers a specific move.
zhen-feng-xiang-dui.title: 针锋相对 (zhen feng xiang dui) — "Sharp, direct confrontation in argument" | Meaning & Origin

zhen-ge-dai-dan.example_en: The security team remained vigilant throughout the night, prepared for any threat
zhen-ge-dai-dan.example_zh: 安保团队整夜保持警惕，准备应对任何威胁

faq.a: 枕戈待旦 (zhěn gē dài dàn) literally means "Pillow spear await dawn" and metaphorically means "Maintain high vigilance awaiting challenge". It belongs to the Strategy & Action category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 枕戈待旦 mean?

faq.a: 枕戈待旦 is pronounced as "zhěn gē dài dàn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 枕戈待旦?

faq.a: 枕戈待旦 is used when The security team remained vigilant throughout the night, prepared for any threat.
faq.q: When is 枕戈待旦 used?

zhen-ge-dai-dan.origin: This comes from the Book of Jin, on Liu Kun, who wrote that he slept with his spear (枕戈) for a pillow waiting for dawn (待旦), determined that a rival should not strike at the invaders before he did. The competitive edge is in the original and usually lost: he was racing a colleague, not only the enemy. Staying ready over a long period and at some cost.
zhen-ge-dai-dan.title: 枕戈待旦 (zhen ge dai dan) — "Maintain high vigilance awaiting challenge" | Meaning & Origin

zhen-liu-shu-shi.example_en: The researcher lived modestly while dedicating everything to her discoveries
zhen-liu-shu-shi.example_zh: 研究员过着简朴的生活，把一切都投入到研究发现中

faq.a: 枕流漱石 (zhěn liú shù shí) literally means "Pillow stream rinse stone" and metaphorically means "Live as a recluse in the wild". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 枕流漱石 mean?

faq.a: 枕流漱石 is pronounced as "zhěn liú shù shí" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 枕流漱石?

faq.a: 枕流漱石 is used when The researcher lived modestly while dedicating everything to her discoveries.
faq.q: When is 枕流漱石 used?

zhen-liu-shu-shi.meaning: Live as a recluse in the wild
zhen-liu-shu-shi.meaning_metaphoric: Live as a recluse in the wild
zhen-liu-shu-shi.origin: Sun Chu, meaning to say he would pillow on stones and rinse in the stream (枕石漱流) — the standard image of the recluse — got it out backwards as pillowing on the stream (枕流) and rinsing with stones (漱石). Asked by Wang Ji how a stream could be a pillow or a stone a mouthwash, he answered without pausing: he pillowed on the current to wash out his ears, and rinsed with stone to sharpen his teeth. The New Account of Tales of the World keeps the exchange. Both forms are now current, and the phrase carries a flavour of the quick save as much as of reclusion.
zhen-liu-shu-shi.title: 枕流漱石 (zhen liu shu shi) — "Live as a recluse in the wild" | Meaning & Origin

zhen-shi-shu-liu.origin: To pillow (枕) on stone (石) and rinse (漱) in the stream (流) is the standard image of the recluse who has declined office and lives off the mountain. Its fame, however, comes from a slip: the New Account of Tales of the World records Sun Chu, meaning to say it, getting it out as 漱石枕流 — rinsing with stone and pillowing on the stream, and then defending the mistake on the spot — he pillowed on the current to wash out his ears, and rinsed with stone to sharpen his teeth. Both forms are now current, and both appear in this collection.

zheng-fen-duo-miao.origin: This modern idiom emerged during China's industrialization period in the 20th century, reflecting the urgency of national development. It combines 'fighting for' (争) minutes (分) and 'seizing' (夺) seconds (秒) to emphasize making the most of every moment. The phrase became particularly popular during the Great Leap Forward era and remains common in contexts requiring urgent action. It expresses the importance of efficiency and the race against time, commonly used in emergency situations, competitive environments, and deadline-driven work.

zheng-lun-bu-xiu.origin: To argue (争论) without (不) ceasing (休). This is a modern four-character phrase built on a productive pattern rather than a classical allusion: 不休 attaches to a verb to mean that the action will not stop, and it yields 喋喋不休 (chattering on and on) the same way it yields this. There is no story behind it and no source text to cite. The force is in 休 — the complaint is not that the disagreement is fierce but that nobody will let it end.

zheng-ren-jun-zi.origin: An upright person (正人), a gentleman (君子) — the compound is old and was straightforwardly complimentary, describing the scholar-official who behaved as the training was supposed to make him behave. Its modern life is almost entirely sarcastic. Said today, 正人君子 usually means someone conspicuously performing rectitude, and the more solemn the delivery the more certain the irony. Learners should treat it as unusable as praise: to compliment integrity, Chinese has 德高望重 or simply 正直, and this phrase will be heard as an accusation.

zheng-ren-mai-lv.origin: A man (人) of Zheng (郑), wanting to buy (买) shoes (履), measured his foot with a cord and left the cord at home. Reaching the market he found he had forgotten it and went back for it, and by the time he returned the market had closed. Asked why he had not simply tried the shoes on his feet, he said: I trust the measurement, I do not trust myself. Han Feizi tells it against rulers who prefer the precedent to the case in front of them, and the punchline is the whole idiom — the foot was available the entire time.

zheng-xian-kong-hou.meaning_metaphoric: Rush eagerly to be first, not last
zheng-xian-kong-hou.origin: The competitive atmosphere of the Han Dynasty imperial court gave birth to this phrase describing the twin drives of striving to be first (争先) while fearing to be last (恐后). Court historians noted how this combination of ambition and anxiety drove official behavior. Tang Dynasty observers saw the same pattern in broader social competition. Modern usage spans from consumer behavior to professional advancement, capturing how social momentum creates both attraction to leading positions and fear of falling behind.
zheng-xian-kong-hou.title: 争先恐后 (zheng xian kong hou) — "Rush eagerly to be first, not last" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-dao-huang-long.origin: The History of Song records Yue Fei telling his officers 直抵黄龙府，与诸君痛饮尔 — we will reach Huanglong Prefecture (黄龙) and drink together there. The modern form swaps 抵, to arrive at, for 捣, to smash into, and comes from the later Yue Fei fiction rather than from the history. Huanglong lay far to the northeast, deep in Jurchen Jin territory, and not at Kaifeng, which had been the Song's own capital before its loss — so naming it meant carrying the war into the enemy's heartland rather than merely recovering what had been taken. Yue Fei was recalled and executed before he could try. Striking at the source of a problem rather than at its symptoms.
zhi-dao-huang-long.title: 直捣黄龙 (zhi dao huang long) — "Strike directly at the heart of enemy territory" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-gao-qi-yang.origin: The Zuo Zhuan records an officer watching the Chu commander Qu Xia set out and predicting his defeat: 举趾高，心不固矣 — he lifts his toes (趾) high (高), and his heart is not steady. The gait gave him away, and he lost. With 气扬, the spirit (气) flying up (扬), the phrase pairs the walk with the mood behind it. What it names is confidence displayed in the body before anything has been achieved, and it gets used of somebody who has just won something small and is being visible about it.
zhi-gao-qi-yang.title: 趾高气扬 (zhi gao qi yang) — "Strut arrogantly; be conceited" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-ji-zhi-bi.origin: Sun Tzu's line in the chapter on attack by stratagem runs 知彼知己，百战不殆 — know the other and know yourself, and a hundred engagements will not endanger you. Two things get lost in the popular version. The order is reversed, the enemy coming first; and the promise is not a hundred victories but a hundred fights without peril, which is a colder and more accurate claim. Sun Tzu grades the rest: knowing yourself alone gives even odds, and knowing neither loses every time.
zhi-ji-zhi-bi.title: 知己知彼 (zhi ji zhi bi) — "Strategic insight" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-lu-wei-ma.meaning: Deliberately distort truth as power display
zhi-lu-wei-ma.meaning_metaphoric: Deliberately distort truth as power display
zhi-lu-wei-ma.origin: Zhao Gao, holding the Qin court after the First Emperor's death, brought a deer (鹿) before the young emperor and, pointing (指) at it, called it (为) a horse (马). The emperor laughed; the officials divided. Those who said deer, Zhao Gao later had killed. The Records of the Grand Historian tells it, and the point is not that anyone was deceived — everyone in the hall could see a deer. It was a loyalty test conducted in public, and Chinese uses the phrase for exactly that: an obvious falsehood that power requires you to affirm.
zhi-lu-wei-ma.title: 指鹿为马 (zhi lu wei ma) — "Deliberately distort truth as power display" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-nan-er-jin.meaning: Press on despite awareness of challenges
zhi-nan-er-jin.meaning_metaphoric: Press on despite awareness of challenges
zhi-nan-er-jin.origin: To know (知) the difficulty (难) and advance (进) anyway. It is built as the deliberate opposite of 知难而退, withdrawing in the face of difficulty, and the pair is used against each other constantly in Chinese. What both share is the first half: the knowing is not in dispute, and the phrase specifically excludes the person who pressed on because they had not understood what they were taking on. It is courage with the information already in hand.
zhi-nan-er-jin.title: 知难而进 (zhi nan er jin) — "Press on despite awareness of challenges" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-nan-er-tui.meaning: Back off once the difficulty is clear; often, give up when it gets hard
zhi-nan-er-tui.meaning_metaphoric: Back off once the difficulty is clear; often, give up when it gets hard
zhi-nan-er-tui.origin: The Zuo Zhuan records the Jin commanders arguing before an engagement with Chu: Chu had already made peace with Zheng, its army was in good order, and the case for withdrawing was that a fight now had nothing left to win. Those who insisted on pressing forward were beaten. In its original setting the phrase is praise for judgement — knowing (知) the difficulty (难) and pulling back (退) is what a competent commander does. Modern use has drifted, and it now often carries a sting: said of somebody else, it usually means they gave up when things got hard.
zhi-nan-er-tui.title: 知难而退 (zhi nan er tui) — "Back off once the difficulty is clear; often, give up when it gets hard" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-sang-ma-huai.origin: To point at (指) the mulberry (桑) and curse (骂) the pagoda tree (槐). It is the twenty-sixth of the Thirty-Six Stratagems, where the technique is discipline by demonstration: an inferior who cannot be rebuked directly is addressed through someone else in the room. The two trees are both ordinary yard trees, which is the point — they are interchangeable, and everyone present knows which one is meant. Criticism aimed past its stated target.
zhi-sang-ma-huai.title: 指桑骂槐 (zhi sang ma huai) — "Indirect criticism of real target" | Meaning & Origin

faq.q: When is 纸上富贵 used?

zhi-shang-fu-gui.origin: Wealth and rank (富贵) that exist on paper (纸上) and nowhere else. The phrase is patterned on 纸上谈兵 — "discussing warfare on paper," the phrase for Zhao Kuo, who had mastered the military texts and lost an army the moment he commanded one — and it borrows that construction's judgement wholesale: 纸上 marks the gap between a thing written down and the same thing in the world. It is not itself a classical idiom with a source of its own. Modern use runs to valuations, projections and holdings that have never been converted into anything.
zhi-shang-fu-gui.title: 纸上富贵 (zhi shang fu gui) — "Success in theory not reality" | Meaning & Origin

faq.q: What does 纸上谈兵 mean?

faq.a: 纸上谈兵 is pronounced as "zhǐ shàng tán bīng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 纸上谈兵?

faq.a: 纸上谈兵 is used when The consultant's theories proved useless when faced with real business challenges.
faq.q: When is 纸上谈兵 used?

zhi-shang-tan-bing.origin: Zhao Kuo had his father's books by heart and could out-argue him on tactics; his father said that war is a matter of life and death and the boy spoke of it far too easily. Qin's agents spread word that the only Zhao general they feared was Zhao Kuo, Zhao replaced the cautious Lian Po with him, and at Changping in 260 BCE the army was encircled and destroyed — the Records of the Grand Historian puts the dead at four hundred thousand. The idiom is much later than the events: there was no paper (纸) in the Warring States to discuss (谈) war (兵) on (上), and the phrase belongs to a much later age looking back.
zhi-shang-tan-bing.title: 纸上谈兵 (zhi shang tan bing) — "All theory no practice" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-tong-dao-he.origin: The same (同) ambition (志) and paths that fit together (道合). 志 is what a person is aiming at and 道 is the way they mean to get there, so the phrase requires agreement on both — people who want the same thing by different means do not qualify. That is a stricter test than friendship, which is why it belongs to founding partners, political allies and collaborators rather than to companions. What it names is the basis on which people joined, and it explains why a group holds.
zhi-tong-dao-he.title: 志同道合 (zhi tong dao he) — "Share the same goals and values" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-xing-he-yi.literal: Knowledge and action unite as one
zhi-xing-he-yi.origin: Wang Yangming reached his enlightenment in exile at Longchang in Guizhou in 1508, and began teaching this doctrine the following year, when he was invited to head the academy at Guiyang: knowing (知) and acting (行) are one (合一) rather than two stages. His claim is stronger than an exhortation to put things into practice — he holds that knowledge which has not issued in action was never knowledge at all, only an opinion about it, so a man who knows what filial conduct is and does not perform it does not in fact know it. That collapses the excuse of weak will, which is exactly what it was built to do. Chinese now uses the phrase of applying principles in practice, in a considerably milder sense than Wang intended.
zhi-xing-he-yi.title: 知行合一 (zhi xing he yi) — "Practice what you know" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-zai-si-fang.example_en: With a clear vision, she set her sights on achieving greatness beyond her hometown.
zhi-zai-si-fang.example_zh: 她志在四方，立志要在更广阔的舞台上展现自己。

faq.a: 志在四方 (zhì zài sì fāng) literally means "Ambition in all directions" and metaphorically means "Broad aspirations". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 志在四方 mean?

faq.a: 志在四方 is pronounced as "zhì zài sì fāng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 志在四方?

faq.a: 志在四方 is used when With a clear vision, she set her sights on achieving greatness beyond her hometown..
faq.q: When is 志在四方 used?

zhi-zai-si-fang.origin: Chong'er, the exiled prince of Jin, had settled comfortably in Qi and shown no further interest in leaving. The Zuo Zhuan gives the reproach to his wife Jiang, who told him that a man's ambition (志) lies (在) in the four directions (四方) — and then had him carried out of the state while drunk, so that he could not refuse. He went on to become one of the great hegemons. The phrase keeps that edge. It is generally said to somebody who is settling for a small life within easy reach, and it means go, not merely aspire.
zhi-zai-si-fang.title: 志在四方 (zhi zai si fang) — "Broad aspirations" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-zhi-du-wai.example_en: He ignored the risks and pursued his dream regardless.
zhi-zhi-du-wai.example_zh: 他将风险置之度外，执着追求自己的梦想。

faq.a: 置之度外 (zhì zhī dù wài) literally means "Place it beyond consideration" and metaphorically means "To disregard; put aside consideration of". It belongs to the Success & Perseverance category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 置之度外 mean?

faq.a: 置之度外 is pronounced as "zhì zhī dù wài" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 置之度外?

faq.a: 置之度外 is used when He ignored the risks and pursued his dream regardless..
faq.q: When is 置之度外 used?

zhi-zhi-du-wai.meaning: To disregard; put aside consideration of
zhi-zhi-du-wai.meaning_metaphoric: To disregard; put aside consideration of
zhi-zhi-du-wai.origin: To place (置) something (之) outside (外) what is being reckoned (度). Emperor Guangwu, holding most of the empire with two hold-outs left, said he would put those two beyond his calculations for the time being; the phrase is his. What it describes is not forgetting a factor but deciding to stop counting it, which is a deliberate act and can be either shrewd or reckless. People who put their own safety outside the reckoning claim it above all, and there it is unambiguous praise.
zhi-zhi-du-wai.title: 置之度外 (zhi zhi du wai) — "To disregard; put aside consideration of" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-zu-bu-ru.example_en: He always finds joy in what he has, knowing that contentment brings peace.
zhi-zu-bu-ru.example_zh: 他总是对自己拥有的感到满足，知道知足不辱。

faq.a: 知足不辱 (zhī zú bù rǔ) literally means "Know contentment avoid disgrace" and metaphorically means "Be content avoid shame". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 知足不辱 mean?

faq.a: 知足不辱 is pronounced as "zhī zú bù rǔ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 知足不辱?

faq.a: 知足不辱 is used when He always finds joy in what he has, knowing that contentment brings peace..
faq.q: When is 知足不辱 used?

zhi-zu-bu-ru.origin: The Daodejing puts it in chapter 44, after asking whether fame or your own person is dearer: 知足不辱，知止不殆 — knowing when you have enough keeps you from disgrace, knowing when to stop keeps you from danger. The two clauses are always quoted together. The Huainanzi illustrates them with Gong Yixiu, the minister of Lu who loved fish and refused every gift of fish, reasoning that a minister who takes presents loses his post and a man without a post cannot afford fish at all. Refusing them was how he kept eating them.
zhi-zu-bu-ru.title: 知足不辱 (zhi zu bu ru) — "Be content avoid shame" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-zu-chang-le.example_en: Despite modest circumstances, the family found contentment in simple pleasures and each other's company
zhi-zu-chang-le.example_zh: 尽管条件简朴，这家人从简单的乐趣和彼此的陪伴中找到了满足

faq.a: 知足常乐 (zhī zú cháng lè) literally means "Know enough constant happiness" and metaphorically means "Contentment with what one has brings happiness". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 知足常乐 mean?

faq.a: 知足常乐 is pronounced as "zhī zú cháng lè" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 知足常乐?

faq.a: 知足常乐 is used when Despite modest circumstances, the family found contentment in simple pleasures and each other's company.
faq.q: When is 知足常乐 used?

zhi-zu-chang-le.meaning: Contentment with what one has brings happiness
zhi-zu-chang-le.meaning_metaphoric: Contentment with what one has brings happiness
zhi-zu-chang-le.origin: The Daodejing supplies the thought in several places: there is no calamity greater than not knowing when one has enough, and the contentment that knows enough (知足) is enough for good (常乐). The claim is stronger than an argument for modest living — it is that sufficiency is a judgement rather than a quantity, so no amount of acquisition reaches it and a decision does. Chinese uses the phrase sincerely and also, quite often, as the thing said to someone who has just been passed over for something.
zhi-zu-chang-le.title: 知足常乐 (zhi zu chang le) — "Contentment with what one has brings happiness" | Meaning & Origin

zhi-zui-jin-mi.example_en: The young heirs lived in luxury, oblivious to the real world's hardships
zhi-zui-jin-mi.example_zh: 这些年轻的继承人生活在奢华中，对现实世界的艰辛毫无察觉

faq.a: 纸醉金迷 (zhǐ zuì jīn mí) literally means "Paper drunk gold confused" and metaphorically means "Decadent luxury lifestyle". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 纸醉金迷 mean?

faq.a: 纸醉金迷 is pronounced as "zhǐ zuì jīn mí" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 纸醉金迷?

faq.a: 纸醉金迷 is used when The young heirs lived in luxury, oblivious to the real world's hardships.
faq.q: When is 纸醉金迷 used?

zhi-zui-jin-mi.origin: A Song collection tells of the physician Meng Fu, who fitted out a small room at home with gilded furnishings and paper so bright it dazzled; a guest who dozed there said afterwards that resting in it left a man gold-dazed and paper-drunk — 此室暂憩，令人金迷纸醉. The gold (金) and the papered walls (纸) are literal in the anecdote, and the pair of verbs — dazed (迷), drunk (醉) — became a byword for luxury that disorients. Nightlife districts and wealth arranged to be looked at, always with disapproval attached.
zhi-zui-jin-mi.title: 纸醉金迷 (zhi zui jin mi) — "Decadent luxury lifestyle" | Meaning & Origin

zhong-kou-shuo-jin.example_en: The social media campaign succeeded in changing the company's policy
zhong-kou-shuo-jin.example_zh: 社交媒体运动成功改变了公司的政策

faq.a: 众口铄金 (zhòng kǒu shuò jīn) literally means "Many mouths melt gold" and metaphorically means "Repeated by enough people, a falsehood passes for truth". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 众口铄金 mean?

faq.a: 众口铄金 is pronounced as "zhòng kǒu shuò jīn" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 众口铄金?

faq.a: 众口铄金 is used when The social media campaign succeeded in changing the company's policy.
faq.q: When is 众口铄金 used?

zhong-kou-shuo-jin.meaning: Repeated by enough people, a falsehood passes for truth
zhong-kou-shuo-jin.meaning_metaphoric: Repeated by enough people, a falsehood passes for truth
zhong-kou-shuo-jin.origin: This is from the Discourses of the States, paired there with another line: many hearts make a city wall, and many mouths (众口) melt (铄) metal (金). Gold does not melt from talk, which is the point — enough voices saying the same thing achieve what should be impossible. The original is a warning about slander rather than a celebration of consensus. Where enough people repeating something have settled it, this is the phrase, and the tone is always uneasy.
zhong-kou-shuo-jin.title: 众口铄金 (zhong kou shuo jin) — "Repeated by enough people, a falsehood passes for truth" | Meaning & Origin

zhong-shi-zhi-di.example_en: As the whistleblower, she became the target of everyone's criticism.
zhong-shi-zhi-di.example_zh: 作为举报人，她成了众矢之的。

faq.a: 众矢之的 (zhòng shǐ zhī dì) literally means "Target of many arrows" and metaphorically means "Target of public criticism". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 众矢之的 mean?

faq.a: 众矢之的 is pronounced as "zhòng shǐ zhī dì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 众矢之的?

faq.a: 众矢之的 is used when As the whistleblower, she became the target of everyone's criticism..
faq.q: When is 众矢之的 used?

zhong-shi-zhi-di.origin: The target (的) that many (众) arrows (矢) are aimed at. 的 is the bullseye — the same character that now does duty as the commonest particle in the language, which regularly surprises learners — and the phrase puts somebody on it. What it describes is not being criticised but being the agreed object of criticism, which is a different and lonelier position: the arrows come from people who are not otherwise coordinated. Public figures, and whoever has become the convenient explanation for a shared problem.
zhong-shi-zhi-di.title: 众矢之的 (zhong shi zhi di) — "Target of public criticism" | Meaning & Origin

zhong-shuo-fen-yun.example_en: In the debate, there were so many conflicting opinions that it was hard to reach a consensus.
zhong-shuo-fen-yun.example_zh: 在辩论中，众多相互矛盾的意见让人难以达成共识。

faq.a: 众说纷纭 (zhòng shuō fēn yún) literally means "Many voices, chaotic opinions" and metaphorically means "Diverse opinions". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 众说纷纭 mean?

faq.a: 众说纷纭 is pronounced as "zhòng shuō fēn yún" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 众说纷纭?

faq.a: 众说纷纭 is used when In the debate, there were so many conflicting opinions that it was hard to reach a consensus..
faq.q: When is 众说纷纭 used?

zhong-shuo-fen-yun.origin: Many (众) accounts (说), tangled and numerous (纷纭). 纷纭 is a reduplicative describing things scattered and interwoven, the same word used of falling blossom and drifting snow. So the phrase is not about disagreement between two sides but about a field of opinion with no shape to it. It is used when the facts are not yet settled — an unexplained event, an unattributed decision — and it implies that none of the accounts has yet earned precedence.
zhong-shuo-fen-yun.title: 众说纷纭 (zhong shuo fen yun) — "Diverse opinions" | Meaning & Origin

zhong-suo-zhou-zhi.example_en: It is widely accepted that regular exercise contributes to better health outcomes
zhong-suo-zhou-zhi.example_zh: 众所周知，经常锻炼有助于改善健康状况

faq.a: 众所周知 (zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī) literally means "Everyone completely knows" and metaphorically means "As everyone knows or is widely recognized". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 众所周知 mean?

faq.a: 众所周知 is pronounced as "zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 众所周知?

faq.a: 众所周知 is used when It is widely accepted that regular exercise contributes to better health outcomes.
faq.q: When is 众所周知 used?

zhong-suo-zhou-zhi.meaning: As everyone knows or is widely recognized
zhong-suo-zhou-zhi.meaning_metaphoric: As everyone knows or is widely recognized
zhong-suo-zhou-zhi.origin: What the many (众) all (周) know (所知). The phrase is doing rhetorical work rather than reporting a fact, which is worth noticing before using it: placing a claim inside 众所周知 asserts that it is settled and puts anyone who disagrees outside the group rather than inside the argument. Chinese official and commercial writing uses it constantly for exactly that reason, and a careful reader treats it as a signal to check what follows.
zhong-suo-zhou-zhi.title: 众所周知 (zhong suo zhou zhi) — "As everyone knows or is widely recognized" | Meaning & Origin

zhong-wang-suo-gui.example_en: The new leader was chosen based on the collective hopes of the community.
zhong-wang-suo-gui.example_zh: 新领导的产生是众望所归。

faq.a: 众望所归 (zhòng wàng suǒ guī) literally means "Where the hopes of the many converge" and metaphorically means "Trusted leadership". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 众望所归 mean?

faq.a: 众望所归 is pronounced as "zhòng wàng suǒ guī" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 众望所归?

faq.a: 众望所归 is used when The new leader was chosen based on the collective hopes of the community..
faq.q: When is 众望所归 used?

zhong-wang-suo-gui.literal: Where the hopes of the many converge
zhong-wang-suo-gui.origin: What the many (众) hope for (望) is where it comes to rest (所归). The Book of Jin uses it, and the metaphor in 归 is of water finding its way to the sea — the expectations of a great many people converging on one person without anyone organising it. That is what distinguishes the phrase from mere popularity. It describes the appointment that surprises nobody — the candidate everyone had already assumed would be chosen.
zhong-wang-suo-gui.title: 众望所归 (zhong wang suo gui) — "Trusted leadership" | Meaning & Origin

zhong-zhi-cheng-cheng.example_en: The community's united effort successfully prevented the development project
zhong-zhi-cheng-cheng.example_zh: 社区齐心协力成功阻止了开发项目

faq.a: 众志成城 (zhòng zhì chéng chéng) literally means "Many wills make wall" and metaphorically means "Unity creates strength". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 众志成城 mean?

faq.a: 众志成城 is pronounced as "zhòng zhì chéng chéng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 众志成城?

faq.a: 众志成城 is used when The community's united effort successfully prevented the development project.
faq.q: When is 众志成城 used?

zhong-zhi-cheng-cheng.origin: This architectural metaphor shows how many wills (众志) can form (成) an impenetrable wall (城), drawing from ancient Chinese defensive architecture. It gained significance during the Warring States period when city walls required massive coordinated effort to construct and defend. Historical records detail how communities united to build city walls in record time when facing invasion. The idiom emphasizes how collective determination creates strong defenses. Modern usage extends to team efforts and community initiatives, highlighting how unity and shared purpose can overcome seemingly impossible challenges.
zhong-zhi-cheng-cheng.title: 众志成城 (zhong zhi cheng cheng) — "Unity creates strength" | Meaning & Origin

zhou-er-fu-shi.example_en: The seasons change, reminding us that life is a continuous cycle of beginnings and endings.
zhou-er-fu-shi.example_zh: 四季更替，让我们意识到生活是一个不断循环的过程。

faq.a: 周而复始 (zhōu ér fù shǐ) literally means "Cycle and start again" and metaphorically means "Endless cycle". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 周而复始 mean?

faq.a: 周而复始 is pronounced as "zhōu ér fù shǐ" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 周而复始?

faq.a: 周而复始 is used when The seasons change, reminding us that life is a continuous cycle of beginnings and endings..
faq.q: When is 周而复始 used?

zhou-er-fu-shi.origin: To go round (周) and then (而) begin again (复始). Chinese thought organises time cyclically by default — the sixty-year calendar, the五行 sequence, the seasons — and this phrase is the plain statement of the pattern. It carries no verdict. Used of nature it is calm, and used of human affairs it is generally weary, describing the meeting that produces the decision that produces the same meeting, and the historical pattern that keeps arriving as though for the first time.
zhou-er-fu-shi.title: 周而复始 (zhou er fu shi) — "Endless cycle" | Meaning & Origin

zhui-ben-su-yuan.example_en: The researcher tracked the problem to its root cause
zhui-ben-su-yuan.example_zh: 研究人员追踪到问题的根源

faq.a: 追本溯源 (zhuī běn sù yuán) literally means "Chase root trace source" and metaphorically means "Trace back to source". It belongs to the Wisdom & Learning category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 追本溯源 mean?

faq.a: 追本溯源 is pronounced as "zhuī běn sù yuán" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 追本溯源?

faq.a: 追本溯源 is used when The researcher tracked the problem to its root cause.
faq.q: When is 追本溯源 used?

zhui-ben-su-yuan.origin: To chase (追) the root (本) and trace (溯) the source (源). Both halves are the same instruction in different terrain, one botanical and one riverine, and 溯 specifically means moving against the current — the work is upstream and harder than going with it. That is the sense the phrase carries: not merely asking why but travelling back through the intervening causes one at a time. It belongs to investigation, etymology and root-cause analysis.
zhui-ben-su-yuan.title: 追本溯源 (zhui ben su yuan) — "Trace back to source" | Meaning & Origin

zhuo-jin-jian-zhou.example_en: The budget constraints left the department financially stretched.
zhuo-jin-jian-zhou.example_zh: 预算限制让部门捉襟见肘。

faq.a: 捉襟见肘 (zhuō jīn jiàn zhǒu) literally means "Pulling the lapel reveals the elbow" and metaphorically means "Hard-pressed; financially stretched". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 捉襟见肘 mean?

faq.a: 捉襟见肘 is pronounced as "zhuō jīn jiàn zhǒu" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 捉襟见肘?

faq.a: 捉襟见肘 is used when The budget constraints left the department financially stretched..
faq.q: When is 捉襟见肘 used?

zhuo-jin-jian-zhou.literal: Pulling the lapel reveals the elbow
zhuo-jin-jian-zhou.origin: The Zhuangzi describes Zengzi in poverty: he had not made a coat in ten years, and when he straightened his cap the chin-strap snapped, when he pulled (捉) his lapel (襟) across, his elbow (肘) came through (见). The clothing is failing at three points at once, and the comedy is exact — every attempt to make himself presentable exposes something else. That is what the phrase carries over. Budgets and staffing, where covering one gap opens another; the sense is of a shortage that can no longer be fixed by rearrangement.
zhuo-jin-jian-zhou.title: 捉襟见肘 (zhuo jin jian zhou) — "Hard-pressed; financially stretched" | Meaning & Origin

zi-bao-zi-qi.example_en: After losing his job, he fell into despair and gave up on life.
zi-bao-zi-qi.example_zh: 失去工作后，他自暴自弃，放弃了生活。

faq.a: 自暴自弃 (zì bào zì qì) literally means "Self-ruin self-abandon" and metaphorically means "Give up on oneself entirely". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 自暴自弃 mean?

faq.a: 自暴自弃 is pronounced as "zì bào zì qì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 自暴自弃?

faq.a: 自暴自弃 is used when After losing his job, he fell into despair and gave up on life..
faq.q: When is 自暴自弃 used?

zi-bao-zi-qi.origin: Mencius distinguishes two failures and the phrase joins them. The man who does violence to himself (自暴) cannot be talked with, because he has decided that right and propriety are not worth discussing; the man who throws himself away (自弃) cannot be worked with, because he has decided he is incapable of them. One is contempt for the standard, the other is despair of meeting it. Chinese uses the compound for the settled version of giving up, and it is a serious thing to say about someone.
zi-bao-zi-qi.title: 自暴自弃 (zi bao zi qi) — "Give up on oneself entirely" | Meaning & Origin

zi-bu-liang-li.example_en: He thought he could easily complete the project, but he underestimated the challenges ahead.
zi-bu-liang-li.example_zh: 他以为自己能轻松完成这个项目，却自不量力。

faq.a: 自不量力 (zì bù liàng lì) literally means "Not measuring one's own strength" and metaphorically means "Overestimate abilities". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 自不量力 mean?

faq.a: 自不量力 is pronounced as "zì bù liàng lì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 自不量力?

faq.a: 自不量力 is used when He thought he could easily complete the project, but he underestimated the challenges ahead..
faq.q: When is 自不量力 used?

zi-bu-liang-li.origin: The Zuo Zhuan lists five faults in the small state of Xi, which attacked its stronger neighbour Zheng: it did not weigh its virtue, did not measure (量) its own (自) strength (力), was not kind to its kin, did not examine the wording of the quarrel, and did not establish who was at fault. Xi's army was routed, and the chronicler adds that this was how one knew the state would eventually fall. Failing to measure one's own force is therefore a specific administrative error rather than mere arrogance. Modern Chinese uses the phrase bluntly, often as a contemptuous dismissal — 自不量力 said of a challenger means they have not done the arithmetic.
zi-bu-liang-li.title: 自不量力 (zi bu liang li) — "Overestimate abilities" | Meaning & Origin

zi-can-xing-hui.example_en: She felt self-conscious and ashamed when she compared herself to her more accomplished peers.
zi-can-xing-hui.example_zh: 她看到更优秀的同龄人时，自惭形秽。

faq.a: 自惭形秽 (zì cán xíng huì) literally means "Ashamed of one's appearance" and metaphorically means "Feeling inferior". It belongs to the Life Philosophy category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 自惭形秽 mean?

faq.a: 自惭形秽 is pronounced as "zì cán xíng huì" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 自惭形秽?

faq.a: 自惭形秽 is used when She felt self-conscious and ashamed when she compared herself to her more accomplished peers..
faq.q: When is 自惭形秽 used?

zi-can-xing-hui.origin: Wang Ji was a handsome man and knew it. The New Account of Tales of the World says that whenever he saw his nephew Wei Jie he would sigh 珠玉在侧，觉我形秽 — with pearl and jade beside me, I am aware of how coarse I look. The idiom supplies the word he left out: shame (惭) at one's own (自) form (形) being coarse (秽) next to another's. Wei Jie's looks were famous enough that crowds gathered to see him, and he died young — the wits said of being stared to death. The phrase describes being diminished by proximity rather than by any criticism, which is what makes it so recognisable.
zi-can-xing-hui.title: 自惭形秽 (zi can xing hui) — "Feeling inferior" | Meaning & Origin

zi-gao-fen-yong.example_en: She volunteered to lead the difficult project.
zi-gao-fen-yong.example_zh: 她自告奋勇，主动承担这个困难的项目。

faq.a: 自告奋勇 (zì gào fèn yǒng) literally means "Self-recommend with vigor and courage" and metaphorically means "Volunteer bravely; step forward willingly". It belongs to the Relationships & Character category of Chinese idioms.
faq.q: What does 自告奋勇 mean?

faq.a: 自告奋勇 is pronounced as "zì gào fèn yǒng" in Mandarin Chinese.
faq.q: How do you pronounce 自告奋勇?

faq.a: 自告奋勇 is used when She volunteered to lead the difficult project..
faq.q: When is 自告奋勇 used?

zi-gao-fen-yong.origin: To put oneself forward (自告) with vigour (奋) and courage (勇). The construction is the point: 自告 means doing the nominating yourself, which inside a hierarchy is the difficult part, and the rest of the phrase supplies what is needed to follow through once you have. It is used where nobody has been asked and something unwelcome needs doing. Chinese treats it as straightforward praise — the volunteer, the person who put a hand up for the job with no obvious reward attached to it.

Chinese speakers still use it straightforwardly for personal independence, but the national resonance is never quite absent from it.

zi-qi-dong-lai.literal: Purple vapour comes from the east
zi-qi-dong-lai.meaning: Good fortune is on its way
zi-qi-dong-lai.meaning_metaphoric: Good fortune is on its way
zi-qi-dong-lai.origin: 紫 is 'purple', 气 is 'vapour' or 'energy', and 东来 is 'coming from the east'. It refers to the legend of Laozi leaving China through the Hangu Pass. The Records of the Grand Historian (《史记》) says only that the pass keeper Yin Xi (尹喜) asked Laozi to write a book before he left, and the received Biographies of Immortals (《列仙传》) says Yin Xi 'saw his qi first'. The purple colour comes in the Tang commentary 《史记索隐》, which quotes a version of the Biographies: Yin Xi 'saw purple qi floating over the pass, and Laozi indeed came riding a black ox' (望见有紫气浮关，而老子果乘青牛而过也). Purple qi became a sign that something auspicious, or someone remarkable, is arriving. It is a classic door inscription and Spring Festival couplet phrase, and works as a written New Year wish for a home or business.
zi-qi-dong-lai.title: 紫气东来 (zi qi dong lai) — "Good fortune is on its way" | Meaning & Origin
